Example: A student takes a Spanish placement test before orientation and skips the first-semester course.

See also: Orientation, Course Registration, AP Credit Transfer

docs.title: Practice Interview
docs.text:
A rehearsal interview with a counselor, teacher, or family member to build comfort and polish answers before the real one.

Example: A parent asks "Tell me about yourself" and "Why this college?" so the student can practice answering out loud.

See also: Interview Preparation, Interviews

docs.title: Priority Deadline
docs.text:
A date before the final deadline by which applying gives a student the best consideration for admission, scholarships, honors programs, or housing.

Example: A university with a priority deadline in December may consider only applicants who meet it for its top merit scholarships.

See also: Application Deadline, Aid Priority Deadline, Automatic Merit Scholarship

docs.title: Private College
docs.text:
A college funded mainly through tuition, donations, and endowment rather than state government, charging the same tuition to all students regardless of residence.

Private colleges often have high sticker prices but may offer generous institutional aid.

See also: Public University, Sticker Price, Institutional Aid

docs.title: Private Loan
docs.text:
A loan from a bank, credit union, or other private lender, typically with fewer protections and less flexible repayment than federal loans.

Example: A family turns to a bank's private student loan only after using all federal loan options.

See also: Federal Direct Loan, Parent PLUS Loan, Total Debt at Graduation

docs.title: Profile Section
docs.text:
The part of the Common App where students enter personal information such as name, address, contact details, citizenship, and demographic background.

See also: Common App, Family Section, Education Section

docs.title: PSAT/NMSQT
docs.text:
A preliminary version of the SAT, usually taken in tenth or eleventh grade, that also serves as the qualifying test for the National Merit Scholarship Program.

Example: A junior's PSAT/NMSQT score helps predict SAT performance and may qualify the student for National Merit recognition.

See also: SAT, Diagnostic Practice Test

docs.title: Public University
docs.text:
A college or university funded and governed in part by a state government, usually charging lower tuition to residents of that state.

Example: A Texas resident attending the University of Texas pays in-state tuition, which is lower than what out-of-state students pay.

See also: In-State Residency, Flagship University, Private College

docs.title: Questions to Ask Interviewer
docs.text:
Thoughtful questions an applicant prepares to ask at the end of a college interview, showing curiosity and helping the student learn what the college is really like.

Example: "What surprised you most about your first year here?" invites a genuine conversation.

See also: Interview Preparation, Informational Interview

docs.title: Reach School
docs.text:
A college where a student's admission is unlikely or uncertain because the student's credentials fall below the typical admitted range or the college admits very few applicants.

Any college with a very low admission rate is a reach for nearly everyone.

Example: A student with a 3.6 GPA applying to a college that admits 8% of applicants treats it as a reach.

See also: Target School, Safety School, Balanced College List

docs.title: Reading an Award Letter
docs.text:
Carefully examining a financial aid award letter to separate grants from loans, identify the true out-of-pocket cost, and spot expenses the letter leaves out.

Example: A student notices that a "$30,000 aid package" includes $12,000 in loans, so the free money is only $18,000.

See also: Award Letter, Free Money vs. Borrowed Money, Out-of-Pocket Cost

docs.title: Recommendation Request Timing
docs.text:
When a student asks for a recommendation, ideally several weeks or more before the first deadline so the recommender has enough time.

Example: Many students ask junior-year teachers in late spring or early fall before senior deadlines.

See also: Asking for a Recommendation, Recommender Deadlines

docs.title: Recommender Deadlines
docs.text:
The dates by which each recommender must submit letters for each college, which the student should communicate clearly and well ahead of time.

Example: A student tells teachers that her earliest letter is due November 1 and sends a reminder two weeks before.

See also: Recommender Packet, Supporting Document Deadline, Assigning Recommenders

docs.title: Recommender Packet
docs.text:
A collection of materials a student gives recommenders, such as a brag sheet, resume, college list, and deadlines, to make letter writing easier.

Example: A student gives each teacher a folder with her resume, a list of colleges with deadlines, and a short note on what she hopes they highlight.

See also: Brag Sheet, Recommender Deadlines, Asking for a Recommendation

docs.title: Recycled Essay Trap
docs.text:
The mistake of reusing an essay for another college without adapting it, which can leave the wrong school's name or generic details in the response.

Example: Submitting a Why Us essay that mentions a different college's mascot is a classic recycled essay trap.

See also: Essay Adaptation, Why Us Essay, Scholarship Essay Reuse

docs.title: Reflection and Insight
docs.text:
The part of an essay where the writer explains what an experience meant, how it changed their thinking, or what it reveals about them.

Reflection is often what separates a strong essay from a simple story.

Example: After describing a failed science fair project, a student explains how it taught her to welcome criticism.

See also: Personal Story, Essay Structure, Small Moment Essay

docs.title: Regular Decision
docs.text:
The standard application round, with a later deadline than early rounds and decisions typically released in spring, carrying no commitment to enroll.

See also: Early Action, Early Decision, Decision Release Date

docs.title: Rejection as Fit
docs.text:
The perspective that a college denial often reflects the college's limited space and institutional priorities rather than a judgment of the applicant's worth.

Example: A student denied by a college that admitted few applicants from her region recognizes the decision was about the college's class, not her worth.

See also: Denial, Institutional Priorities, Long-Term Perspective

docs.title: Renewable Scholarship
docs.text:
A scholarship that can be awarded again in later years of college as long as the student continues to meet the award's stated requirements.

Example: A $5,000 scholarship renewable for four years is worth up to $20,000 if the student keeps qualifying.

See also: Scholarship Renewal Criteria, Aid Renewal, Four-Year Cost Projection

docs.title: Rescinded Admission
docs.text:
The withdrawal of an admission offer by a college after acceptance, typically due to a significant grade drop, disciplinary issue, or dishonesty on the application.

Example: A college rescinds an offer after a student's final transcript shows several failing grades in spring semester.

See also: Senioritis, Final Transcript, Double Depositing

docs.title: Research University
docs.text:
A university, typically larger, that emphasizes faculty research and graduate programs alongside undergraduate education, often offering many majors and research opportunities.

Undergraduates may find large introductory lectures but also labs and specialized programs.

See also: Liberal Arts College, Flagship University, School Size

docs.title: Restrictive Early Action
docs.text:
A non-binding early round that limits applicants from applying early to certain other colleges, while still allowing them to decline the offer if admitted.

Each college defines its restrictions differently, so read the exact policy before applying.

See also: Early Action, Early Decision, Application Rounds

docs.title: Retention Rate
docs.text:
The percentage of first-year students who return to the same college for their second year, often used as a sign of student satisfaction and support.

Example: A 95% retention rate means nearly all freshmen chose to come back sophomore year.

See also: Graduation Rate, College Scorecard

docs.title: Retesting Decision
docs.text:
The choice of whether to take the SAT or ACT again, weighing likely score gains against the time, cost, and stress of another attempt.

Example: A student whose practice tests consistently beat the official score may decide one more attempt is worthwhile.

See also: Superscoring, Test Date Planning, Diagnostic Practice Test

docs.title: Revision
docs.text:
Rewriting an essay to improve its content, structure, and clarity, often through several rounds of substantial changes rather than small word fixes.

Example: A student cuts the first paragraph and moves the reflection earlier in the second draft.

See also: Drafting, Feedback on Essays, Editing and Proofreading

docs.title: Rolling Admission
docs.text:
An admissions approach in which a college reviews applications as they arrive and releases decisions on an ongoing basis until the class is full.

Applying early in a rolling cycle can improve your chances because spaces may fill.

Example: A student submits to a rolling-admission university in September and receives a decision four weeks later.

See also: Application Rounds, Application Deadline

docs.title: Room and Board
docs.text:
The combined charge a college sets for on-campus housing and a meal plan, usually listed as a major part of the cost of attendance for students who live on campus.

Example: A student living in a dorm with a full meal plan pays room and board to the college each term.

See also: Cost of Attendance, Housing Application, Tuition

docs.title: Roommate Selection
docs.text:
The process by which an incoming student chooses a roommate or is matched with one for on-campus housing, often through a questionnaire about habits and preferences.

Example: A student matches with a roommate through the college's housing questionnaire about sleep schedules and tidiness.

See also: Housing Application, Move-In Day

docs.title: Safety School
docs.text:
A college where a student is very likely to be admitted and can afford to attend, and that the student would be genuinely happy to enroll in.

A school is only a true safety if it is affordable and you would actually go there.

Example: A student with a 3.7 GPA applies to an affordable in-state university that admits most applicants with a 3.2.

See also: Reach School, Target School, Financial Fit

docs.title: SAT
docs.text:
A standardized college admissions exam from the College Board that measures reading, writing, and math skills, delivered digitally and scored on a 400-1600 scale.

Example: A student who scores 650 in Reading and Writing and 700 in Math has a total SAT score of 1350.

See also: ACT, PSAT/NMSQT, SAT-ACT Concordance

docs.title: SAT-ACT Concordance
docs.text:
An official table that converts scores between the SAT and ACT so colleges and students can compare results on the two tests.

Example: A concordance table shows roughly which SAT total corresponds to an ACT composite of 30.

See also: SAT, ACT, Score Benchmark Comparison

docs.title: Scam Warning Signs
docs.text:
Red flags that suggest a scholarship or aid offer is fraudulent, such as upfront fees, guaranteed winnings, or requests for bank details.

Example: "You've won! Pay a $50 processing fee to claim your award" is a common warning sign.

See also: Scholarship Scams

docs.title: Scholarship Eligibility
docs.text:
The specific requirements a student must meet to apply for or receive a scholarship, such as major, location, GPA, or background.

Example: A scholarship open only to residents of one county who plan to study nursing has narrow eligibility.

See also: Scholarship Search Engine, Competitive Scholarship, Scholarship Renewal Criteria

docs.title: Scholarship Essay Reuse
docs.text:
Adapting essays already written for college applications to answer similar scholarship prompts, saving time while tailoring each version to the specific award.

Example: A student turns her Common App essay about leadership at work into a 500-word scholarship essay on leadership.

See also: Essay Adaptation, Recycled Essay Trap, Scholarship Prioritization

docs.title: Scholarship Prioritization
docs.text:
Deciding which scholarships to apply for first by weighing how well the student fits, the award amount, the likely competition, and the effort required.

Example: A student applies first to local awards she clearly qualifies for before tackling a large national contest.

See also: Expected Value of Applying, Local Scholarship, Scholarship Essay Reuse

docs.title: Scholarship Renewal Criteria
docs.text:
The conditions a student must keep meeting, such as a minimum GPA or full-time enrollment, to continue receiving a renewable scholarship.

Example: A scholarship requiring a 3.0 college GPA may be lost if the student's GPA drops to 2.8.

See also: Renewable Scholarship, Aid Renewal

docs.title: Scholarship Scams
docs.text:
Fraudulent offers that pretend to provide scholarships, grants, or financial aid help but are designed to take a student's money or personal information.

Example: A website promising guaranteed scholarships for a $99 fee is likely a scam.

See also: Scam Warning Signs, Scholarship Search Engine

docs.title: Scholarship Search Engine
docs.text:
A website that matches students with possible scholarships by comparing a profile of their interests, background, location, and achievements against a database of awards.

Example: A student creates a profile on a scholarship search site and receives matches for awards for future teachers in her state.

See also: Outside Scholarship, Scholarship Scams, Scholarship Eligibility

docs.title: Scholarships
docs.text:
Money awarded to students for college that does not have to be repaid, based on merit, need, talents, or other criteria.

See also: Merit Aid, Outside Scholarship, Grants

docs.title: School Counselor
docs.text:
The high school staff member who guides students through course planning and college applications and who sends transcripts and a counselor recommendation.

Counselors often have large caseloads, so meeting early helps them know you.

See also: Counselor Meeting, Counselor Recommendation, Independent Counselor

docs.title: School Size
docs.text:
The number of students enrolled at a college, which shapes class sizes, the variety of programs, and the feel of campus life.

Example: A college with 2,000 students feels very different from one with 40,000 students.

See also: Campus Setting, Liberal Arts College, Research University

docs.title: School-Specific Research
docs.text:
Investigating a particular college's programs, courses, traditions, and opportunities so that supplemental essays and interviews include specific, accurate details about that school.

Example: A student names a specific undergraduate research program and professor in a Why Us essay after reading the department website.

See also: Why Us Essay, Why This Major Essay, Demonstrated Interest

docs.title: Score Benchmark Comparison
docs.text:
The practice of comparing one's test score against a college's reported middle 50% range to judge whether the score helps the application.

Example: A student with a 30 ACT compares it to one college's 27-31 range and another's 33-35 range to decide where to send it.

See also: Middle 50% Range, Score Submission Decision, Common Data Set

docs.title: Score Choice
docs.text:
A testing option that lets students select which test dates' scores to send to colleges, subject to each college's own reporting rules.

Example: A student who tested three times uses Score Choice to send only her strongest test date to a college that allows it.

See also: Superscoring, Sending Test Scores, Official Score Report

docs.title: Score Submission Decision
docs.text:
The choice an applicant makes, at a test-optional college, about whether sending an SAT or ACT score is likely to strengthen the application.

Example: A student whose SAT falls above a college's middle 50% range sends it, but withholds it from a college where it falls below.

See also: Test-Optional Policy, Score Benchmark Comparison, Middle 50% Range

docs.title: Section Scores
docs.text:
The individual scores a student earns on each part of a standardized test, such as SAT Math or ACT English.

See also: Composite Score, Superscoring

docs.title: Selective Admissions
docs.text:
An admissions approach in which a college admits only a portion of qualified applicants, choosing among them based on academic and personal factors rather than accepting everyone who meets minimum requirements.

At highly selective colleges, strong grades alone do not guarantee admission.

See also: Admission Rate, Holistic Review, Reach School

docs.title: Self-Assessment
docs.text:
The process of reflecting on one's own strengths, interests, values, and preferences to identify what a student needs from a college.

Example: Listing the classes you enjoyed most and the settings where you felt most motivated is a quick self-assessment.

See also: Personal Priorities, College Fit, Brainstorming

docs.title: Self-Care Routine
docs.text:
A set of regular habits, such as enough sleep, physical activity, healthy meals, and downtime, that support a student's physical and emotional health during busy periods.

See also: Healthy Coping Strategies, Balancing Rigor and Burnout

docs.title: Self-Reported Academic Record
docs.text:
A record of courses and grades that an applicant enters directly into an application, which colleges verify later against the official transcript.

Entries must match your transcript exactly, so work from a copy of it.

Example: A student enters her grades on a college's self-report form, and the college later checks them against her final transcript.

See also: Courses and Grades Section, Transcript Copies, Final Transcript

docs.title: Self-Reported Scores
docs.text:
Test scores an applicant types into an application, which some colleges accept for review and verify with an official report only after admission.

Example: A college may let a student enter an SAT score on the Common App and send the official report only if enrolling.

See also: Official Score Report, Testing Section, Self-Reported Academic Record

docs.title: Sending Official Transcripts
docs.text:
The process by which a high school sends a student's verified transcript directly to colleges, usually through the counselor or an electronic service.

See also: High School Transcript, Supporting Document Deadline, School Counselor

docs.title: Sending Test Scores
docs.text:
Arranging for official test scores to be delivered to colleges from the testing organization, or reporting them on the application where allowed.

See also: Official Score Report, Institution Codes, Score Choice

docs.title: Senior Grades
docs.text:
The grades a student earns during senior year, which colleges see on mid-year and final reports and can affect admission even after acceptance.

See also: Mid-Year Report, Final Transcript, Senioritis

docs.title: Senior Year Calendar
docs.text:
A schedule that maps key application, testing, financial aid, and decision tasks across a student's twelfth-grade year, from late summer through spring.

See also: Month-by-Month Planner, Admissions Timeline, Calendar Reminders

docs.title: Senior Year Course Load
docs.text:
The set of classes a student takes in twelfth grade, which colleges review to see whether the student continued to challenge themselves.

Example: A student keeps AP Literature, Calculus, Physics, and Spanish 4 in senior year instead of dropping to an easier schedule.

See also: Course Rigor, Senior Grades, Course Selection Strategy

docs.title: Senioritis
docs.text:
A decline in effort and motivation during senior year, often after applications are submitted, which can lower grades and put admission offers at risk.

Example: A student who skips assignments after being admitted in December may see grades drop enough to trigger a warning letter from the college.

See also: Senior Grades, Rescinded Admission, Final Transcript

docs.title: Shared Tracker
docs.text:
A deadline tracker that a student shares with a parent, guardian, or counselor so everyone can see progress and upcoming tasks.

See also: Deadline Tracker, Parent and Family Role, Getting Organized

docs.title: Short-Answer Questions
docs.text:
Brief application prompts, often limited to a few sentences, words, or characters, that ask about interests, preferences, or quick facts about the applicant.

Example: "What is your favorite word, and why?" is a typical short-answer question.

See also: Supplemental Essays, Essay Word Limit

docs.title: Show Don't Tell
docs.text:
A writing technique that reveals a person's qualities through concrete details, actions, and scenes instead of simply stating those qualities outright.

Example: Instead of "I am determined," a student describes rewriting a failed code program at 2 a.m. until it finally ran.

See also: Personal Story, Authentic Voice, Opening Hook

docs.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
docs.text:
A chart or spreadsheet that lines up colleges using the same categories, such as cost, programs, and location, to make differences clear.

Example: A student builds a table with one column per college and rows for net price, distance, major, and campus feel.

See also: Comparing Offers, Award Letter Comparison, Personal Priorities

docs.title: Small Moment Essay
docs.text:
An essay built around a brief, ordinary experience that reveals something meaningful about the writer, rather than a large dramatic event.

Example: An essay about the nightly ritual of making tea with a grandmother can reveal more than a list of accomplishments.

See also: Personal Story, Reflection and Insight, Overused Essay Topics

docs.title: Social Fit
docs.text:
How well a college's student body, campus life, traditions, and community match the kind of environment in which a student feels comfortable and engaged.

Example: A student who loves outdoor activities might feel most at home at a college with an active hiking club and nearby trails.

See also: College Fit, Campus Culture, Campus Setting

docs.title: Social Media Boundaries
docs.text:
Personal limits on when and how a student uses social media during the application season, aimed at reducing comparison, distraction, and decision-day stress.

Example: Muting decision-day posts or taking a week off apps after results come out.

See also: Limiting Comparison, Healthy Coping Strategies

docs.title: Standardized Testing
docs.text:
Exams given under uniform conditions and scored on a common scale, such as the SAT and ACT, used by some colleges to compare applicants.

See also: SAT, ACT, Test-Optional Policy

docs.title: State Aid
docs.text:
Financial aid funded by a state government, such as grants or scholarships, typically for residents of that state who attend eligible colleges within it.

Example: A student who files the FAFSA and stays in her home state qualifies for a state grant toward tuition.

See also: In-State Residency, FAFSA, Federal Aid

docs.title: Sticker Price
docs.text:
The published full cost of attending a college for one year, before any grants, scholarships, or other financial aid are subtracted.

Most students pay less than the sticker price once aid is applied.

Example: A private college has a sticker price of $80,000 per year, but many students pay far less after grants.

See also: Cost of Attendance, Net Price

docs.title: Student Aid Index
docs.text:
An eligibility number calculated from FAFSA information that colleges use to determine how much need-based federal aid a student qualifies for.

The SAI is not the amount your family will pay; it is an index used in aid formulas.

Example: A family with a very low income may receive an SAI of zero or below, qualifying the student for the maximum Pell Grant.

See also: FAFSA, Demonstrated Financial Need, Pell Grant

docs.title: Student Reviews
docs.text:
First-hand opinions about a college posted by current or former students, offering insight into daily life that official materials may not show.

Treat individual reviews as one perspective, not a verdict.

See also: Campus Culture, College Search Website

docs.title: Submission Confirmation
docs.text:
The on-screen message, email, or portal status that proves a college received an application, serving as a record in case questions arise later.

Save these confirmations in case questions arise.

See also: Application Submission, Applicant Portal, Digital Document Folder

docs.title: Subsidized Loan
docs.text:
A need-based federal student loan for which the government pays the interest while the student is in school at least half-time.

Example: A student borrows a subsidized loan, and no interest builds while she is enrolled full-time.

See also: Unsubsidized Loan, Federal Direct Loan

docs.title: Summer Before Senior Year
docs.text:
The months between junior and senior year, often used to finalize the college list, visit campuses, draft essays, and prepare for fall testing.

Example: A student uses July to draft the Common App essay and August to finalize her list and visit two campuses.

See also: Senior Year Calendar, Brainstorming, Campus Visit

docs.title: Summer Experiences
docs.text:
Activities a student pursues during summer breaks, such as paid jobs, academic programs, volunteering, family duties, or independent projects, which can show initiative and growth.

Costly summer programs are not required; a job or personal project can be just as valuable.

See also: Extracurricular Activities, Part-Time Job, Personal Interests

docs.title: Summer Melt
docs.text:
The situation in which students who plan to attend college in the fall never enroll, often because of missed tasks, costs, or lack of support over the summer.

Example: A student who committed in May never completes housing or registration forms and does not show up in the fall.

See also: Summer Transition Planning, Getting Ready for Fall

docs.title: Summer Transition Planning
docs.text:
Organizing the tasks, deadlines, and preparations a student must complete between high school graduation and the first day of college.

Example: A student makes a checklist with housing, health forms, orientation, and the first tuition bill, each with a date.

See also: Summer Melt, Getting Ready for Fall, Move-In Day

docs.title: Superscoring
docs.text:
A college practice of combining a student's highest section scores from different test dates into a new, highest possible total score.

Example: If a student scored highest in math in March and in reading in June, a superscoring college uses both best sections.

See also: Section Scores, Score Choice, Retesting Decision

docs.title: Supplement Planning
docs.text:
Mapping every supplemental essay prompt across a college list to spot overlaps, plan where material can be reused, and schedule writing time before deadlines.

Example: A student finds that four colleges ask a community question and drafts one core essay to adapt for each.

See also: Supplemental Essays, Essay Adaptation, Deadline Tracker

docs.title: Supplemental Essays
docs.text:
Additional essays required or offered by specific colleges beyond the main personal essay, often asking about fit, interests, or community.

See also: Why Us Essay, Short-Answer Questions, Supplement Planning

docs.title: Support Network
docs.text:
The people a student can rely on for encouragement, advice, and practical help, such as family members, friends, teachers, coaches, and counselors.

Example: A student relies on her aunt for essay feedback, her counselor for deadlines, and friends for encouragement.

See also: Healthy Coping Strategies, School Counselor, Parent and Family Role

docs.title: Supporting Document Deadline
docs.text:
The date by which materials sent separately from the application, such as transcripts, recommendations, and test scores, must reach a college.

Example: A college may let the counselor's transcript arrive a week or two after the student's application deadline.

See also: Application Deadline, Sending Official Transcripts, Recommender Deadlines

docs.title: Sustained Commitment
docs.text:
Continued involvement in the same activity over several years, showing dedication, growth, and reliability rather than short-term or one-time participation.

See also: Depth Over Breadth, Hours per Week, Leadership Roles

docs.title: Target School
docs.text:
A college where a student's academic credentials fall within the typical range of admitted students, giving a reasonable chance of admission.

Example: A student whose GPA and scores sit near the middle of a college's middle 50% range would treat it as a target.

See also: Reach School, Safety School, Middle 50% Range

docs.title: Teacher Recommendation
docs.text:
A letter from a teacher, usually in a core academic subject from junior or senior year, describing the student's work and engagement in class.

See also: Letters of Recommendation, Choosing Recommenders, Counselor Recommendation

docs.title: Test Accommodations
docs.text:
Approved changes to standard testing conditions, such as extra time, breaks, or a separate room, for students with documented disabilities or other qualifying needs.

Requests usually go through the testing organization and school well before the test date.

Example: A student with a documented learning disability is approved for extended time on the SAT through the school's coordinator.

See also: Test Registration, School Counselor

docs.title: Test Date Planning
docs.text:
Choosing SAT or ACT test dates so that scores arrive before application deadlines and leave room for a retake if the student wants one.

Example: A student applying early in November takes the ACT in September so scores arrive before the deadline.

See also: Test Registration, Retesting Decision, Admissions Timeline

docs.title: Test Registration
docs.text:
The process of signing up for a specific SAT or ACT date and test center, typically done online in advance of the exam.

See also: Test Date Planning, Fee Waiver, Test Accommodations

docs.title: Test-Blind Policy
docs.text:
A college admissions policy under which SAT and ACT scores are not considered in admission decisions at all, even when an applicant submits them.

See also: Test-Optional Policy, Test-Required Policy

docs.title: Test-Optional Myth
docs.text:
The mistaken belief that test-optional means test scores never matter, when strong scores may still help and some colleges, programs, or scholarships still use them.

Example: A college may admit students without scores but still use scores to award certain merit scholarships.

See also: Admissions Myths, Test-Optional Policy, Score Submission Decision

docs.title: Test-Optional Policy
docs.text:
A college admissions policy that lets applicants choose whether to submit SAT or ACT scores, with no penalty for applying without them.

Example: A student with strong grades but a low ACT score applies to a test-optional college without submitting the score.

See also: Test-Required Policy, Test-Blind Policy, Score Submission Decision

docs.title: Test-Required Policy
docs.text:
A college admissions policy that requires every applicant to submit an SAT or ACT score as part of a complete application.

Several selective colleges have returned to requiring tests, so always verify current rules.

See also: Test-Optional Policy, Test-Blind Policy, Verifying Current Policies

docs.title: Testing Section
docs.text:
The part of the Common App where students choose whether to report standardized test scores and enter them if they do.

See also: Self-Reported Scores, Score Submission Decision

docs.title: Thank-You Notes
docs.text:
Brief written messages of appreciation sent to recommenders, interviewers, and others who helped with an application, often followed by an update on the outcome.

Example: A handwritten card to a teacher after letters are submitted, plus an update when decisions arrive.

See also: Asking for a Recommendation, Interview Follow-Up

docs.title: Timed Practice
docs.text:
Working through test sections under the same time limits as the real exam to build pacing, stamina, and comfort with the pressure of test day.

See also: Official Practice Tests, Error Log

docs.title: Total Debt at Graduation
docs.text:
The full amount of student loans, and sometimes parent loans, that will be owed after a student completes a degree, including any interest that has accrued.

Example: A student who borrows $5,500 each year for four years graduates owing about $22,000 plus any interest.

See also: Four-Year Cost Projection, College Scorecard, Federal Direct Loan

docs.title: Transcript Copies
docs.text:
Unofficial copies of a student's high school transcript kept on hand for entering self-reported grades, completing scholarship forms, and preparing recommender packets.

See also: High School Transcript, Self-Reported Academic Record, Digital Document Folder

docs.title: Tuition
docs.text:
The amount a college charges for instruction each term or year, listed separately from fees, housing, meals, and other parts of the cost of attendance.

Example: A state university charges in-state students lower tuition than out-of-state students for the same classes.

See also: Cost of Attendance, Room and Board, In-State Residency

docs.title: Undeclared Major
docs.text:
The status of a student who has not yet chosen a field of study, typically allowed for the first year or two of college.

Being undeclared is common and rarely hurts an application.

See also: Intended Major, Academic Fit

docs.title: Unmet Need
docs.text:
The portion of a student's demonstrated financial need that remains after all aid in the financial aid package is applied, which the family must cover another way.

Example: A student with $30,000 in demonstrated need who receives $22,000 in aid has $8,000 in unmet need.

See also: Meets Full Need, Out-of-Pocket Cost, Financial Aid Appeal

docs.title: Unsubsidized Loan
docs.text:
A federal student loan available regardless of need, on which interest builds from the time the money is paid out.

Example: A student who borrows an unsubsidized loan freshman year owes more than she borrowed by graduation because interest has built up.

See also: Subsidized Loan, Federal Direct Loan, Total Debt at Graduation

docs.title: Unweighted GPA
docs.text:
A grade point average in which every course counts on the same scale, typically 0 to 4.0, regardless of the course's difficulty level.

Many colleges recalculate GPAs their own way, so they may look at your unweighted grades alongside course rigor.

See also: Weighted GPA, Grade Point Average, Course Rigor

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
A process in which a college asks a student to confirm the information reported on the FAFSA by submitting documents such as tax records.

Example: A student selected for verification uploads a parent's tax transcript to the financial aid office.

See also: FAFSA, Applicant Portal

docs.title: Verifying Current Policies
docs.text:
The practice of checking each college's official website for its latest requirements, deadlines, and testing rules, because policies change from year to year.

Example: Before applying, a student confirms on a college's admissions page that it is still test-optional this year.

See also: College-Specific Requirements, Test-Optional Policy

docs.title: Virtual Interview
docs.text:
A college interview held over a video platform instead of in person, following the same format and expectations as a face-to-face conversation with an alum or admissions officer.

Example: A student tests the camera and lighting, picks a quiet room, and joins five minutes early.

See also: Interviews, Interview Preparation

docs.title: Virtual Tour
docs.text:
An online walkthrough of a college campus, using video, photos, or interactive maps, that lets students explore buildings and grounds without traveling.

See also: Campus Visit, College Research Tools, Demonstrated Interest

docs.title: Waiting Period
docs.text:
The stretch of time between submitting applications and receiving admission decisions, during which the applicant has little control over outcomes and often feels anxious.

Example: Between a November submission and a March decision, a student might focus on senior grades and scholarships.

See also: Managing Uncertainty, Decision Release Date, Healthy Coping Strategies

docs.title: Waitlist
docs.text:
A decision that places a qualified applicant on a list of students who may be admitted later if spaces open in the class.

Example: A student is offered a waitlist spot in March and is admitted in May when a space opens.

See also: Waitlist Strategy, Letter of Continued Interest, Admission Decision

docs.title: Waitlist Strategy
docs.text:
A plan for responding to a waitlist offer, including accepting a spot, sending updates, and committing elsewhere in the meantime.

Example: A waitlisted student deposits at another college by the deadline while sending a continued-interest letter to the waitlist school.

See also: Waitlist, Letter of Continued Interest, Enrollment Deposit

docs.title: Weighted GPA
docs.text:
A grade point average that awards extra points for grades earned in more demanding courses, such as honors, AP, or IB classes, so the scale can exceed the standard maximum.

Example: At a school that weights AP courses, an A in AP Biology might count as 5.0 instead of 4.0.

See also: Unweighted GPA, Honors Courses, Advanced Placement

docs.title: Well-Rounded Applicant Myth
docs.text:
The mistaken belief that colleges want applicants who do a little of everything, when many value focused depth in a few areas that builds a well-rounded class overall.

Example: A student deeply committed to theater and stage design can be more compelling than one who joined ten unrelated clubs.

See also: Admissions Myths, Depth Over Breadth, Sustained Commitment

docs.title: Why This Major Essay
docs.text:
A supplemental essay asking why an applicant wants to study a chosen field, connecting past experiences to future academic plans.

Example: A student connects her experience volunteering at a vet clinic to her plan to study animal science.

See also: Intended Major, School-Specific Research, Supplemental Essays

docs.title: Why Us Essay
docs.text:
A supplemental essay asking why an applicant wants to attend a particular college, answered best with specific details linking the school to the student's goals.

Example: A student mentions a specific marine biology field station and a student-run research journal at the college.

See also: School-Specific Research, Supplemental Essays, Recycled Essay Trap

docs.title: Work-Study
docs.text:
A financial aid program that provides part-time jobs to students with financial need, letting them earn money for college expenses.

Example: A work-study student earns a paycheck working at the campus library 10 hours a week.

See also: Federal Aid, Need-Based Aid, Award Letter

docs.title: Writing Section
docs.text:
The part of the Common App that holds the personal essay along with other writing, such as optional statements about challenges or disciplinary history.

See also: Personal Essay, Additional Information Section, Common App Essay Prompts

docs.title: Writing Supplements
docs.text:
The college-specific essays and short-answer questions that appear in an applicant's Common App account after a particular college is added to the list.

See also: Supplemental Essays, Member Questions, Supplement Planning

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: This textbook is organized into 20 chapters covering 342 concepts.

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text:
1. The College Landscape and Application Rounds - An introduction to the admissions process and timeline, the kinds of four-year colleges, residency and selectivity, and how Early Decision, Early Action, Regular Decision, and rolling admission work.
  2. How Colleges Evaluate Applicants - How admissions offices read applications, from holistic and formula-based review to transcripts, GPA, rigor, class rank, and institutional priorities, plus the myths that distort how students see the process.
  3. Finding Your Fit - A self-assessment of priorities, major, size, setting, culture, and cost that turns into academic, social, and financial fit and a list balanced across reach, target, and safety schools.
  4. Researching and Narrowing Your College List - Using the College Scorecard, Common Data Set, outcome data, visits, fairs, and reviews to research schools, then narrowing a long list to a final eight to twelve.
  5. Getting Organized - Setting up the systems that carry you through senior year: deadline trackers, filing systems, a dedicated email, portals and the Common App account, counselors, family roles, and five first steps.
  6. The SAT and ACT Question - Deciding whether and where to submit SAT or ACT scores under test-optional, test-required, and test-blind policies, with superscoring, retesting, registration, and free, effective prep.
  7. Your Senior Year Course Load - Why senior grades, the mid-year report, and the final transcript still count, and how to choose AP, IB, or dual enrollment while balancing rigor against burnout.
  8. Activities and Resume - Presenting extracurriculars, jobs, and family responsibilities as strengths, showing depth and impact, and turning them into a strong activities list and resume.
  9. The Personal Essay - Writing the Common App personal essay from brainstorming and topic choice through structure, authentic voice, reflection, drafting, feedback, and revision.
  10. Supplemental Essays - Researching each school to write specific Why Us, major, community, and activity essays and short answers, and adapting material without falling into the recycled-essay trap.
  11. Letters of Recommendation - Choosing and asking teacher and counselor recommenders, preparing a brag sheet and recommender packet, the FERPA waiver, and following up with thanks.
  12. Filling Out the Common App and Coalition App - A section-by-section walkthrough of the Common App and Coalition App, from profile to supplements, plus fees and waivers, submission, and sending transcripts and scores.
  13. Interviews - The kinds of college interviews, how to prepare and practice, what questions to ask, and how to follow up.
  14. Understanding Financial Aid - How college pricing and aid work, from net price and the FAFSA and CSS Profile to demonstrated need, types of aid, need-blind admissions, grants, verification, and priority deadlines.
  15. Scholarships - Finding automatic, competitive, outside, and local scholarships, deciding which are worth applying for, reusing essays, keeping renewable awards, and avoiding scams and award displacement.
  16. Comparing Award Letters - Reading and comparing award letters line by line, separating grants from loans and work-study, projecting four-year cost and debt, and requesting a reconsideration.
  17. Waiting and Managing Anxiety - What happens to an application after submission and healthy ways to get through the wait, from portal checking to limiting comparison, self-care, and support.
  18. Handling Decisions - Responding to acceptances, denials, deferrals, and waitlists, handling Early Decision release and rescinded admission, appealing aid, and seeing rejection as a question of fit.
  19. Making Your Final Choice - Comparing offers side by side, using admitted-student days and revisits, committing by May 1 with an enrollment deposit, and declining other offers the right way.
  20. Getting Ready for Fall - Every step from deposit to move-in, including housing, orientation, health forms, AP credit, placement, registration, and summer melt, closing with the senior-year planner and capstone roadmap.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text:
The chapters follow the order of senior year: understanding how admissions works, building your list, testing, writing and submitting applications, paying for college, and making your decision. Each chapter only builds on concepts introduced in earlier chapters, so reading in order gives the smoothest path. Because every chapter lists its prerequisites, you can also jump straight to the topic that is most urgent for you right now and look back only where needed.

Note: Each chapter includes a list of concepts covered. Make sure to complete prerequisites before moving to advanced chapters.

docs.title: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces the admissions process and timeline, the kinds of four-year colleges, residency and selectivity, and how Early Decision, Early Action, Regular Decision, and rolling admission work. This chapter builds the vocabulary the rest of the book relies on. After it, students can place any college on the map of public, private, and specialized institutions and explain which application rounds are binding and which are not.

docs.title: Why Start With the Map
docs.text:
Before you build a list or write a word of an essay, it helps to know the ground you're crossing. Applying to college has its own vocabulary — Early Action, flagship, admit rate, binding — and admissions offices use those words as if everyone already knows them. Students with a parent or private counselor who has done this before pick the vocabulary up at the dinner table. Everyone else has to learn it from scratch, usually in a panic in October.

This chapter is that vocabulary, in the order you'll need it. You'll start with the process as a whole and the calendar it runs on. Then you'll look at the kinds of four-year colleges you can apply to and what "selective" really means. You'll meet the people who read your application. Finally, you'll learn the different application rounds, which ones lock you in, and which ones keep your options open. Every later chapter builds on these terms.

docs.title: The College Admissions Process
docs.text:
The college admissions process is the full sequence of steps a student goes through to get from "I want to go to college" to "I'm enrolled at a college this fall." It is not one application. It's a project with six stages, and each stage hands its results to the next one:

  1. Build your list. Decide which colleges to apply to, based on fit, cost, and your chances of admission.
  2. Test. Decide whether to take the SAT or ACT, and whether to send your scores to each school.
  3. Apply. Complete each application: forms, essays, activities, and recommendations.
  4. Seek aid. File the financial aid forms and apply for scholarships so each school can tell you what you'd actually pay.
  5. Decide. Compare the offers you receive and choose one school.
  6. Enroll. Pay a deposit, decline the other offers, and complete the steps that get you to campus in the fall.

The stages overlap. You'll usually be filing financial aid forms while you're still finishing applications, and testing often happens while you're still settling your list. But the order matters, because each stage depends on the one before it. You can't write a "Why this college?" essay for a school that isn't on your list yet. You can't compare financial aid offers for schools you never applied to.

The process is long. For most students, it runs from the summer before senior year to the fall after graduation, about fifteen months. That length is the reason so many students feel behind: there's rarely a single moment when someone tells you to start. The good news is that a long process is forgiving. Most of it is small tasks done steadily, not one heroic weekend.

The diagram below shows the six stages as a single roadmap. Click any stage to see what it involves, roughly when it happens, and which chapter of this book covers it.

docs.title: Diagram: College Admissions Process Roadmap
docs.text:

When: spring of junior year through October of senior year. Chapter 6. 3. "Apply" — Complete forms, essays, activities, and recommendations. When: August through January. Chapters 8–13. 4. "Seek Aid" — File the FAFSA (and CSS Profile where required) and apply for scholarships. When: October through February. Chapters 14–16. 5. Correct drops turn green; incorrect drops bounce back. A "Show answers" button restores the labels.

docs.title: Worked Example: Where Is Priya Right Now?
docs.text:
It's late September. Priya, a senior, has a list of ten colleges, took the SAT once in June, and has a rough draft of her personal essay. She hasn't opened a financial aid form yet.

  • Build your list: mostly done. She has a list, but she still needs to check that it includes schools she's very likely to get into.
  • Test: in progress. She needs to decide whether to retake the SAT in October or stop here.
  • Apply: started. The essay is drafted, but nothing has been submitted.
  • Seek aid: not started, and that's fine for September. The main federal form opens in the fall.
  • Decide and Enroll: not yet.

Placing yourself on the roadmap like this turns "I'm so behind" into a short list of the next moves. Priya's next moves are to settle her testing plan and finish one application completely before starting the others.

docs.title: The Admissions Timeline
docs.text:
The admissions timeline is the calendar the process runs on: the months when each stage usually happens and the fixed dates the whole system shares. Individual colleges set their own deadlines, but most of them cluster around the same few anchor points, so the senior year of nearly every applicant has the same rhythm.

Here are the anchor points worth knowing now. Later chapters explain each one in depth.

  • August 1: The Common App, the shared application most colleges accept, opens for the new year. You'll set it up in Chapter 5.
  • Fall (traditionally October 1): The FAFSA, the federal financial aid form, opens. Its exact opening date has shifted in recent years, so confirm the current one. Chapter 14 covers it.
  • November 1 and November 15: The most common early application deadlines.
  • Mid-December: Most early decisions arrive.
  • January 1 to February 1: The most common regular deadlines.
  • Mid-March to early April: Most regular decisions arrive.
  • May 1: The national deadline for choosing one college and paying a deposit. Chapter 19 covers it.
  • June through August: Housing forms, orientation, and final transcripts.

Notice how lopsided the calendar is. Almost all of the work (lists, testing, essays, applications, aid forms) is packed into August through January. February is quiet. Then March and April bring a rush of decisions that require careful comparison, and May 1 forces a choice. Planning around that shape is most of what it means to "start early."

The interactive timeline below lays these anchor points across the senior year. You can switch between three sample students with different plans and see how the same calendar fills up differently for each.

docs.title: Worked Example: Planning Backward From a Deadline
docs.text:
Suppose your earliest application is due November 1, and one of your recommending teachers asks for at least four weeks' notice. Work backward:

  • November 1: Application due. Aim to submit by October 25 to leave room for technical problems.
  • October 25: Final proofread of the essays and the whole application.
  • Around October 1: The teacher needs the request by now, four weeks before the deadline. Ask in September to be safe.
  • Mid-September: A full essay draft should exist so there's time for two rounds of revision.

The deadline on the college's website is November 1, but your real deadline for asking a teacher is September. Planning backward like this is how the timeline turns into a to-do list. Chapter 5 shows how to put it in a tracker.

docs.title: Application Deadlines
docs.text:
An application deadline is the date and time by which a college must receive your application for it to be considered in a given round. That definition has two details worth slowing down on.

First, receive, not start. If the Common App's servers are slow at 11:30 p.m. on deadline night, which happens nearly every year, that is your problem, not the college's. Submitting a few days early is the only reliable protection.

Second, a "deadline" is usually several deadlines. Most colleges separate the application form itself from the materials that support it, and some set additional dates for financial aid or scholarships. A single college can easily have three or four dates that matter to you:

  • Application deadline: the form and essays must be submitted.
  • Supporting document deadline: transcripts, recommendations, and test scores, often a week or two later.
  • Financial aid priority deadline: the date to file aid forms for the best chance at the full range of aid.
  • Scholarship deadline: sometimes earlier than the application deadline itself.

Deadlines also come with a time and a time zone. Many are 11:59 p.m. in your local time, but some colleges use their own time zone or a different hour entirely. Read the fine print on each school's admissions page, and record the exact time, not just the date.

docs.title: Worked Example: One College, Four Dates
docs.text:
The University of Iowa, which this book uses as its running example, shows how one college's "deadline" splits apart. Iowa's own published dates change slightly from year to year, so treat these as an illustration and check the current ones.

What's due Early Action round Regular round Application submitted November 2 February 1 Supporting documents (transcript, scores) November 9 February 8 Financial aid priority (FAFSA filed) December 1 December 1 Merit scholarship consideration Complete application by early February Complete application by early February

Two things stand out. First, the financial aid priority date of December 1 falls before the regular application deadline. A student applying in the regular round who waits until January to think about aid has already missed the best aid window. Second, applications completed after February 1 lose merit scholarship consideration. A missed deadline here costs real money, not just a spot.

The deadline you see is rarely the only one

For every college on your list, record the application deadline, the supporting document deadline, the financial aid deadline, and any scholarship deadline, along with the exact time and time zone. Chapter 5 shows how to keep them in one tracker.

docs.title: Four-Year Colleges
docs.text:
A four-year college is a school that awards the bachelor's degree, the undergraduate degree designed to take about four years of full-time study. This book is about applying to four-year colleges, as opposed to community colleges, which mainly award two-year associate degrees and generally admit anyone with a high school diploma.

"College" and "university" are used loosely in everyday speech, and the names on campus signs aren't always consistent. Dartmouth College is a research university with graduate schools; some places called "university" are small and focus on undergraduates. So don't judge a school by its name. Ask what kind of institution it actually is.

There are more than two thousand four-year colleges in the United States. They are sorted along two main lines that you'll use to describe any school on your list:

  • How it's funded and governed: public or private.
  • What it focuses on: research and graduate study, or teaching undergraduates.

The next sections define each of these categories one at a time. After that, a summary table and an interactive sorter let you put them together.

docs.title: Public Universities
docs.text:
A public university is a college funded in part by a state government and governed by a state board. Because state taxpayers help pay for it, a public university usually charges much lower tuition to students who live in that state. Examples include the University of Iowa, Iowa State University, the University of Michigan, and the University of California campuses.

Public universities tend to be large. Many enroll more than 20,000 undergraduates, which brings a wide range of majors, courses, and activities. Size also shapes how they admit students. With tens of thousands of applications and a duty to serve their state, many public universities lean more heavily on grades and test scores than smaller private colleges do. Some use a formula in which an application that clears a set academic threshold is admitted. You'll see how that works in Chapter 2.

Public universities also have a responsibility to the state's own students, so they treat applicants differently based on where they live. That's where residency comes in, covered later in this chapter.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading a Public University's Profile
docs.text:
Here is how you'd read the key facts about the University of Iowa:

  • Public: funded partly by the state of Iowa, so Iowa residents pay a lower tuition rate.
  • Large: over 20,000 undergraduates, with many majors to choose from.
  • Admission style: largely formula-driven. Iowa computes a Regent Admission Index from grades and courses, and the minimum required score for its main college is lower for residents (245) than for nonresidents (255).
  • Rounds offered: Early Action and Regular, both non-binding, with no Early Decision.

That short profile already tells an applicant a lot. Iowa residents get a cost advantage and an admissions advantage. The application is less essay-driven than at a small private college. And applying early carries no commitment.

docs.title: Private Colleges
docs.text:
A private college is a college that is not run by a state government. It is funded mainly by tuition, donations, and its endowment, the pool of invested money a college has built up over time. Most private colleges are nonprofits. Harvard, Stanford, Grinnell College, and Drake University are all private.

Private colleges usually charge the same tuition to every student no matter where they live, and their listed price is often much higher than a public university's. But many have large financial aid budgets of their own, so the price a student actually pays can be far lower than the listed price. Sometimes it's lower than a public university's. Chapter 14 explains how to find the real price.

docs.title: Research Universities
docs.text: A research university is a university where professors are expected to produce research as well as teach, and where there are graduate programs (master's and doctoral degrees) alongside the undergraduate college. Research universities can be public, like the University of Iowa, or private, like Stanford. For an undergraduate, that means access to labs, research projects, and a huge course catalog. It can also mean large introductory lectures and some classes taught by graduate students.

docs.title: Liberal Arts Colleges
docs.text: A liberal arts college is a college, usually small and private, that focuses on undergraduate education across the arts, humanities, social sciences, and sciences rather than on graduate programs or job-specific training. Classes are typically small and taught by professors, and students are expected to explore broadly before going deep in a major. Grinnell College in Iowa, Williams College in Massachusetts, and Pomona College in California are well-known examples. Most liberal arts colleges enroll somewhere between a few hundred and a few thousand students.

docs.title: Flagship Universities
docs.text: A flagship university is the best-known and usually oldest public research university in a state, often the one whose name is the state's own. The University of Iowa, the University of Michigan, and the University of Texas at Austin are flagships. A flagship usually gets the most state attention and offers the widest range of programs, and in many states it is the hardest public university to get into. Every flagship is a public research university, but not every public research university is a flagship. Iowa State is a major public research university, but the University of Iowa is the state's flagship.

docs.title: Putting the Categories Together
docs.text:
Now that each category is defined, here is how they combine. The two lines of sorting, funding and focus, are independent of each other, so a single school always sits in one box of each.

Kind of college Funded by Typical size Focus Example Public research university State plus tuition Large Research, graduate and undergraduate Iowa State University Flagship university State plus tuition Large The state's leading public research university University of Iowa Private research university Tuition, donations, endowment Medium to large Research, graduate and undergraduate Stanford University Liberal arts college Tuition, donations, endowment Small Teaching undergraduates Grinnell College

Practice sorting real colleges with the interactive sorter below. It works best if you add a few of the schools you're already considering.

docs.title: In-State Residency and Out-of-State Applicants
docs.text:
Because public universities are funded by state taxpayers, they distinguish between applicants who live in the state and those who don't.

In-state residency is the legal status of a student whose home is officially in a public university's state, which qualifies that student for the lower in-state tuition rate. Each state sets its own rules. For most high school seniors, residency follows where your parents or guardians live and pay taxes. Most states require at least a year of living there before you enroll. Moving to a state just to attend college usually doesn't make you a resident right away.

An out-of-state applicant is a student applying to a public university in a state where they are not a legal resident. Out-of-state students pay a higher tuition rate, often two to three times the in-state rate. At some public universities they also face a tougher admissions bar, because the school reserves most of its seats for residents. The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, for example, limits out-of-state students to about 18 percent of each first-year class by state policy.

The tuition gap is the reason residency matters so much. According to the College Board's Trends in College Pricing, average published tuition and fees for 2024–25 were roughly:

Student type Average published tuition and fees (2024–25) In-state student at a public four-year college about $11,600 Out-of-state student at a public four-year college about $30,800 Any student at a private nonprofit four-year college about $43,400

These are sticker prices, before any financial aid. A few regional programs, such as the Western Undergraduate Exchange in the western states, let students attend participating public colleges in nearby states at a reduced rate. Check whether your state belongs to one.

docs.title: Admission Rate
docs.text:
An admission rate, also called an acceptance rate or admit rate, is the percentage of applicants a college admits in a given year. It's the single number people use most often to describe how hard a college is to get into.

You calculate it by dividing the number of students admitted by the number who applied, then multiplying by 100 to get a percentage:

Admission rate = (students admitted ÷ students who applied) × 100%

Colleges report this number every year, and you can find it on their websites and on federal and third-party college search tools, covered in Chapter 4.

docs.title: Worked Example: Calculating and Comparing Admission Rates
docs.text:
Two colleges report last year's numbers:

  • College A received 40,000 applications and admitted 6,000 students.

  • College B received 9,000 applications and admitted 6,300 students.

  • College A: 6,000 ÷ 40,000 × 100% = 15%

  • College B: 6,300 ÷ 9,000 × 100% = 70%

College A admits about 3 of every 20 applicants. College B admits about 7 of every 10. College B admitted more students, yet College A is far harder to get into, because so many more people applied.

The admission rate is useful, but it hides as much as it shows. Keep three cautions in mind:

  • It describes the whole applicant pool, not you. A 15 percent rate doesn't mean you have a 15 percent chance. Your odds depend on how your academic record compares with the students the college actually admits, which Chapter 2 covers.
  • Who applies changes the number. A college that encourages lots of applications, even from students unlikely to be admitted, will see its rate fall without becoming any more demanding.
  • Rates differ by round and by program. Early rounds often have higher admit rates, partly because of who tends to apply early. Engineering or nursing programs inside a university can be much harder to get into than the university's overall rate suggests.

Try the calculator below to see how the rate responds when applications or admits change.

docs.title: Selective Admissions
docs.text:
Selective admissions describes a college that admits only some of its qualified applicants, choosing among them rather than accepting everyone who meets a minimum standard. Selectivity is a spectrum, not a yes-or-no label, and the admission rate is the most common way to place a school on it.

There's no official definition of each level, but these rough bands, which this book uses, match how counselors and college guides talk about schools:

Band Approximate admission rate What it means for applicants Most selective Under 10% Nearly every applicant is academically strong; essays, activities, and recommendations decide most cases. A reach for everyone. Highly selective 10–30% Strong grades in hard courses are expected; the rest of the application matters a great deal. Selective 30–60% Solid academic records are usually admitted; the rest of the application can tip borderline cases. Less selective 60–90% Most students who meet the academic requirements are admitted. Open or nearly open Over 90% Almost everyone who applies with a high school diploma is admitted.

The most important fact about this table is how few colleges sit at the top. Most four-year colleges admit more than half of the students who apply. The handful of famous schools that admit fewer than one in ten get most of the news coverage. That gives a distorted picture of college admissions as a whole.

docs.title: Worked Example: Same Student, Different Odds
docs.text:
Marcus has a strong record: mostly A's in a demanding course load. He's considering three schools:

  • School X admits 6% of applicants. Most of the students it turns down have records like his, so even with a strong application his chances are low. This is a reach for him, as it would be for any applicant.
  • School Y admits 45%. Marcus's grades are above those of most students it admits, so his chances are good, though not guaranteed.
  • School Z admits 80%. His record is well above its typical admit, so he is very likely to be admitted.

Marcus's application is the same in all three cases. What changes is how selective the school is and where his record falls among its admitted students. Chapter 3 turns this reasoning into reach, target, and safety categories for your own list.

Selectivity isn't quality

A low admission rate tells you a school is hard to get into. It doesn't tell you the school is a good fit for you, that it teaches your intended major well, or that you can afford it. Many excellent colleges admit most of their applicants.

docs.title: Inside the Admissions Office
docs.text:
The admissions office is the department of a college that recruits students, reads applications, makes admission decisions, and manages the process of turning admitted students into enrolled ones. When you email a question, attend an information session, or submit an application, you're dealing with the admissions office. At most colleges it works closely with, but separately from, the financial aid office, which decides what you'll pay.

An admissions office has two jobs that pull in opposite directions. It wants as many good applications as possible, so it markets the college to students: visits to high schools, college fairs, emails, campus tours. Then it has to turn most of those applicants away, or at least choose among them, to build a class that fits the college's goals. Understanding both jobs explains a lot of what you'll experience. The glossy brochures are the first job. The careful reading of your file is the second.

Admissions offices also run on the calendar you saw earlier. Fall is travel season, when staff visit high schools and fairs. Winter is reading season, when the office reads applications almost full time. Spring is decision and recruitment season, when admitted students are invited to campus. Summer is planning for the next cycle.

The people in a typical admissions office fill a few distinct roles:

Role What they do When you'll meet them Dean or director of admissions Sets admissions policy and class goals; signs off on final decisions Rarely; perhaps at a large information session Admissions officer (counselor) Recruits in a region, reads applications, presents files in committee At school visits, college fairs, emails, interviews Application reader Reads and rates files during reading season; may be seasonal staff Never directly Operations staff Processes documents, matches transcripts and letters to files, sends missing-items notices Through portal messages and emails about missing items

docs.title: Worked Example: Who Do You Email?
docs.text:
You notice your application portal says your transcript is missing, and your school counselor says they sent it two weeks ago. Who do you contact?

  • Not the dean. This is a processing problem, not a policy question.
  • Start with the portal message or the general admissions email. Operations staff match incoming documents to files, and a transcript is often received but not yet matched.
  • Include the details they need: your full name, birth date, high school, and the date the counselor sent it.
  • If it's still unresolved in a week, email your regional admissions officer. That's the person assigned to your area, usually listed on the college's website under "Find your counselor."

Knowing who does what saves days, and in deadline season a few days matter.

docs.title: Admissions Officers
docs.text:
An admissions officer, often called an admissions counselor, is a staff member of an admissions office who recruits students and evaluates applications. At most colleges each officer is assigned a territory: a group of states, regions, or high schools. They visit those schools in the fall, get to know the counselors there, and are usually the first to read applications from that territory in the winter.

That territory system matters to you for three reasons:

  • The officer reading your file usually knows your high school. They've seen its course list, know how hard its grading is, and may have read applications from your classmates in earlier years. They read your record against what your school offers, not against an ideal applicant.
  • They're a real person you can contact. If you have a question that's specific to you, your regional officer is the right person to ask.
  • They often argue for applicants. At colleges that use a committee, the first reader summarizes the file and may advocate for the student when the committee meets.

Admissions officers read a lot. During reading season, an officer at a selective college may read dozens of files a day and spend somewhere around ten to fifteen minutes on each. That doesn't mean your application is skimmed carelessly. It means it has to be clear. A reader should be able to tell who you are and what you care about without hunting for it.

The interactive diagram below follows one application from the moment it's submitted to the moment a decision is released. Click each step to see who handles it and what they're looking at.
