docs.title: Worked Example: Naming a Culture You Want
docs.text:
On visits and virtual sessions, Priya noticed that the colleges she liked shared some patterns. Students talked about working in study groups, not about class rank. Campus events filled the weekends. People seemed interested in ideas without being competitive about them. She also realized she didn't care much about big-time athletics, though she liked the idea of a school with traditions.

She turned those observations into a short list of culture priorities: collaborative academics, an active campus social life, a reading-and-talking culture, and traditions without a sports-centered calendar. That list became a filter. When a college's students described it as "cutthroat," or when every student she met talked about game days first, she knew to look more closely before keeping it.

docs.title: Social Fit
docs.text:
Social fit is how well you'd feel at home in a college's community: whether you'd find friends, activities, and a sense of belonging there. It's the personal result of campus culture meeting your own personality and needs. Campus culture describes the college. Social fit describes you at the college.

Social fit is the dimension students most often judge too quickly, from a single visit on a rainy day or one conversation with a tour guide. It's also closely tied to whether students stay in college. Students who feel isolated or out of place are more likely to transfer or leave. So it deserves careful attention, and a few concrete questions help:

  • Would I find people who share my interests, background, or values? Is there a club, team, or community I'd want to join on day one?
  • Do students seem happy and engaged when they talk about their lives, not just the college's features?
  • How do students who are like me describe their experience? Talk to students in your intended major, your activities, or your community, not just the official tour guides.
  • Where do students live after the first year, and does most social life happen on or off campus?

Social fit isn't about finding a college where everyone is like you. Many students thrive by meeting people very different from themselves. It's about being able to see yourself belonging there.

docs.title: Worked Example: Testing Social Fit
docs.text:
Marcus wants to make sure the university four hours away will feel like home. He takes three steps. First, he looks up its student organization directory and finds an active game-development club and a robotics team. Second, he joins a virtual session for prospective computer science students and asks a current student what a typical weekday looks like. Third, he notices that most first-years live on campus and many sophomores do too, which suggests a social life centered on campus.

That's good evidence of social fit. He adds one more check, since he works in his family's restaurant: does the university have a commuter or working-student community, for students who go home on weekends? It does. The university stays near the top of his list.

docs.title: Cost of Attendance
docs.text:
The cost of attendance (COA) is a college's estimate of the total cost of one year there, including everything a student needs to pay for, not just classes. Every college that offers federal financial aid is required to publish one. It's the starting point for understanding what a college will actually cost your family.

The cost of attendance has several parts. Each gets a short section below, but here's how they fit together:

  • Tuition and fees: the price of classes and required campus charges.
  • Room and board: housing and meals.
  • Books and supplies: textbooks, a laptop, lab materials.
  • Transportation: travel to and from campus and getting around.
  • Personal expenses: phone, toiletries, clothing, laundry, and similar costs.

The cost of attendance changes with your situation. A public university publishes different tuition for in-state and out-of-state students. Living at home lowers housing costs, but it adds transportation costs. Colleges usually publish separate cost of attendance figures for these situations, so make sure you're reading the one that matches yours.

Two cautions matter most. First, the cost of attendance is a price before financial aid. Most students don't pay it in full, because grants and scholarships lower what they owe, as you'll see under sticker price. Second, it's an estimate. The college sets the figures for books, transportation, and personal costs, and they may not match your habits. Check whether they seem realistic for you.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading a Cost of Attendance
docs.text:
A fictional public university, Midland State, publishes this cost of attendance for one year. The numbers are illustrative, but the structure matches what real colleges publish.

Item In-state, on campus Out-of-state, on campus Tuition and fees $11,500 $32,000 Room and board $12,500 $12,500 Books and supplies $1,000 $1,000 Transportation $1,200 $2,400 Personal expenses $2,500 $2,500 Total cost of attendance $28,700 $50,400

Notice three things. Room and board, books, and personal expenses are the same for both groups. The difference comes from tuition, which is nearly three times higher for out-of-state students, and from transportation, which costs more for students coming from far away. And tuition is only about 40% of the in-state total. A student who looks only at tuition would underestimate the real cost by more than half. The interactive below lets you build a cost of attendance yourself and change one assumption at a time.

docs.title: Tuition
docs.text:
Tuition is the price a college charges for instruction, the classes themselves. It's usually listed alongside fees, which are required charges for things like the student center, technology, health services, and athletics. Fees are often a few hundred to a few thousand dollars a year, so always look at "tuition and fees" together.

Tuition varies more than any other part of the cost of attendance. Public universities charge much less to in-state residents than to out-of-state students, because state taxes help pay for residents' education. Private colleges charge the same tuition to everyone, and it's usually higher than public in-state tuition. Some states also have reciprocity agreements that let students from neighboring states pay reduced out-of-state tuition at participating public colleges. These agreements are worth checking if you live near a state line.

docs.title: Worked Example: Tuition Across Three Options
docs.text:
Casey lives in Iowa and is comparing three illustrative tuition-and-fees figures for one year:

  • In-state public university: $11,000
  • Out-of-state public university in a neighboring state: $31,000
  • Private college: $58,000

Across four years, the in-state public school's tuition totals $44,000, the out-of-state public school's $124,000, and the private college's $232,000. Those differences look decisive, but tuition isn't the whole story. The private college might offer large grants that bring its price below the out-of-state public school, which is why sticker price, covered below, is only a starting point.

docs.title: Room and Board
docs.text:
Room and board is the cost of housing ("room") and meals ("board"). For students living on campus, it's what the college charges for a residence hall and a meal plan. It's often the second-largest part of the cost of attendance, and sometimes the largest at public universities for in-state students.

Room and board depends on choices you make. A single room costs more than a double. A large meal plan costs more than a small one. Living off campus replaces room and board with rent, utilities, and groceries, which can cost more or less depending on the area. Living with family removes most housing costs but adds commuting. Many colleges also require first-year students to live on campus, so the off-campus option may not apply until later.

docs.title: Worked Example: Room and Board Choices
docs.text: Midland State lists room and board at $12,500, based on a double room and the standard meal plan. Priya checks the college's housing page and finds that a single room adds $1,800, while the smallest meal plan saves $900. If she chose a double with the small plan, her room and board would be $11,600. If she chose a single with the standard plan, it would be $14,300. That's a $2,700 difference a year, or more than $10,000 over four years, from two choices she controls.

docs.title: Indirect Costs
docs.text:
Indirect costs are expenses included in the cost of attendance that the college doesn't bill you for: books and supplies, transportation, and personal expenses. In contrast, direct costs are charges the college bills you for, such as tuition, fees, and on-campus room and board. Indirect costs don't appear on your college bill, so they're easy to forget. But you still pay them, usually out of pocket over the course of the year.

Colleges estimate indirect costs for an average student, and your real costs may be quite different. Distance from home is the biggest variable, since a student who flies home twice a year spends much more on transportation than one who drives an hour. Your intended major matters too. Art supplies, engineering software, or nursing equipment can push book and supply costs well above the college's estimate.

docs.title: Worked Example: Indirect Costs That Don't Show Up on the Bill
docs.text: Midland State estimates indirect costs at $4,700 a year for in-state students: $1,000 for books, $1,200 for transportation, and $2,500 for personal expenses. Marcus checks these against his own situation. He'll drive home about six times a year, four hours each way, which he estimates at $900 for gas. That's less than the college's figure. But he needs a new laptop for computer science, about $1,200 in his first year. Adding the college's figures for books and personal expenses, his estimate comes to about $5,600, nearly $900 above the college's, mostly because of the laptop. The real value of the exercise is that he now knows which costs are his to control, and that the laptop is a first-year cost he needs to plan for.

docs.title: Sticker Price
docs.text:
Sticker price is a college's published cost of attendance, before any financial aid is subtracted. The name comes from the price sticker on a new car, which few buyers actually pay. Many families see a sticker price like $85,000 a year and cross the college off at once. Sometimes that's right. Often it's a mistake.

The price a family actually pays is the sticker price minus grants and scholarships. That number is called the net price, and Chapter 14 covers it in detail. At colleges with large endowments and generous aid, the gap between sticker price and net price can be enormous. A private college with a high sticker price can end up costing a family less than a public university with a lower one. It works the other way too. A college with a modest sticker price and little aid may end up costing more than it first appears.

The practical lesson is that sticker price tells you where to start, not where you'll end up. Every college is required by law to post a net price calculator on its website, a tool that estimates your net price from your family's financial information. Use it for every college on your list, early in your search, before you get attached.

docs.title: Worked Example: When Sticker Price Misleads
docs.text:
Priya's family can pay about $25,000 a year. She compares two colleges:

  • Hillcrest College (private) has a sticker price of $82,000. Its net price calculator estimates that, based on her family's income, Hillcrest would offer about \(60,000 in grants, for a net price of about **\)22,000**.
  • An out-of-state public university has a sticker price of $50,000. Its calculator estimates about \(8,000 in aid, for a net price of about **\)42,000**.

Judging by sticker price alone, Priya would have cut Hillcrest first. Judging by net price, Hillcrest fits her family's budget and the public university doesn't. Calculators give estimates, not promises, but they're accurate enough to keep you from cutting the wrong school.

docs.title: Financial Fit
docs.text:
Financial fit is whether your family can afford a college's real cost, its net price after grants and scholarships, without taking on unmanageable debt. It's the third leg of the fit stool, and it's the one that most often fails late, after a student has been admitted and has their heart set on a school.

Financial fit depends on two numbers: what the college will cost you, and what your family can pay. You estimate the first with a net price calculator. You learn the second through the family conversation the self-assessment asked for. With both numbers, you can sort each college into one of three groups:

  • Affordable: the estimated net price is within what your family can pay.
  • A stretch: the price is somewhat above what your family can pay, and would require loans, outside scholarships, or more aid than estimated.
  • Out of reach: the gap is so large that no realistic combination of aid or loans would close it.

A stretch college can stay on your list, but you should know which ones they are. An out-of-reach college usually should come off, unless it's known for meeting full financial need or offering large merit scholarships to students with records like yours. Those colleges can surprise you, and their net price calculators tell you whether they might.

Financial fit isn't just about the first year. Costs rise over four years, and aid offers can change. Ask whether merit scholarships are renewable and what GPA you need to keep them. Also ask whether the college typically maintains need-based aid in later years. Chapters 14–16 cover aid and award letters in depth.

docs.title: Worked Example: Sorting by Financial Fit
docs.text:
Marcus's family can contribute about $15,000 a year, and he's willing to borrow up to about $5,500 a year in federal student loans. That gives him an affordable ceiling of about $20,500 a year. He runs net price calculators for five colleges:

College Sticker price Estimated net price Financial fit In-state public university $28,000 $16,000 Affordable Public university 4 hours away (out of state, reciprocity) $36,000 $21,000 Stretch Private college with strong aid $79,000 $19,000 Affordable Out-of-state flagship $52,000 $41,000 Out of reach Regional public university $24,000 $13,000 Affordable

Marcus cuts the out-of-state flagship. He keeps the reciprocity school as a stretch and plans to apply for outside scholarships to close the gap. The private college, which he'd almost skipped because of its sticker price, turns out to be one of his most affordable options.

docs.title: Reach, Target, and Safety Schools
docs.text: With your priorities set and fit in mind, you can sort the colleges you're considering by your chances of admission. Admissions counselors use three categories for this, and they all depend on two numbers from earlier chapters: a college's admission rate (Chapter 1) and its middle 50% range (Chapter 2).

docs.title: Reach School
docs.text:
A reach school is a college where admission is unlikely, even with a strong application. A college is a reach for you if either of these is true:

  • Your numbers fall below its middle 50% range. If your GPA or test scores are below the 25th percentile, most admitted students had stronger numbers.
  • It admits very few applicants. At colleges in Chapter 1's "most selective" band, under 10%, almost every applicant is qualified, so admission is unpredictable for everyone. These are reaches even for students at the top of the range.

Reach schools belong on a list. They're how you give yourself a shot at a college that would be wonderful if it worked out. But they need to be named honestly. A list with five or six reaches, and too few other schools, is how strong students end up with no good options in April.

docs.title: Worked Example: Is It a Reach?
docs.text:
Priya, with a 3.71 GPA and a 1280 SAT, checks three colleges:

  • College A admits 6% of applicants, with a middle 50% SAT range of 1500–1560. Her score is well below the range, and the college is in the most selective band. This is a clear reach.
  • College B admits 22% of applicants, with a range of 1350–1480. Her score is below the 25th percentile. This is a reach.
  • College C admits 45% of applicants, with a range of 1220–1390. Her score is inside the range. That's not a reach. It's the next category.

docs.title: Target School
docs.text:
A target school, sometimes called a match school, is a college where your academic record is typical of admitted students, so you have a solid, realistic chance of admission, though not a guaranteed one. A college is usually a target when:

  • Your numbers fall inside its middle 50% range, ideally in the middle or upper half.
  • Its admission rate isn't extremely low. A college that admits 15% of applicants is rarely a true target, even if your numbers are inside the range.

Targets are the core of a good list. They're the colleges you're most likely to choose from in April, so they need to be places you'd genuinely want to go, not just names that look safe. A useful rule is that if you'd be disappointed to end up at one of your targets, it doesn't belong on your list.

docs.title: Worked Example: Is It a Target?
docs.text:
College C from the previous example admits 45% of applicants, with a middle 50% SAT range of 1220–1390 and a GPA range of 3.5–3.9. Priya's 1280 and 3.71 are both inside the range, near the middle. College C is a target for her.

If Priya's SAT were 1210, just below the range, but her GPA were 3.85, near the top, College C would be a harder call. Most counselors would label it a target leaning toward reach, and they'd say the rest of her application would decide it. When a college falls between categories, place it in the more cautious one.

docs.title: Safety School
docs.text:
A safety school, sometimes called a likely school, is a college where you are very likely to be admitted and that your family can afford and that you'd be glad to attend. All three parts matter.

  • Very likely to be admitted: your numbers are above its 75th percentile, and it admits a large share of applicants. Formula-based schools whose published thresholds you clear by a comfortable margin, like Iowa's Regent Admission Index from Chapter 2, can be especially reliable safeties.
  • Affordable: a college you can get into but can't afford isn't a safety. It's an admission you can't use. Check financial fit with a net price calculator for every safety.
  • A place you'd want to go: a safety is a real option, not a backup you'd resent. If you can't picture yourself happy there, keep looking.

Many students treat their safety as an afterthought and choose it in a hurry. That's backward. Your safety is the one college you're almost certain to be choosing from in April, so it deserves as much research as any other.

docs.title: Worked Example: Is It a Safety?
docs.text:
Casey, an Iowa resident with an RAI of 259, considers the University of Iowa. Iowa's resident threshold is 245 for its main college, so Casey clears it by 14 points, a comfortable margin. Using Iowa's net price calculator, Casey's family finds the in-state cost manageable. And Casey has visited, liked the campus and its writing programs, and could picture living there.

All three tests pass, so Iowa is a true safety for Casey. Compare that with an out-of-state student with the same RAI. They'd also clear Iowa's nonresident threshold of 255, but by only 4 points, and they'd face a much higher out-of-state price. For that student, Iowa is closer to a target, and possibly not affordable. The same college can sit in different categories for different students.

The classifier below combines all of these tests. Enter your numbers and a college's data, and it suggests a category and explains why.

docs.title: Diagram: Reach, Target, Safety Classifier
docs.text:
Reach, Target, Safety Classifier

Type: microsim sim-id: reach-target-safety-classifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Let students classify a college as a reach, target, or safety using their own numbers, the college's middle 50% range and admission rate, and financial fit.

Bloom Level: Apply (L3) Bloom Verb: classify, apply Learning Objective: Students will apply admission-rate, middle 50% range, and affordability criteria to classify colleges as reach, target, or safety schools for themselves.

Canvas layout: - Left: inputs for the student (GPA, test score with an SAT/ACT select) and the college (admission rate, 25th and 75th percentile GPA, 25th and 75th percentile test score, and a select for financial fit: Affordable / Stretch / Out of reach / Not checked yet). Also a checkbox "I'd be glad to attend." - Center: a horizontal number line for GPA and another for test score, each showing the college's middle 50% band in blue and the student's value as a gold marker. - Right: a large result badge, "Reach" (purple), "Target" (blue), or "Safety" (green), with a three-line explanation of the deciding factors.

Classification rules (stated on screen as a simplified guide, not a prediction): 1. If admission rate < 10%: Reach, regardless of numbers ("Most selective colleges are reaches for everyone."). 2. Else if either value is below the 25th percentile: Reach. 3. Else if both values are above the 75th percentile AND admission rate ≥ 50%: candidate Safety. 4. Otherwise: Target. If admission rate < 25%, label "Target leaning reach." 5. A candidate Safety becomes a Safety only if financial fit is Affordable AND "I'd be glad to attend" is checked. Otherwise the badge reads "Likely admit — not yet a safety," with the missing test named ("Check net price" or "Would you be glad to attend?").

Presets (createButton): "Priya → College A" (6%, SAT 1500–1560 → Reach), "Priya → College C" (45%, SAT 1220–1390, GPA 3.5–3.9 → Target), "Casey → Iowa (resident)" (admission rate shown as 85% for illustration, GPA and ACT above the 75th percentile, affordable, glad to attend → Safety), "Likely admit, can't afford" (→ Likely admit — not yet a safety).

Controls (all created in setup() before positioning): createInput for numeric fields, createSelect for test type and financial fit, createCheckbox, and createButton presets.

Interaction: Any change recomputes the badge immediately. Hovering the badge shows which rule fired.

Color scheme: Reach purple, Target blue, Safety green, "not yet a safety" orange.

Responsive behavior: Call updateCanvasSize() first in setup(); panels stack vertically on narrow screens and controls reposition on resize.

Implementation: p5.js with createInput, createSelect, createCheckbox, and createButton; canvas parented to the main element.

docs.title: The Balanced College List
docs.text:
A balanced college list is a list that includes reach, target, and safety schools in proportions that make a good outcome likely, while still leaving room for ambition. Every school on it should be a genuine fit. Balance is what protects you from both kinds of bad spring: being admitted nowhere you want to go, and being admitted only to colleges you can't afford.

A common guideline for a final list of eight to twelve colleges is:

  • 2–3 reach schools, for the possibility of a stretch that works out.
  • 4–6 target schools, the core of the list and your most likely choices.
  • 2–3 safety schools, each one affordable and a place you'd be glad to go.

These numbers aren't rules. A student applying mostly to formula-based public universities, where outcomes are predictable, might need fewer schools. A student aiming at highly selective colleges, where outcomes are unpredictable, might need more targets and a firm safety. What matters is the principle: at least one affordable college you'd love should be very likely to say yes.

Two checks keep a list honest. First, check the categories against financial fit. A list with three safeties, all of them out of reach financially, has no safeties at all. Second, check every school against your priorities. If a college is on your list only because of its name, and you can't say why it fits you, it's taking up a slot. Chapter 4 walks you through narrowing a long list to a final one. The aim here is to know what balance looks like before you start cutting.

docs.title: Worked Example: Priya Rebalances Her List
docs.text:
Priya's original list had seven reaches, two targets, and one school she'd called a safety, which turned out to be out of reach financially. After her self-assessment and net price calculations, she rebuilt it:

Category Colleges Notes Reach (3) College A, College B, one more highly selective college Kept her two favorites from the original list, plus one with strong aid Target (5) College C, Hillcrest College, three others found in her research All suburban or college-town campuses with collaborative cultures Safety (2) Her state flagship (in-state, honors college likely), a regional public university Both affordable by net price calculator; she visited both and liked them

Her new list has ten schools. Every one fits her priorities, every safety is affordable, and she'd be glad to attend any of them. She didn't give up her ambition. She kept three reaches. But no matter what happens in the reach round, she has a good outcome waiting. The builder below lets you sort your own list the same way and checks it for balance.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Your college list sets the limits of your final choice, so build it from your own personal priorities, identified through a written self-assessment, not from reputation. Name your dealbreakers first.
  • College fit has three dimensions, and a college must work on all three. Academic fit is your major and level of challenge, social fit is belonging, and financial fit is affordability.
  • There's no single right school. Most students could thrive at many colleges.
  • Check your intended major at every college. Capped majors can be far harder to enter than the university's admit rate suggests. Applying undeclared is normal.
  • School size, campus setting, distance from home, and campus culture shape daily life. Judge them with evidence from your own experience.
  • The cost of attendance combines tuition and fees, room and board, and indirect costs. The sticker price comes before aid, so run a net price calculator for every college early.
  • A reach school is unlikely for you, a target school is realistic, and a safety school is very likely, affordable, and a place you'd be glad to go.
  • A balanced college list of eight to twelve schools usually holds 2–3 reaches, 4–6 targets, and 2–3 safeties, with at least one affordable school you'd love that's very likely to say yes.

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
Why is a college you're certain to be admitted to, but can't afford, not a safety school?

A safety must be very likely to admit you, affordable, and a place you'd be glad to attend. An admission you can't afford isn't a usable option, so it doesn't protect you the way a safety should.

A university admits 60% of applicants, but its nursing program, which you'd apply to directly, admits 20%. Your numbers are inside the university's middle 50% range. How should you classify it?

As a reach (or at best a target leaning reach). Because you apply directly to a capped major, the 20% program rate matters more than the 60% university rate.

A college's cost of attendance is $30,000: tuition and fees $12,000, room and board $12,000, and $6,000 in books, transportation, and personal expenses. What are its direct and indirect costs?

Direct costs (billed by the college) are tuition and fees plus room and board: \(24,000**. **Indirect costs** (not billed) are books, transportation, and personal expenses: **\)6,000.

Your numbers are above a college's 75th percentile, but it admits only 8% of applicants. Is it a target?

No, it's a reach. At colleges admitting under 10%, nearly every applicant is qualified, so admission is unpredictable even for students above the range.

A list has six reaches, two targets, and one safety. What's the main risk, and how would you fix it?

The risk is ending up with few or no options you'd want. Too much of the list depends on unlikely outcomes. Cut the reaches to 2–3 and add targets and at least one more affordable safety you'd be glad to attend.

docs.title: Researching and Narrowing Your College List
Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers using the College Scorecard, Common Data Set, outcome data, visits, fairs, and reviews to research schools, then narrowing a long list to a final eight to twelve. It applies the fit criteria from the previous chapter to real data. Students finish with a researched, balanced final list of eight to twelve schools.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 14 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score College Research Tools 356 College Search Website 1 Graduation Rate 3 College Scorecard 1 Common Data Set 1 Retention Rate 1 Virtual Tour 1 Campus Visit 36 College Fair 1 Admissions Information Session 1 Student Reviews 1 Long List 299 Narrowing the List 298 Final College List 297

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
  • Chapter 2: How Colleges Evaluate Applicants
  • Chapter 3: Finding Your Fit

docs.title: From Priorities to Evidence
docs.text:
At the end of Chapter 3, you had a set of personal priorities, a way to judge academic, social, and financial fit, and a definition of a balanced list. What you probably don't have yet is enough real information about specific colleges to apply any of it. You may know a college's name, its mascot, and what a friend said about it. That's not enough to judge fit.

This chapter is about getting that information and using it. You'll learn which research tools answer which questions, starting with federal data and the standardized reports colleges publish about themselves, then moving to the first-hand experience of visits, fairs, and student voices. Then you'll put the research to work. You'll build a long list, narrow it in deliberate passes, and finish with a final list of eight to twelve colleges you can defend school by school.

Throughout the chapter, you'll follow Marcus from earlier chapters. His priorities are a cost ceiling of about $20,500 a year, a strong computer science program, a campus within a day's drive, and a mid-sized school.

docs.title: College Research Tools
docs.text:
College research tools are the sources you use to learn about specific colleges: data about admissions, cost, and outcomes, and first-hand impressions of what it's like to study and live there. No single tool tells you everything. Each one is good at answering certain questions and weak at others, so effective research means knowing which tool to reach for.

It helps to sort research tools into two groups:

  • Data tools give you numbers that are reported in a standard way, so you can compare colleges fairly. They include the U.S. Department of Education's College Scorecard, each college's Common Data Set, net price calculators, and college search websites. They're best for questions about admission chances, cost, and outcomes.
  • Experience tools give you a feel for a place: what students are like, what a weekday looks like, whether you could see yourself there. They include campus visits, virtual tours, information sessions, college fairs, and student reviews. They're best for questions about culture and social fit.

You need both kinds. Data alone can make a college look perfect on paper even though you'd be unhappy there. Experience alone can make you fall for a beautiful campus you can't afford or have little chance of getting into. A good habit is to use data to decide which colleges to look at, and experience to decide which ones feel right.

Before you look at the matrix below, keep one more distinction in mind. Some tools come from neutral sources, such as the federal government or standardized reports. Others come from the college itself, such as its website, tours, and information sessions, which are designed to recruit you. Both are useful, but marketing should be read as marketing.

docs.title: Diagram: Research Tool Matrix
docs.text:
Research Tool Matrix

Type: infographic sim-id: research-tool-matrix Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Show students which college research tool best answers which question, so they can choose the right tool instead of relying on one source for everything.

Bloom Level: Analyze (L4) Bloom Verb: select, differentiate Learning Objective: Students will select the research tool best suited to a given question about a college and differentiate between data tools and experience tools.

Visual style: A grid. Rows are nine research tools in two labeled groups: Data tools (College Scorecard, Common Data Set, Net price calculator, College search website) and Experience tools (Campus visit, Virtual tour, Information session, College fair, Student reviews). Columns are six questions students ask: "Can I get in?", "What will it cost me?", "Do students graduate?", "Is my major strong?", "What's the culture like?", "Could I see myself there?" Each cell shows a filled circle (strong source), half circle (partial), or empty circle (weak), plus a small tag "Neutral" or "From the college" on each row.

Ratings (illustrative): - College Scorecard: cost strong, graduation strong, can I get in partial, major partial (field-of-study earnings), culture weak, see myself weak. Neutral. - Common Data Set: can I get in strong, graduation strong, cost partial, major weak, culture weak, see myself weak. Reported by the college in a standard format. - Net price calculator: cost strong, others weak. From the college. - College search website: can I get in partial, cost partial, graduation partial, major partial, culture partial, see myself weak. Third party. - Campus visit: culture strong, see myself strong, major partial, others weak. From the college. - Virtual tour: culture partial, see myself partial, others weak. From the college. - Information session: can I get in partial, cost partial, major partial, culture partial. From the college. - College fair: can I get in partial, major partial, culture weak, see myself weak. From the college. - Student reviews: culture strong, see myself partial, major partial, others weak. Third party, unverified.

Interaction: - Click a cell: open an infobox explaining why the tool is strong, partial, or weak for that question, with one tip (for example, Common Data Set × "Can I get in?": "Section C has admit counts and middle 50% ranges in the same format at every college."). - Click a column header: highlight the best tools for that question in gold. - A createSelect "I want to know..." with the six questions does the same as clicking a column header. - A "Quiz me" button shows a random question and asks the student to click the best tool; correct picks turn green with an explanation, wrong picks show a hint.

Color scheme: data-tool rows tinted pale blue, experience-tool rows tinted pale green; strong circles dark, partial half-filled, weak outlined.

Responsive behavior: Call updateCanvasSize() first in setup(); on narrow screens the grid collapses to one tool card at a time with a "Next tool" button.

Implementation: p5.js with createSelect and createButton; canvas parented to the main element.

docs.title: Worked Example: Matching Questions to Tools
docs.text:
Marcus has four questions about a public university four hours from home. He matches each to a tool:

  1. "Can I afford it?" → The university's net price calculator, using his family's income. His estimate comes to $21,000, just above his ceiling.
  2. "Is the CS program strong, and can I get into it?" → The university's CS department website for program rules, and its Common Data Set for overall admission numbers. He learns that CS is open to any admitted student, with no separate application.
  3. "Do students actually finish?" → The College Scorecard, which shows the university's graduation rate and the typical earnings of its CS graduates.
  4. "Would I like living there?" → A campus visit during a school break, plus student reviews and a conversation with a current CS student.

Without the matching step, Marcus might have tried to answer all four questions from the university's glossy website, and he would have learned mostly what the university wanted him to know. With it, each question goes to the source most likely to answer it honestly.

docs.title: College Search Websites
docs.text:
A college search website is a third-party site that lets you search and filter many colleges at once by traits like size, location, majors, cost, and selectivity. Examples include the College Board's BigFuture, Niche, and Cappex. These sites are good for casting a wide net. You can find colleges you've never heard of that match your priorities, which is exactly what a long list needs.

Use them with two cautions. First, their numbers usually come from federal data or the Common Data Set, sometimes a year or two old, so check important figures against the source. Second, treat any "match score," "grade," or ranking as a starting point, not a verdict. Those scores reflect someone else's choices about what matters, not your priorities.

docs.title: The College Scorecard
docs.text:
The College Scorecard is a free website from the U.S. Department of Education, at collegescorecard.ed.gov, that reports standardized data for nearly every college that accepts federal financial aid. Because the federal government collects the data the same way from every college, it's one of the fairest ways to compare schools side by side.

The Scorecard is strongest on cost and outcomes. For each college it shows the average annual net price, including how that price varies by family income. It also shows the graduation rate, the typical student debt at graduation, and the typical earnings of former students several years after they leave. Many of those figures are also broken down by field of study, so Marcus can compare earnings for computer science graduates specifically, not just graduates overall. Its admissions data is thinner, so pair it with the Common Data Set for questions about getting in.

docs.title: The Common Data Set
docs.text:
The Common Data Set (CDS) is a standardized report that many colleges publish each year, answering the same questions in the same format. To find one, search for the college's name plus "Common Data Set." It's usually posted on the college's institutional research page. Because every college uses the same sections, you can compare colleges question by question. Chapter 2 used it for middle 50% ranges and demonstrated interest.

The sections you'll use most are:

Section What it covers Questions it answers B Enrollment and persistence How large is it? What are its graduation and retention rates? C First-year admission How many apply and get in? Middle 50% ranges (C9)? How much does each factor matter, including demonstrated interest (C7)? G Annual expenses What are tuition, fees, and room and board? H Financial aid How much need-based and merit aid does the college give, and to how many students? I Faculty and class size How many classes are small, and how many are large?

Two cautions apply. Not every college publishes a CDS, and the most recent one may describe the class that entered a year or two ago. Still, it's the best single source for a college's admissions numbers. It's also where you'll find the class-size data Chapter 3 recommended checking.

docs.title: Graduation Rate
docs.text:
A college's graduation rate is the percentage of students who start there as first-time, full-time students and finish a bachelor's degree within a set time. The standard federal measure uses six years, which is 150% of the normal four. Many colleges also report a four-year rate, which is usually lower. The College Scorecard uses a broader measure: the share of all entering students, full-time and part-time, who finish within eight years. Its numbers won't match a college's six-year rate, so compare colleges using the same source.

Graduation rate matters because a college you start but don't finish costs time and money without giving you the degree. A high rate suggests that students are well supported, can get the classes they need, and can afford to stay. A low rate isn't automatically a dealbreaker, since colleges that serve many working or part-time students often have lower rates for reasons beyond the college's control. But it's a reason to ask questions. When you compare, look at the four-year rate too. A college where most students take five or six years to finish costs you an extra year or two of tuition and living expenses.

docs.title: Retention Rate
docs.text:
A college's retention rate is the percentage of first-time, full-time first-year students who return for their second year. It's an early warning signal. Students who leave after one year usually do so because of cost, academic difficulty, or poor social fit. A high retention rate suggests most first-years found what they needed. Retention is reported in the Common Data Set (Section B) and on many college search websites.

Retention and graduation rates usually move together, but retention reacts faster. If you see a college with a decent graduation rate and a retention rate noticeably lower than similar colleges, ask what happens to students in their first year.

docs.title: Worked Example: Comparing Outcomes
docs.text:
Marcus compares three colleges on his list using the Scorecard and each college's CDS. The colleges are fictional, but the comparison is the kind real data supports.

College Retention rate 4-year graduation rate 6-year graduation rate Midland State 88% 52% 74% Lakeshore University 94% 71% 86% Ridgeview Polytechnic 81% 30% 61%

Lakeshore stands out: students stay, and most finish in four years. Midland's six-year rate is solid, but only about half its students finish in four, which means an extra year of costs is common. Ridgeview's lower retention, 81% compared with 88% and 94%, and its 30% four-year rate are red flags. Marcus doesn't cut Ridgeview yet, but he adds a question to ask on his visit: why do students leave after their first year, and why do so many take longer than four years? The chart below lets you compare up to four colleges this way.

docs.title: Diagram: College Outcomes Comparison
docs.text:

Chart type: Grouped vertical bar chart. Each college is a group of three bars: Retention rate, 4-year graduation rate, 6-year graduation rate. Y-axis 0–100%.

An "Add college" button adds a row (max 4) and "Remove" buttons delete rows. - A checkbox "Show the four-to-six-year gap," which overlays a bracket between each college's 4-year and 6-year bars labeled with the difference in percentage points. - A "Reset to example" button.

docs.title: Campus Visits
docs.text:
A campus visit is a trip to a college to see it in person, usually including a guided tour and often an admissions information session. It's the single best way to judge campus culture and social fit, because it shows you things no website can: how students talk to each other, how the place feels on an ordinary day, and whether you can picture yourself there.

A visit is worth more when you plan it. A few habits make the difference:

  • Visit while classes are in session if you can, so you see the campus on a normal day rather than an empty one.
  • Go beyond the tour. Tour guides are trained, enthusiastic volunteers. Also eat in a dining hall, sit in on a class if the college allows it, walk through the neighborhood, and read the student newspaper or bulletin boards.
  • Talk to students who weren't assigned to talk to you. Ask a student in the library or the student center what they like least about the college. Their answer often tells you more than the tour.
  • Take notes right away. After three visits, campuses blur together. Write down what you liked, what bothered you, and any questions within an hour of leaving.
  • Register with the admissions office. At colleges that track demonstrated interest, signing in for a tour counts.

Visits cost time and money, and many students can't visit every college on their list. That's fine. Prioritize visits to colleges you're seriously considering, especially ones that are close, ones where you're unsure about fit, and your likely safeties. For the rest, use virtual tours and information sessions, which the next sections cover. Many colleges also offer travel grants or fly-in programs for low-income and first-generation students. Search the admissions website for "fly-in" or "diversity visit program."

docs.title: Worked Example: Getting More From One Visit
docs.text:
Marcus visits Lakeshore University on a Friday in October. He signs in at admissions, attends the information session, and takes the tour. Then he does three more things:

  • He eats lunch in a dining hall and asks two students at his table what they'd change about Lakeshore. Both mention that the CS department's intro courses are huge, but the clubs make it feel smaller.
  • He sits in on the last half hour of an intro CS lecture and notices that teaching assistants are walking the aisles helping students.
  • He walks ten minutes off campus and finds a main street with cheap food and a bus stop to the nearest city.

In his notes he writes: Big intro CS but good support. Friendly, collaborative. Town is small but enough. Can picture myself here: yes. Those three extra hours told him more than the tour, and they confirmed that Lakeshore belongs on his final list.

docs.title: Admissions Information Sessions
docs.text:
An admissions information session is a presentation by a college's admissions staff, usually about an hour long, that explains the college's academics, student life, admissions process, and financial aid. Sessions are held on campus, often before tours, and many colleges also run them online or in high schools and hotels as part of regional travel.

Sessions are useful because they give you the college's own description of what it looks for and how its process works, sometimes including details you won't find online, such as how it reads applications by region or which majors are hardest to enter. They're also a chance to ask questions. Come with one or two specific ones, and remember that the session is a recruiting event, so pair what you hear with neutral data.

docs.title: Virtual Tours
docs.text: A virtual tour is an online version of a campus visit: a guided video, a 360-degree photo walk-through, or a live online tour led by a current student. Nearly every college offers one on its admissions website, and some search platforms collect many in one place. Virtual tours cost nothing and take minutes, so they're ideal for early screening and for colleges you can't afford to visit. They can't show you how a campus feels or let you talk freely with students, so for colleges high on your list, pair them with a live online session or a conversation with a current student.

docs.title: College Fairs
docs.text: A college fair is an event where representatives from many colleges set up tables in one place, usually a school gym, convention center, or online platform, to meet prospective students. The National Association for College Admission Counseling (NACAC) runs large national fairs, and many high schools and regions hold their own. Fairs are an efficient way to learn about colleges you hadn't considered and to meet the admissions officer who may read your application. Bring a short list of questions, have a few colleges in mind, and fill out the inquiry card at colleges you're serious about. At colleges that track interest, that card counts too.

docs.title: Student Reviews
docs.text:
Student reviews are first-hand descriptions of a college written by current or former students, posted on review sites such as Niche or Unigo, on social media, or in online forums. They can reveal things marketing materials don't, such as how hard it is to get into popular classes, what dorms are really like, or how students feel about campus life.

Read them carefully, though. Reviews are unverified and self-selected. Students with very good or very bad experiences post far more often than everyone in between. Look for patterns across many reviews, not single dramatic posts, and give more weight to specific details ("advising helped me switch majors in a semester") than to general feelings ("this place is the worst"). Where you can, confirm what you read with a real conversation.

docs.title: The Long List
docs.text:
A long list is your first, broad list of colleges worth researching, usually fifteen to twenty-five schools. It's built from your priorities and filled out through research, so it includes colleges you already know and colleges you discovered by looking. At this stage, you're still gathering options, not deciding.

A good long list has three traits:

  • It comes from your priorities. Every school on it meets your dealbreakers, as far as you know. A college that obviously fails one shouldn't be on it.
  • It's wider than your comfort zone. Use college search websites to find colleges you've never heard of that match your profile. Students who build lists only from familiar names miss many good fits, often less-known colleges that offer generous aid.
  • It spans every category. Include likely reaches, targets, and safeties from the start, so you aren't scrambling to find a safety in October.

Use a simple tracking sheet from the beginning. For each college, record the information you'll need to narrow the list: admission rate, middle 50% range, your category guess, estimated net price, graduation rate, and a few notes on fit. Chapter 5 shows how to turn that sheet into a full application tracker.

docs.title: Worked Example: Marcus Builds a Long List
docs.text:
Marcus starts with the three colleges he already knew: his in-state public university, the regional public university nearby, and Lakeshore. Then he opens a college search website and filters for: computer science major, 5,000–20,000 undergraduates, within 400 miles of home, and a published average net price under $25,000 for families in his income range. The search returns more than forty colleges. He skims each one and keeps those with a CS program that looks strong and a campus that seems like a plausible fit.

After an evening of research, Marcus has eighteen colleges. Five were new to him, including two private colleges with strong aid that he'd never have found by name. His long list is more than double the size of his final list will be, which is exactly right.

docs.title: Narrowing the List
docs.text:
Narrowing the list is the process of cutting a long list down to a final list by applying your priorities and the three kinds of fit, college by college, in deliberate passes. It's the step where research turns into decisions. It works best as a sequence of passes, each with one clear question, rather than one long, agonizing review.

Pass 1: Cut on dealbreakers and fit. For each college, ask: Does it clearly fail one of my priorities? Use your research. If the net price calculator shows a college is out of reach, if the CS program turns out to be weak, or if a virtual tour shows a campus that doesn't match what you want, cut it, no matter how famous it is.

Pass 2: Classify and balance. Sort what remains into reach, target, and safety using the Common Data Set numbers and the criteria from Chapter 3. Then compare the counts with a balanced list. You may need to cut from a crowded category, usually reaches, or add to a thin one, usually safeties.

Pass 3: Test each school. For every college still on the list, ask one question: Could I picture myself happy here, and could I say why in a sentence? If you can't, the college is on your list for its name, not its fit. Cut it, or research it more until you can answer.

The order matters. Cutting on fit first means you never waste time classifying colleges that wouldn't work anyway. Balancing second means you trim and fill by category, not by gut feeling. Testing last catches the colleges that survived the first two passes on numbers alone. The simulation below runs a long list through all three passes.

docs.title: Diagram: List Narrowing Funnel
docs.text:
List Narrowing Funnel

Type: microsim sim-id: list-narrowing-funnel Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Let students run a long college list through the three narrowing passes and see how each pass removes colleges for a specific reason, ending with a balanced final list.

Bloom Level: Evaluate (L5) Bloom Verb: judge, justify Learning Objective: Students will judge which colleges to cut from a long list at each narrowing pass and justify each cut using fit criteria and list balance.

Canvas layout: - Left: a vertical funnel with three labeled bands: "Pass 1: Fit," "Pass 2: Balance," "Pass 3: Picture yourself." Above the funnel, a pool of college cards; below it, a "Final list" tray. - Each college card shows a name and four small icons: category (R/T/S), financial fit (green/yellow/red dot), major strength (star filled or empty), and campus match (check or X). - Right: a "Cut log" panel listing each cut and its reason.

Default data: Marcus's 18-college long list (fictional names) with attributes chosen so that Pass 1 cuts 5 (two out of reach financially, one weak CS program, one too far, one too large), Pass 2 cuts 2 reaches from a crowded reach category and flags that one more safety would help, and Pass 3 cuts 1 college Marcus "can't say why" he wants. Final list: 10 (3 reach, 5 target, 2 safety).

Controls (all created in setup() before positioning): - createButton "Run Pass 1," "Run Pass 2," "Run Pass 3" (each enabled after the previous one), and "Reset." - createCheckbox "Let me decide," which switches from automatic cuts to manual mode: the student clicks cards to cut them during each pass and must choose a reason from a createSelect (Out of reach financially / Weak in my major / Fails campus priority / Too many in this category / Can't say why I want it). The log records the student's reasons. - After Pass 3, a summary shows counts by category and runs the balance checks from Chapter 3 (8–12 total, 2–3 reach, 4–6 target, 2–3 safety, at least one affordable safety).

Interaction: Cut cards slide out of the funnel into a "Cut" pile with their reason; kept cards drop to the next band. Hovering a card shows its full attributes. In manual mode, if a student cuts a college that meets all their criteria, a gentle prompt asks "Are you sure? This one fits every priority."

Color scheme: funnel bands in three shades of blue; cut cards grayed; final-list tray in green.

Responsive behavior: Call updateCanvasSize() first in setup(); on narrow screens the cut log moves below the funnel and cards shrink to name plus icons.

Implementation: p5.js with createButton, createCheckbox, and createSelect; canvas parented to the main element.

docs.title: Worked Example: Marcus Narrows Eighteen to Ten
docs.text:
Pass 1 (fit): Marcus runs net price calculators for all eighteen and cuts two private colleges whose estimates came in above $35,000. He cuts one university when he discovers its CS major is new and small, and another that turns out to be a ten-hour drive. He cuts one more, a 35,000-student university, after a virtual tour confirms it's bigger than he wants. Thirteen left.

Pass 2 (balance): He classifies the thirteen: five reaches, six targets, two safeties. Five reaches is too many for a list he wants to keep to ten, so he cuts the two reaches where his CS admission chances are lowest. Eleven left: 3 reaches, 6 targets, 2 safeties.

Pass 3 (picture yourself): For each college, Marcus writes one sentence on why he'd be happy there. For ten, the sentence comes easily. For one target, all he can write is "my friend is applying." He cuts it. Ten left.

docs.title: The Final College List
docs.text:
Your final college list is the set of colleges you'll actually apply to, usually eight to twelve, each researched, balanced across reach, target, and safety, and chosen because it fits you. It's the end product of everything in this chapter and the last, and it becomes the starting point for everything that follows: the deadlines you track in Chapter 5, the testing choices in Chapter 6, and the applications and essays in later chapters.

A strong final list passes a short checklist:

  • Every college fits your dealbreakers and has a clear reason to be there.
  • The list is balanced, usually 2–3 reaches, 4–6 targets, and 2–3 safeties.
  • At least one safety is affordable and a place you'd be glad to attend.
  • You've run a net price calculator for every college.
  • You've seen every college in some form: a visit, a virtual tour, or a conversation with a student.

"Final" doesn't mean frozen. You can still add a college in the fall, for example a late-discovered school with a strong program or rolling admission. You can also drop one if new information changes your view. But aim to settle your list by early fall of senior year, before early deadlines arrive. A list that keeps changing in November usually means an application is being rushed.

docs.title: Worked Example: Marcus's Final List
docs.text:
Here is Marcus's final list, with a one-line reason for each school.

Category College Why it's on the list Reach Two highly selective universities with strong CS and full-need aid Long shots, but affordable if admitted Reach Public university with direct-admit CS Excellent CS and affordable; the CS major's low admit rate makes it a reach Target Lakeshore University Strong CS support, collaborative culture, affordable estimate; visited and loved it Target Private college with strong aid Net price $19,000; small classes in CS Target Public university 4 hours away (reciprocity) Strong CS; a stretch on cost, so he's applying for outside scholarships Target Two mid-sized regional universities Good CS programs, both affordable, both within a day's drive Safety In-state public university Clears the admission thresholds; affordable; strong CS open to all admitted students Safety Regional public university nearby Very likely admit; lowest net price on the list; could live at home if needed

Every college has a reason that ties back to his priorities. The list is balanced at 3 reaches, 5 targets, and 2 safeties, and both safeties are affordable. If every reach says no, Marcus still has several good options he'd be glad to choose from.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• College research tools come in two kinds: data tools for admission chances, cost, and outcomes, and experience tools for culture and social fit. Use data to decide which colleges to look at and experience to decide which feel right.
  • College search websites are good for casting a wide net. Treat their match scores as starting points.
  • The College Scorecard gives neutral federal data on net price, graduation rates, debt, and earnings. The Common Data Set gives each college's admissions numbers, costs, aid, and class sizes in a standard format.
  • Retention rate is an early warning signal. A gap between four- and six-year graduation rates means extra years of cost are common.
  • Campus visits are the best test of culture. Go beyond the tour. Information sessions, virtual tours, college fairs, and student reviews fill in where you can't visit. Read reviews for patterns, not single posts.
  • A long list of fifteen to twenty-five colleges is built from your priorities and stretched by research.
  • Narrowing the list works in three passes: cut on fit, then balance categories, then test each school with "Could I picture myself happy here, and say why?"
  • Your final college list of eight to twelve colleges is balanced, fully researched, and includes at least one affordable safety you'd be glad to attend.

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
Which tool would you use to find a college's middle 50% SAT range, and which section would you look in?

The college's Common Data Set, Section C (first-year admission), which reports middle 50% test ranges in item C9.

A college's six-year graduation rate is 80%, but its four-year rate is 45%. What does that suggest, and why does it matter for cost?

Many students take five or six years to finish. Each extra year adds a year of tuition and living costs, so budget for the possibility, and ask the college why students take longer.

You read six reviews of a college. One says the dorms are 'disgusting.' Five mention that it's hard to get into required courses in your major. Which deserves more weight?

The pattern across five reviews about required courses. Single dramatic posts are less reliable than specific details that many students repeat.

Why does narrowing the list cut on fit before balancing categories?

Cutting on fit first means you never spend time classifying colleges that wouldn't work for you. Balancing then trims and fills categories using only colleges that genuinely fit.

A student's final list has ten colleges, but they can't say why they'd be happy at three of them. What should they do?

Apply the picture-yourself test: research those three until they can name a specific reason, or cut them and, if needed, replace them with colleges that clearly fit.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers setting up the systems that carry you through senior year: deadline trackers, filing systems, a dedicated email, portals and the Common App account, counselors, family roles, and five first steps. Organization is what keeps a dozen applications from turning into chaos. After this chapter, students have their trackers, accounts, and filing system in place and know who can help them.
