docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
  • Chapter 2: How Colleges Evaluate Applicants
  • Chapter 4: Researching and Narrowing Your College List

docs.title: Systems Before Essays
docs.text:
Applications rarely fall apart because of one hard step. They fall apart because of dropped threads: a deadline you knew about but forgot to write down, a teacher who never got your resume, a password you can't remember in December, an email from a college that landed in a folder you never check. Each mistake is small. With ten colleges and five months, there are hundreds of chances to make one.

This chapter sets up the systems that prevent that. You'll begin with what getting organized means and why it pays off. Then you'll build the core tools: a deadline tracker you share with your family, a checklist for each college, and a filing system for your documents and logins. Next come the accounts that every application runs through, starting with a dedicated email address and the Common App. You'll also learn who can help you, from your school counselor to your family, and how senior year's calendar fits together. The chapter ends with five first steps you can take this week.

The good news is that none of this is hard. Most of it takes an afternoon or two. That small investment pays off every week for the rest of the year.

docs.title: Getting Organized
docs.text:
Getting organized means setting up, before your applications begin, the tools and habits that keep every task, date, document, and login in a known place. It's not busywork that comes before the real work. It's what lets the real work, like writing strong essays and comparing aid offers, happen without a last-minute scramble.

Organization rests on three principles:

  1. One source of truth. Every deadline lives in one tracker, every document in one folder, every password in one secure place. When information is scattered across texts, sticky notes, and memory, something always gets lost.
  2. Visible to the people helping you. A parent, guardian, or counselor can only catch a missed date if they can see the plan. Sharing your tracker turns your helpers into a safety net.
  3. Early buffers. Set your own deadlines a few days before the real ones. Portals crash on deadline night, recommenders run late, and files refuse to upload. A buffer turns those problems into minor annoyances instead of emergencies.

The payoff is easy to underestimate. Think about how many separate items the process involves. Ten colleges, each with an application, a supplement or two, a supporting document deadline, and an aid deadline, already add up to more than forty dates. Add in testing, recommendations, scholarship applications, and the FAFSA, and the total climbs past a hundred. No one can track that from memory.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Cost of a Dropped Thread
docs.text:
Two students apply to the same set of colleges.

Student 1 keeps deadlines in their head and in a few phone notes. In late October, they realize their top choice's Early Action deadline is November 1, not November 15 as they'd remembered. They rush their supplemental essay and submit it at 11:40 p.m. with two typos. They also discover that one teacher never received the resume they meant to send, so that letter arrives a week late.

Student 2 spent one Saturday in August building a tracker and shared it with a parent. Every deadline has a personal due date five days earlier, and phone reminders go off a week before each one. Their supplemental essays are done by October 25. When a teacher's letter hasn't appeared in the portal by November 3, the tracker flags it, and a polite email fixes it the same day.

Both students are equally capable. The difference in their applications comes entirely from one Saturday of setup.

docs.title: The Deadline Tracker
docs.text:
A deadline tracker is a single document, usually a spreadsheet, that lists every college on your list along with every date and requirement attached to it. It's the center of your organizational system. Chapter 1 explained why one college can have several deadlines. The tracker is where you record all of them.

For each college, a good tracker includes:

  • Application round and deadline, with the exact time and time zone.
  • Supporting document deadline for transcripts, recommendations, and test scores.
  • Financial aid and scholarship deadlines, including any priority deadlines.
  • Your personal due date, a few days before the real deadline.
  • Application platform, whether the Common App or the college's own application.
  • Supplemental essays, with their prompts and word limits.
  • Recommendations required, and from whom.
  • Testing policy, and whether you plan to submit scores.
  • Status: not started, in progress, submitted, or complete.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Rows of Priya's Tracker
docs.text:
College Round Deadline My due date Docs due Aid priority Platform Supplements Recs Status State flagship EA Nov 1, 11:59 p.m. local Oct 27 Nov 8 Dec 1 (FAFSA) Own application 1 short answer (250 words) None required In progress Hillcrest College RD Jan 15, 11:59 p.m. ET Jan 9 Feb 1 Feb 15 (CSS Profile) Common App "Why Hillcrest" (300 words) 2 teachers + counselor Not started

Notice that Priya's flagship row has an aid priority date (December 1) that comes after her application but before she'd hear back. Without the tracker, she might assume aid comes after admission. Also notice that Hillcrest requires the CSS Profile, an extra aid form Chapter 14 explains, so it gets its own deadline.

docs.title: The Shared Tracker
docs.text: A shared tracker is your deadline tracker made visible to the people helping you, usually a parent or guardian and sometimes your counselor, through a shared online spreadsheet or document. Sharing it doesn't hand over control. You still own the process. What it does is give someone else a chance to notice a problem you're too close to see, like a missing aid deadline, two essays due the same week, or a status that hasn't changed in a month. Decide together how you'll use it. For example, your parent might check it every Sunday and add questions as comments rather than sending reminders all week. One caution: never put passwords in a shared tracker. They belong in your private login record, covered later in this chapter.

docs.title: Supporting Document Deadlines
docs.text: A supporting document deadline is the date by which a college must receive the materials that accompany your application: your transcript, recommendation letters, test scores, and any school report. Chapter 1 introduced it. Here's why it gets its own column in your tracker. Most of these documents are sent by other people, such as your counselor, your teachers, and testing agencies, so your job is to request them early and then confirm they arrived. Record each document's status separately, and check your applicant portal a week or so after the deadline to make sure everything was matched to your file.

docs.title: Priority Deadlines
docs.text: A priority deadline is an earlier date that gives you the best chance at something limited, such as financial aid, merit scholarships, honors programs, or housing, even though the college still accepts applications or forms after it. "Priority" is easy to misread as "optional." In practice, students who miss a priority deadline are still considered, but often for whatever money or spots are left. Iowa's December 1 FAFSA priority date, for example, comes before its regular application deadline. Treat every priority deadline as a real deadline.

docs.title: Calendar Reminders
docs.text: Calendar reminders are alerts you set on your phone or computer calendar for each date in your tracker, so deadlines come to you instead of depending on you to check. A tracker only helps when you look at it. Reminders make sure you do. A useful pattern is to set two reminders for each deadline: one a week before your personal due date, to start finishing, and one the day before, to submit. Add reminders for checking your portals and email, too.

docs.title: The Application Checklist
docs.text:
An application checklist is a list of every component one specific college requires, which you check off as you complete each one. Your tracker gives the overview across all your colleges. The checklist gives the detail for one. You might keep one checklist per college as a tab in your spreadsheet, a note, or a printed page in that college's folder.

A typical checklist includes the application form, the personal essay, each supplemental essay, the activities list, each recommendation, the transcript request, test scores if submitting, the application fee or fee waiver, and any extras such as a portfolio, interview, or specific form for a program. It ends with two items students often forget: "Submitted (confirmation saved)" and "Portal checked: all documents received."

docs.title: College-Specific Requirements
docs.text:
College-specific requirements are the parts of an application that differ from one college to another: extra essays, extra recommendations, testing rules, portfolios, interviews, program-specific forms, and the specific deadlines each college sets. Even when ten colleges share one application platform, they rarely ask for exactly the same things. Missing one college's unique requirement is one of the most common ways an otherwise complete application ends up incomplete.

Requirements vary in several ways:

  • Essays. Some colleges ask for no supplemental essays. Others ask for two, three, or more, with different word limits.
  • Recommendations. Some require none, some require one teacher, and some require two teachers plus a counselor. A few accept an optional additional letter.
  • Testing. Policies range from test-required to test-optional to test-blind, and can differ by program or for merit scholarships.
  • Program requirements. Art, music, theater, and architecture programs often require portfolios or auditions. Nursing and engineering may ask for extra essays or have different deadlines.
  • Course requirements. Some colleges, or some majors, require specific high school courses, such as four years of math or a year of chemistry.
  • Interviews. Some colleges offer them, some recommend them, and a few require them for certain programs.

Where do you find them? Always on the college's own admissions website, usually on a page called "first-year requirements" or "how to apply." The Common App also lists each member college's requirements, but treat the college's own site as the final word, since it's updated most directly. Policies change from year to year, so check them in the fall of the year you apply, not from a friend's experience last year.

Before the matrix below, here's how to read it. Each row is a college and each column is a requirement type. Filled cells show what that college asks for, so you can see at a glance which requirements are shared and which are unique.

docs.title: Diagram: College Requirements Matrix
docs.text:
College Requirements Matrix

Type: microsim sim-id: college-requirements-matrix Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Show students how requirements differ across the colleges on one list, so they can spot unique requirements before they're missed and plan the total workload.

Bloom Level: Analyze (L4) Bloom Verb: compare, organize Learning Objective: Students will compare application requirements across colleges and organize them to identify which requirements are shared and which are unique to one college.

Canvas layout: - A grid. Rows are colleges (up to 10). Columns are requirement types: Platform (Common App or own application), Supplemental essays (count), Teacher recs (count), Counselor rec, Testing policy, Interview, Portfolio or audition, Special course requirement, Fee. - Each cell shows a short value ("2 essays," "Test-optional," "Required") on a colored background: gray for not required, blue for required and shared by most colleges on the list, gold for required and unique to that college. - A totals row at the bottom: total supplemental essays, number of colleges needing a counselor rec, and so on. - A summary line: "Your list requires X supplemental essays and Y teacher letters. Z requirements are unique to one college."

Default data: Priya's ten-college list from Chapter 3 with fictional but realistic requirements (for example, the state flagship uses its own application with one short answer and no recs; Hillcrest uses the Common App with one supplement and two teacher letters; one reach requires an optional interview; one target requires a graded writing sample, marked gold).

Controls (all created in setup() before positioning): - createButton "Add college," which opens a row of createSelect and createInput controls for each column. - createButton "Edit selected" and "Remove selected" for the clicked row. - createCheckbox "Highlight unique requirements only," which dims shared cells. - createButton "Load Priya's list."

Interaction: Hovering a cell shows a tooltip explaining the requirement type ("Test-optional: you choose whether to send scores; see Chapter 6"). Clicking a column header sorts rows by that column. Unique (gold) cells pulse once when the list changes, so new unique requirements are noticed.

Color scheme: gray not required, blue shared, gold unique; selected row outlined.

Responsive behavior: Call updateCanvasSize() first in setup(); on narrow screens the grid becomes one card per college with requirement chips, and controls reposition on resize.

Implementation: p5.js with createButton, createSelect, createInput, and createCheckbox; canvas parented to the main element.

docs.title: Worked Example: Finding the Unique Requirement
docs.text:
Priya fills in her requirements matrix for all ten colleges. Most columns look similar: eight colleges use the Common App, most want two teacher letters, and all ten are test-optional. But one cell stands out in gold. One of her target colleges asks applicants to submit a graded analytical paper from a high school class, with the teacher's comments. It's mentioned only on that college's own "first-year requirements" page, not on its Common App page.

Because she found it in September, Priya has time to pick her best AP U.S. History paper, ask her teacher whether she can submit it, and scan it into her files. If she'd found it the week of the deadline, she might not have had a graded paper on hand at all.

docs.title: The Filing System
docs.text:
A filing system is an organized set of folders, digital, paper, or both, where every document in your application process has a known place. You'll create and receive dozens of documents this year: transcripts, score reports, essay drafts, recommendation requests, financial forms, confirmation emails, and award letters. Without a system, finding the right one in a hurry becomes a scavenger hunt.

A simple structure works best. Create one main folder with these subfolders:

  • Transcripts: unofficial copies for your own reference, and records of official transcript requests.
  • Test scores: score reports from the College Board or ACT.
  • Essays: your personal essay drafts, plus a subfolder for each college's supplements.
  • Activities: your activities resume and notes for the activities list.
  • Recommendations: the resume and notes you gave each recommender, and confirmations that letters were submitted.
  • Financial aid: tax documents and other paperwork for the FAFSA and CSS Profile, kept securely.
  • Colleges: one subfolder per college for its checklist, confirmation emails, portal screenshots, and decision letters.

Name files clearly so you can find them later, for example "Hillcrest_WhyHillcrest_v3.docx" rather than "essay final FINAL.docx."

docs.title: Worked Example: Finding a Document in Thirty Seconds
docs.text:
In early December, Marcus gets an email from Lakeshore University's portal: "We have not received your mid-year report or your counselor recommendation." He's sure his counselor sent them. In his "Colleges › Lakeshore" folder, he finds the screenshot he took on November 10 showing the counselor recommendation marked "received." He replies to the admissions office with the screenshot attached. An hour later, they confirm a matching error and fix it. (The mid-year report isn't due until February. The automated email was simply early.)

Without the filing system, Marcus would have spent his evening worrying and emailing his counselor. With it, he had proof in thirty seconds.

docs.title: The Digital Document Folder
docs.text: A digital document folder is the online version of your filing system, kept in a cloud storage service such as Google Drive, OneDrive, or iCloud so you can reach it from any device. Digital storage has three advantages over paper: you can search it, you can't lose it in a move, and you can upload directly from it to application portals. Back it up, keep it under your own account rather than a school account you'll lose after graduation, and share only specific subfolders with the people who need them, never the financial aid folder by default.

docs.title: Transcript Copies
docs.text: Transcript copies are unofficial copies of your high school transcript that you keep for your own use. Colleges need official transcripts, which your school sends directly. But you'll need an unofficial copy too, because many applications ask you to enter your own courses and grades, and you'll want to check them against the record. Ask your counselor or school office for an unofficial copy at the end of junior year, and again after fall grades come out in senior year. Save each one in your Transcripts folder, and check it for errors. Mistakes on transcripts happen, and it's much easier to fix one in September than in January.

docs.title: The Login Credentials Record
docs.text: A login credentials record is a secure, private record of every account you create during the process, including the site, your username, and your password. By spring you may have twenty or more accounts: the Common App, several college portals, the College Board, ACT, the FAFSA, the CSS Profile, and scholarship sites. You'll need to get back into many of them months after creating them. The safest option is a password manager, an app that stores passwords securely behind one master password. If you don't use one, keep a single document protected with a strong password, not a note on your phone and never your shared tracker. Use a different password for each account.

docs.title: The Dedicated Email Address
docs.text:
A dedicated email address is a personal email account you create just for the college process and use for every application, portal, testing account, and college you contact. It sounds like a small thing, but it matters more than nearly anything else you'll set up, because almost every important message in the process arrives by email: login links, missing-document notices, interview invitations, financial aid requests, and decisions.

A dedicated address solves three problems:

  • Nothing gets buried. College messages don't compete with social media notifications, store promotions, and group chats in your main inbox. When something arrives, you'll see it.
  • You keep access. Many students apply using their high school email, then lose access to it after graduation, often just when colleges send housing and orientation information. A personal account you control stays with you.
  • You look like an adult. Admissions officers see your email address. firstname.lastname@ reads better than a nickname you picked in middle school.

Set it up with a few habits in mind. Use a free provider and a simple, professional address that includes your name. Use the same address everywhere, since colleges match records partly by email. Check it at least every other day during application season, and daily from March through May. Set up filters or labels so messages from each college, testing agencies, and financial aid sort themselves. Check your spam folder weekly, since important college emails sometimes land there. Finally, consider sharing access or forwarding with a parent if your family agrees. Some families find that helpful. Others prefer that the student own it fully.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Missed Email
docs.text:
Ana's older cousin, Luis, applied to a university using his high school email account. In February, the university's financial aid office emailed to say his aid file was missing a tax form, with a two-week deadline. His school's email filter flagged the message as outside mail and sent it to a quarantine folder he didn't know existed. He found it a day after the deadline. The aid office still processed his file, but his grant offer came weeks later than his friends' offers, and some of the university's limited grant money had already been awarded.

Ana learned from Luis's experience. She created a dedicated address before opening any accounts, set up a "Colleges" label, and checks it every day. When a college asks her for something, she'll see it within hours.

docs.title: Applications and Accounts
docs.text: Every college application is completed through one of two kinds of system: a college's own application, or a shared platform used by many colleges. Most students use both, because their lists include colleges of both kinds.

docs.title: The Institutional Application
docs.text:
An institutional application is a college's own application form, completed on the college's website rather than through a shared platform. Many public universities use one, and some private colleges do too. Some colleges accept only their institutional application. The University of California system, MIT, and Georgetown, for example, don't accept the Common App. Others, like the University of Iowa, accept both, so you choose.

The term covers more than the form itself. In a sense, every application is institutional at heart. Even when you apply through a shared platform, each college sets its own deadlines, its own supplements, and its own requirements, and it makes its own decision. Shared platforms only bundle the parts many colleges have in common.

When a college offers both options, choosing between them is a real decision:

Consideration Institutional application Shared platform (Common App) Effort if it's your only college of this kind Often shorter and simpler More sections to complete Effort if you're already using the platform A separate set of forms to fill out Little extra work beyond any supplements Personal essay Sometimes not required Your Common App essay goes to every college you send it to Fees and waivers Set by the college Set by the college; fee waivers handled through the platform

Iowa shows the trade-off. Its own application requires no personal essay for general admission, while the Common App sends along the essay you wrote for other colleges. If Iowa is one of several colleges on your list and you already have an essay, the Common App is little extra work. If it's your only application, the institutional application is simpler.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Platforms, One List
docs.text:
Marcus's final list of ten includes eight colleges that accept the Common App, the in-state public university, which accepts both, and the nearby regional university, which uses only its own application. He decides:

  • Eight colleges → Common App. One set of core sections, one personal essay.
  • In-state public university → Common App too. He's already completing it, so adding the college takes minutes.
  • Regional university → its own application. It's short. He blocks out one evening for it in his tracker.

He records the platform for each college in his tracker. That way he won't open the Common App in December, wonder why the regional university isn't there, and panic.

docs.title: The Applicant Portal
docs.text:
An applicant portal is a personal online account a college creates for you after you apply, where you check your application status, see which documents have arrived, upload missing items, and eventually view your decision and financial aid. After you submit, each college typically emails you instructions to set up your portal login within a few days to a couple of weeks. That's one more reason the dedicated email matters.

Portals are where problems surface. A transcript that arrived but wasn't matched to your file, or a recommendation listed as missing, appears there long before anyone emails you about it, if anyone does. Make checking portals part of your routine. Look about a week after each submission and again after each supporting document deadline. Record every new portal login in your credentials record the day you create it.

docs.title: The Common App
docs.text:
The Common App (short for the Common Application) is a shared online application platform accepted by more than 1,000 colleges, including most private colleges and many public universities. You complete one set of core sections, covering your profile, family, education, testing, activities, and a personal essay, and send it to every member college on your list. Each college may then add its own questions and supplemental essays.

The main advantage is efficiency. Without it, you'd type your address, your parents' information, your activities, and your courses separately for every college. With it, you do that once. The Common App also lets your counselor and teachers upload their documents once for all your colleges, and it handles application fee waivers in one place.

A few facts about how it works:

  • It runs on a yearly cycle. The new application year opens on August 1, when that year's essay prompts and college-specific questions go live.
  • You can add up to 20 colleges. That's far more than most students need.
  • Each college sets its own rules. Deadlines, supplements, recommendation requirements, and testing policies all come from the college, not the Common App.
  • You'll see a separate list of requirements for each college. It shows that college's deadlines, supplements, and documents, the same information your requirements matrix collects.

The Common App isn't the only shared platform. Chapter 12 also covers the Coalition App, which some colleges accept, and gives a section-by-section walkthrough of the Common App itself. For now, the important step is the account.

docs.title: The Common App Account
docs.text:
Your Common App account is the personal login you create on the Common App website to complete and submit your applications. You can create it any time, including as a junior. Most of what you enter rolls over when the new application year begins on August 1, so starting early is safe. Creating it early has real benefits. The process starts to feel concrete, you can explore each college's requirements, and you can finish the long factual sections over the summer, leaving fall for essays.

When you create the account, get four details right from the start:

  1. Use your dedicated email address. Every Common App and college message will go there.
  2. Use your legal name, exactly as it appears on your school records, test registrations, and eventually financial aid forms. Mismatched names are a common cause of documents not being matched to your file. You can list a preferred name separately.
  3. Choose "first-year student" as your applicant type, unless you've already attended college after high school graduation.
  4. Record the login in your credentials record right away.

After that, add the colleges on your list and invite your counselor through the Education section. The Common App connects you with your counselor, and from there, to your teachers. Chapter 12 explains how recommenders are invited.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Summer Head Start
docs.text:
Priya creates her Common App account in June after junior year. Over July, she fills in the Profile, Family, and Education sections, using her unofficial transcript to enter her courses. She drafts her activities list from her activities resume. On August 1, the new year opens and her information carries over. She adds her eight Common App colleges, reads each one's requirements page, and copies every supplemental essay prompt into her tracker.

By mid-August, the only parts of her application left are essays and recommendations. While some of her classmates spend September typing addresses and course names, she spends it writing.

docs.title: The People Who Help
docs.text: You own your applications, but you shouldn't do them alone. Several people can help, and knowing what each one does keeps you from asking the wrong person or asking too late.

docs.title: The School Counselor
docs.text:
Your school counselor is the staff member at your high school who guides students through academic planning and college applications, and who represents your school to colleges. In the admissions process, the counselor does several things only they can do. They send your official transcript and school profile. They write the counselor recommendation and complete the school report, including the course-rigor rating from Chapter 2. They send your mid-year and final grades. They're also often the person who knows how students from your school have done at specific colleges in past years.

Counselors are often stretched thin. At many public high schools, one counselor works with several hundred students, and senior fall is their busiest time. That means two things for you. First, help them help you. Give them your list, your deadlines, and any information they'll need well ahead of time. Second, don't wait for them to come to you. Request a meeting yourself, early.

docs.title: Worked Example: Helping a Busy Counselor
docs.text:
Ana's high school has one counselor for about 400 students. Ana is first-generation, and her family doesn't know the process, so her counselor matters a lot to her. In May of junior year, she sends a short email asking for a meeting before summer. She attaches her draft college list and a one-page summary of her activities. At the meeting, the counselor tells her about a fee waiver she qualifies for, a fly-in program at one of her colleges, and a local community organization that helps first-generation students with essays.

In September, Ana shares her tracker with her counselor and sends a short reminder two weeks before her first deadline. Her counselor later mentions that Ana was one of the easiest students to write for, because she'd made it simple to know her.

docs.title: The Counselor Meeting
docs.text: A counselor meeting is a scheduled conversation with your school counselor to plan your applications. Ideally, you have one in spring of junior year and another early in senior fall. Come prepared. Bring your draft college list, your unofficial transcript, a list of questions, and your activities resume. Good questions include: Is my list balanced? How have students from our school done at these colleges? What do you need from me, and by when? How does our school handle transcript and recommendation requests? Take notes, and add any new dates to your tracker that day.

docs.title: Independent Counselors
docs.text: An independent counselor, also called an independent educational consultant, is a private admissions advisor a family hires and pays, separate from the school. Some are former admissions officers or school counselors. They can offer more individual time than a busy school counselor, but they typically charge anywhere from a few hundred dollars for a single consultation to several thousand for full support. You don't need one to apply successfully. This book, your school counselor, and free resources cover the process. Many community organizations and nonprofit programs offer free counseling, especially for first-generation and low-income students. If your family does hire one, check credentials and references, and be wary of anyone who promises admission to specific colleges. An independent counselor never replaces your school counselor, who still sends your official documents.

docs.title: The Parent and Family Role
docs.text:
The parent and family role is the part that parents, guardians, and other family members play in the process: supporting, informing, and helping with specific tasks, while the student leads. Families matter most in three areas. The first is money. Parents usually complete parts of the financial aid forms and are central to the conversation about what the family can afford. The second is logistics, such as visits, deadlines, and paperwork. The third is encouragement through a long, uncertain year.

The hardest part is balance. Too little family involvement can leave a student alone with a complicated process, especially if no one has done it before. Too much can take the process away from the student. Essays written by parents tend to sound like parents, and admissions readers can tell. A useful division looks like this:

Task Student leads Family supports Building the college list Researches, decides, explains choices Shares cost limits, asks questions, joins visits Applications and essays Writes everything, meets deadlines Reads drafts if asked, offers general feedback Deadlines Owns the tracker Checks the shared tracker, flags problems Financial aid Learns the process, completes student sections Provides financial information, completes parent sections Final decision Makes the choice Helps compare costs and offers

Families who've never done this, or who are new to the U.S. education system, have just as important a role. Their job isn't to know the process. It's to support the student in learning it, to show up for the money conversation, and to help with the forms only they can complete. Many colleges and community organizations offer financial aid workshops for families, often in several languages.

docs.title: Worked Example: Dividing the Work
docs.text:
Ana and her parents sit down in August to divide the work. Ana's mother doesn't know the application process, but she manages the family's paperwork. Her father works evenings and can't attend events, but wants to help.

They agree on three things. Ana owns her tracker and applications and shares the tracker with her mother. Her mother gathers the tax documents for the FAFSA by October and attends a free financial aid workshop at Ana's school. Her father reads Ana's essays on Sunday mornings when she asks him to, and tells her whether they sound like her. Each person's role fits what they can actually do, and none of them is pretending to be an expert.

docs.title: The Summer Before Senior Year
docs.text: The summer before senior year is the stretch between the end of junior year and the start of senior year, the last long block of free time before deadlines begin. Use it for the tasks that take time but not urgency. Finalize your college list, visit nearby campuses, create your Common App account and fill in its factual sections, build your activities resume, draft your personal essay, and decide whether to take or retake a standardized test in the fall. Students who use the summer well start senior year with essays in progress. Students who don't start it with everything at once. You don't need to work every day. A few hours a week adds up.

docs.title: The Senior Year Calendar
docs.text:
The senior year calendar is the month-by-month sequence of admissions tasks from the start of senior year through May 1, built from the shared admissions timeline in Chapter 1 and your own application rounds. Its overall shape is the same for nearly everyone:

  • August–September: Finish your list, open the Common App, ask for recommendations, write essays.
  • October: Test if you're testing, file the FAFSA once it opens, finish early applications.
  • November: Submit early applications, then turn to regular-round essays.
  • December: Early decisions arrive. Finish regular applications.
  • January–February: Submit the remaining applications, send mid-year grades, apply for scholarships.
  • March–April: Decisions and aid offers arrive. Compare and decide.
  • May 1: Commit to one college.

Your personal calendar shifts with your rounds. An Early Decision applicant's fall is busier, and a Regular Decision applicant's winter is. Chapter 1's Senior Year Admissions Timeline shows both, and the Month-by-Month Planner in Chapter 20 turns this outline into a detailed checklist.

docs.title: Five First Steps
docs.text:
The five first steps are five concrete tasks that start the process and set up its foundations. You can do all of them in a week, even before your list is final:

  1. Set up a shared tracker. Create the spreadsheet, add the colleges you're considering, and share it with a parent or guardian.
  2. Create your Common App account, using your dedicated email address and legal name. Create the email first if you haven't already.
  3. Ask two teachers for recommendations. Teachers get many requests in the fall, and asking early gets you a better letter, not just a faster one. Chapter 11 covers whom to ask and how.
  4. Draft an activities resume. List your jobs, clubs, sports, volunteering, and family responsibilities. You'll use it for the Common App, for your recommenders, and for essay ideas. Chapter 8 covers it in detail.
  5. Start a running list of essay material. Keep a note on your phone for moments, stories, and details as they occur to you. The best essay material often shows up when you're not trying to write.

The checklist below tracks your progress on these five steps and the setup tasks from this chapter.

docs.title: Diagram: Getting Organized Setup Checklist
docs.text:
Getting Organized Setup Checklist

Type: microsim sim-id: organized-setup-checklist Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Give students an interactive checklist of the five first steps and the chapter's setup tasks, showing progress and explaining why each task matters.

Bloom Level: Apply (L3) Bloom Verb: implement, carry out Learning Objective: Students will carry out the five first steps and the core setup tasks of getting organized, tracking their progress toward a complete organizational system.

Canvas layout: - Top: a circular progress ring showing tasks completed out of the total, with the percentage in the center. - Middle: two groups of tasks with createCheckbox controls: - "Five First Steps": Shared tracker set up; Common App account created; Two teachers asked; Activities resume drafted; Essay-material list started. - "Foundations": Dedicated email created; Login credentials record set up; Digital document folder created with subfolders; Unofficial transcript saved; Calendar reminders set for first deadlines; Counselor meeting scheduled; Family roles discussed. - Right side (below on narrow screens): an infobox that shows, for the most recently hovered or clicked task, one sentence on why it matters and which chapter covers it.

Order dependencies (shown as small lock icons that open when the prerequisite is checked): "Common App account created" shows a hint "Create your dedicated email first" until the email task is checked, though it can still be checked. "Calendar reminders set" shows a hint to set up the tracker first.

Controls (all created in setup() before positioning): createCheckbox for each task; createButton "Reset"; createButton "Show me what's next," which highlights the first unchecked task in gold.

Completion: When all tasks are checked, the ring turns green and a message reads "Your systems are in place. Next: testing decisions in Chapter 6."

Persistence: Use localStorage (wrapped in try/catch) to remember the checked state for the viewer, so the checklist survives a page reload; render correctly if storage is unavailable.

Responsive behavior: Call updateCanvasSize() first in setup(); task groups stack on narrow screens and controls reposition on resize.

Implementation: p5.js with createCheckbox and createButton; canvas parented to the main element.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Getting organized rests on one source of truth, visibility to your helpers, and early buffers. One afternoon of setup prevents most dropped threads.
  • A deadline tracker lists every college's dates and requirements. A shared tracker lets a parent or counselor catch problems. Calendar reminders bring deadlines to you. Track supporting document deadlines and priority deadlines as real deadlines.
  • Keep an application checklist for each college, and capture college-specific requirements from the college's own website.
  • A filing system in a digital document folder gives every document a home. Keep transcript copies and a private login credentials record, never in the shared tracker.
  • A dedicated email address that you control and check often is the single most important account you'll create.
  • Colleges use an institutional application, the Common App, or both. After you apply, each college's applicant portal shows what's missing.
  • Create your Common App account early, with your dedicated email and legal name. Your information rolls over on August 1.
  • Your school counselor sends key documents and knows your school's history. Prepare for each counselor meeting. An independent counselor is optional. Your family's role is to support while you lead.
  • Use the summer before senior year for slow tasks, and follow the senior year calendar. Start with the five first steps this week.

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
Why should you avoid using your high school email address for college applications?

You'll likely lose access after graduation, often just as colleges send housing and orientation information. School filters may also block or quarantine college emails. A dedicated personal address avoids both problems.

A college lists a 'priority deadline' of December 1 for merit scholarships and a regular deadline of January 15. You apply January 10. What's the risk?

You'll still be considered for admission, but you may be considered for merit scholarships only from whatever money is left, or not at all. Priority deadlines should be treated as real deadlines.

Your Common App shows eight colleges, but your final list has ten. What's the most likely explanation, and where should you check?

The other two probably use their own institutional applications. Check your tracker's platform column and each college's admissions website.

Where should you store your applicant portal passwords, and where should you never store them?

In a password manager or a single secure, private document, your login credentials record. Never in your shared tracker, which other people can see.

Name two things only your school counselor can do in the application process.

Any two of: send your official transcript and school profile; complete the school report and counselor recommendation, including the course-rigor rating; send mid-year and final grades.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers deciding whether and where to submit SAT or ACT scores under test-optional, test-required, and test-blind policies, with superscoring, retesting, registration, and free, effective prep. It replaces guesswork about testing with a clear decision rule. Students finish able to compare their scores against each school's range and plan any retest with free resources.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
  • Chapter 2: How Colleges Evaluate Applicants

docs.title: A Question With a Different Answer for Each College
docs.text:
Testing used to be simple. Nearly every four-year college required the SAT or ACT, so nearly every applicant took one and sent the score everywhere. That's no longer true. Today, some colleges require scores, many let you decide whether to send them, and a few won't look at them at all. The same score can help you at one college on your list and hurt you at another.

That makes testing less a single decision than a series of small ones. Should you take a test at all? Which one? How do you read the score you got? Is it worth taking again? And for each college on your list, should you send it? This chapter gives you a clear way to answer each question.

You'll start with what standardized tests are and the three testing policies colleges use. Then you'll learn how the SAT and ACT are built and scored, and how to compare scores across the two. The heart of the chapter is a decision rule: compare your score with each college's range, then decide college by college whether to submit. The chapter ends with the practical side, including score reports, registration, test dates, and how to prepare well without paying for expensive tutoring.

Testing policies and test formats change often. The details here reflect the tests as they are given in the mid-2020s. Before you register or decide, check the College Board and ACT websites and each college's admissions page for current rules.

docs.title: Standardized Testing
docs.text:
Standardized testing means giving every test-taker the same kind of test, under the same conditions, scored the same way, so results can be compared fairly across students from different schools. In college admissions, the term refers mainly to two tests: the SAT and the ACT.

Colleges use standardized tests because grades aren't standardized. As Chapter 2 showed, an A at one high school may not mean the same thing as an A at another, and GPA scales differ. A test score, by contrast, means the same thing whether you took the test in Iowa or Florida. That gives admissions readers one common measure to set beside a transcript they're still learning to interpret.

Tests have real limits, though. A score reflects one morning, not four years. Scores tend to rise with family income, partly because wealthier families can pay for tutoring and repeat attempts. And for many students, grades in challenging courses predict college success at least as well as a test does. Those concerns are why so many colleges stopped requiring scores around 2020, and why the debate continues. Some colleges have since brought requirements back, arguing that scores help them find talented students at less-known high schools.

For you, the practical takeaways are simple:

  • Scores are one factor among several. At almost every college, your academic record outweighs your test score.
  • Scores can still matter a lot. At test-required colleges, for merit scholarships, and in formulas like Iowa's Regent Admission Index, a score can change an outcome.
  • The decision is yours more often than it used to be. That makes it worth understanding, not guessing.

docs.title: Worked Example: What a Score Adds to a File
docs.text:
A reader at a selective college is looking at two applicants from high schools the reader doesn't know well. Both have 3.8 GPAs with strong rigor.

  • Applicant 1 submitted a 1450 SAT. The reader now has an outside measure that confirms the transcript. The 3.8 at an unfamiliar school is backed by a score near the top of the college's range.
  • Applicant 2 submitted no score. The reader relies on the transcript, the school profile, the counselor's rigor rating, and teacher letters. These can show academic strength just as clearly. They just do it differently.

Neither applicant is penalized. But the example shows what a strong score does: it adds a piece of evidence that's easy to compare. That's also why a weak score can hurt. It adds evidence that points the other way.

docs.title: Testing Policies
docs.text: Every college sets a testing policy, its rule about whether applicants must submit test scores and how they'll be used. There are three main types, and the colleges on a single list often use all three.

docs.title: Test-Required Policy
docs.text:
A test-required policy means a college requires every applicant to submit an SAT or ACT score. An application without one is incomplete and won't be reviewed. Before 2020, this was the norm. Many colleges then went test-optional, and a number of them have since gone back to requiring scores. Highly selective private colleges such as MIT, Dartmouth, and Harvard require them, as do the public university systems of a few states, including Florida and Georgia. A few colleges, such as Purdue, call themselves test-expected: they ask every applicant for a score and accept an application without one only in exceptional cases. For planning purposes, treat test-expected as test-required.

At a test-required college, the submission decision is made for you. You must send a score, so the question becomes how to make that score as strong as you reasonably can, and whether to retest. Some test-required colleges also accept other exams in place of the SAT or ACT, such as AP or IB scores. Read the policy closely, because it may be more flexible than the headline suggests.

docs.title: Test-Optional Policy
docs.text:
A test-optional policy means applicants choose whether to submit test scores. If you submit, the college considers your score. If you don't, the college reviews your application fully without it, and says it won't hold the missing score against you. Most four-year colleges today are test-optional. The University of Iowa is one.

Test-optional policies have fine print worth reading:

  • Scholarships may still use scores. At Iowa, scores at or above about a 26 ACT or 1230 SAT open access to larger merit scholarships, even though admission doesn't require a test.
  • Some programs may require scores even when the college as a whole doesn't, for example honors colleges, nursing, or engineering.
  • Some applicants may need scores, such as homeschooled students or applicants from schools without traditional grades.
  • Formulas may change how you're reviewed. Iowa's Regent Admission Index needs a test score to calculate. Applicants who apply without one can still be admitted, but they're reviewed individually instead of by formula.

So "test-optional" really means "optional for admission, under the rules on this college's page." Check each college's own wording.

docs.title: Test-Blind Policy
docs.text:
A test-blind policy means a college won't consider SAT or ACT scores for admission at all, even if you send them. It's rarer than test-optional. The University of California and California State University systems are the best-known examples. At a test-blind college, the decision is simple: don't bother sending scores for admission. Some test-blind colleges still use scores after enrollment, for example to place students in the right first math or writing class, so check whether they ask for scores once you've committed.

The table below summarizes the three policies covered in the sections above.

Policy Must you submit? Will the college look at a score you send? Your decision Test-required Yes Yes Make your score as strong as you reasonably can Test-optional No Yes Compare your score with the college's range, then decide Test-blind No No (for admission) Don't send scores for admission

docs.title: Worked Example: One List, Three Policies
docs.text:
Priya checks the testing policy for every college on her ten-school list and records it in her tracker:

  • College A, her top reach, is test-required. She must send a score no matter what.
  • Seven colleges, including College B, College C, Hillcrest, and her state flagship, are test-optional.
  • One college in California is test-blind. She won't send anything there.
  • One test-optional college offers merit scholarships with a published score cutoff. She marks it, because a score could be worth money there even if it doesn't affect admission.

Before checking, Priya had assumed she'd either send her score everywhere or nowhere. Now she sees that she has one required decision, seven real choices, one non-decision, and one scholarship question. The rest of this chapter shows how she makes each choice.

docs.title: The Test-Optional Myth
docs.text: The test-optional myth is the belief that "test-optional" means test scores no longer matter. In reality, test-optional means you get to choose whether a score is part of your application. A strong score that you submit can still help. A weak one you leave off won't hurt you. Scores can also still matter for merit scholarships, specific programs, and colleges that have gone back to requiring them. Students who believe the myth often skip testing entirely and then discover a scholarship cutoff or a test-required college too late to test. A better approach for most students is to take the test at least once, then decide school by school what to do with the score.

docs.title: The SAT and the ACT
docs.text: The SAT and the ACT are the two standardized tests used for U.S. college admissions. Every college that accepts one accepts the other, and none prefers one over the other. So the choice between them is about which test suits you better.

docs.title: The SAT
docs.text:
The SAT is a standardized college admissions test made by the College Board. Since 2024 it has been given digitally, in the College Board's Bluebook app on a laptop or tablet. It has two sections:

  • Reading and Writing: short passages, each followed by one question, testing reading comprehension, vocabulary in context, grammar, and editing.
  • Math: algebra, advanced math, problem solving and data analysis, and geometry and trigonometry. A graphing calculator is built into the app and allowed for the whole section.

Each section is scored from 200 to 800, for a total of 400 to 1600. The test takes a little over two hours. It's adaptive by section. Each section has two parts, called modules, and how you do on the first module determines whether the second is harder or easier. That's why you can't compare raw question counts between students. The scoring accounts for difficulty.

docs.title: The ACT
docs.text:
The ACT is a standardized college admissions test made by ACT, Inc. It's given on paper or online, depending on the test center. Its core sections are:

  • English: grammar, punctuation, and editing of passages.
  • Math: algebra, geometry, and some trigonometry, with a calculator allowed throughout.
  • Reading: comprehension of longer passages.
  • Science (optional): interpreting data, graphs, and experiments. Science reasoning, not memorized facts.

Each section is scored from 1 to 36. Since 2025, Science has been optional, and the composite score is based on English, Math, and Reading. An optional writing test is also available, though few colleges ask for it. The core ACT takes about two hours, or longer with Science.

docs.title: Choosing Between Them
docs.text:
Because colleges treat the two tests equally, choose the one that fits you. The tests reward slightly different strengths:

Feature SAT ACT Format Digital, adaptive by section Paper or online, not adaptive Sections Reading and Writing, Math English, Math, Reading, optional Science Score range 400–1600 (two sections, 200–800 each) 1–36 composite (each section 1–36) Pace More time per question Faster; more questions in less time Math share About half the score About one-third of the composite Reading style Short passages, one question each Longer passages, several questions each

The best way to choose is to take a free official practice test of each under timed conditions and compare the results using the concordance tables later in this chapter. If your scores are about the same, pick the test whose format you found more comfortable.

docs.title: Worked Example: Choosing a Test
docs.text:
Marcus takes one official practice SAT and one official practice ACT on two Saturdays in the spring of junior year:

  • SAT practice: 1310 (Reading and Writing 610, Math 700).
  • ACT practice: 26 composite. He ran out of time on Reading and left six questions blank.

Using the concordance table, his 1310 SAT is about equal to a 28 ACT, so his SAT result is about two points stronger. The reason is pace. The ACT's faster timing cost him on Reading, while the SAT's math-heavy scoring rewarded his strength. Marcus chooses the SAT and focuses his prep there.

docs.title: The PSAT/NMSQT
docs.text: The PSAT/NMSQT (Preliminary SAT/National Merit Scholarship Qualifying Test) is a practice version of the SAT, usually taken at school in October of 10th or 11th grade. It uses the same digital format and question types as the SAT, scored from 320 to 1520. It doesn't go to colleges, so a low score costs you nothing. Two things make it worth taking seriously. First, it's a free diagnostic. Your score report shows your strengths and weaknesses and links to free practice. Second, in 11th grade only, high scorers can qualify for recognition and scholarships through the National Merit Scholarship Program. The cutoffs vary by state.

docs.title: Section Scores
docs.text:
Section scores are the scores you earn on each separate part of a test: Reading and Writing and Math on the SAT, and English, Math, Reading, and the optional Science section on the ACT. They show where your strengths are, which a single total can hide.

Section scores matter for three reasons. First, they guide your prep. A 1200 SAT made up of 700 Reading and Writing and 500 Math calls for a very different plan than one made up of 600 and 600. Second, some colleges and programs look at them directly. An engineering program may care more about your Math score than your total. Third, they're the building blocks of superscoring, which combines your best section scores across test dates, as you'll see later.

docs.title: Composite Score
docs.text:
A composite score is the single overall score that combines your section scores. On the SAT it's called the total score, and it's the sum of your two section scores:

\[ \text{SAT total} = \text{Reading and Writing} + \text{Math} \]

On the ACT, the composite is the average of the core section scores, rounded to the nearest whole number:

\[ \text{ACT composite} = \frac{\text{English} + \text{Math} + \text{Reading}}{3} \]

Colleges report their score ranges using composite scores, so the composite is the number you'll compare against each college. When people say "I got a 1350" or "I got a 29," they mean the composite.

docs.title: Worked Example: Calculating Composites
docs.text:
Priya's June SAT section scores were Reading and Writing 680 and Math 600:

\[ \text{SAT total} = 680 + 600 = 1280 \]

Casey's ACT section scores were English 25, Math 22, and Reading 26:

\[ \text{ACT composite} = \frac{25 + 22 + 26}{3} = \frac{73}{3} \approx 24.3 \rightarrow 24 \]

Both composites hide a pattern. Priya's Math score is 80 points below her Reading and Writing score, and Casey's Math is three or four points below the other sections. For both students, math is where extra prep would most likely raise the composite.

docs.title: SAT-ACT Concordance
docs.text:
SAT-ACT concordance is the official way of matching an SAT score to the ACT score that represents about the same level of performance. The College Board and ACT publish joint concordance tables, built from students who took both tests. Concordance matters because colleges often report only one test's range, or because you took the other test. To compare your score with a college's range, you sometimes need to convert it.

Here's a selection of values from the official tables. Each ACT composite corresponds to a short range of SAT totals.

ACT composite Equivalent SAT total range 36 1570–1600 34 1490–1520 32 1420–1440 30 1360–1380 28 1300–1320 27 1260–1290 26 1230–1250 25 1200–1220 24 1160–1190 22 1100–1120 20 1030–1050 18 960–980

Two cautions. Concordance is approximate, since the tests measure slightly different things. And because the ranges are short, a one-point difference in ACT terms is often within the normal variation from one test day to another. Use concordance to place your score, not to split hairs.

docs.title: Worked Example: Converting a Score
docs.text: Casey's 24 ACT concords to an SAT total between 1160 and 1190. A college Casey is considering reports only SAT ranges, with a middle 50% of 1100–1280. Casey's converted score falls inside the range, a little below the midpoint. Iowa's merit threshold works the other way. It's stated as a 26 ACT or 1230 SAT, and Casey's 24 is two composite points short. That gap will matter when Casey decides whether to retest. The converter below lets you translate any score.

docs.title: Score Benchmark Comparison
docs.text:
A score benchmark comparison is the step of placing your composite score against a college's middle 50% range, which you learned to read in Chapter 2, to see whether the score is likely to help or hurt your application there. It's the core of every test-optional decision.

To make one, you need two things for each college: your composite score, converted if necessary, and the college's 25th and 75th percentile scores, usually from its Common Data Set (Section C9) or admissions website. Colleges don't usually publish the 50th percentile, the median, so estimate it as the midpoint of the range. A college with a middle 50% SAT range of 1220–1390 has an estimated midpoint of about 1305.

Your score then falls into one of three zones:

  • At or above the midpoint: your score is a strength at this college.
  • Below the 25th percentile: your score is weaker than at least three-quarters of the students in the range, so it's more likely to hurt than help.
  • Between the 25th percentile and the midpoint: a gray zone where other factors decide.

Remember Chapter 2's caution: at test-optional colleges, published ranges include only students who chose to submit, and those tend to be the higher scorers. That pushes the range up. A score slightly below a test-optional college's midpoint may be closer to typical among all admitted students than it looks.

docs.title: The Score Submission Decision
docs.text:
The score submission decision is your choice, made separately for each test-optional college, about whether to send your test score. The benchmark comparison gives you a starting rule:

  • At or above the midpoint → submit. Your score strengthens your application.
  • Below the 25th percentile → don't submit. Your application will be read fully without it.
  • In between → it's a judgment call. Lean toward submitting if the score is close to the midpoint, or if the rest of your record is ordinary and the score adds strength. Lean toward withholding if your GPA and rigor are strong and the score sits near the 25th percentile, so it would undercut an otherwise strong academic record.

Three other factors can override the rule:

  • Merit scholarships. If a college awards scholarships by score cutoff and your score clears it, submit, even if the score is only average for admission.
  • Program requirements. If your intended program requires scores, you must submit.
  • Formula-based admission. Where a formula like Iowa's RAI uses the score, run the formula both ways and submit if the score raises your result.

Make the decision college by college, not once for your whole list. Students often submit everywhere or nowhere, which almost guarantees sending a weak score somewhere or withholding a strong one somewhere else.

docs.title: Worked Example: Priya Decides College by College
docs.text:
Priya's SAT is 1280. Here's her comparison for five of her colleges:

College Policy Middle 50% SAT Estimated midpoint Where 1280 falls Decision College A Test-required 1500–1560 1530 Well below 25th Must submit; consider retesting College B Test-optional 1350–1480 1415 Below 25th Don't submit College C Test-optional 1220–1390 1305 Between 25th and midpoint Judgment call State flagship Test-optional 1150–1320 1235 Above midpoint Submit Merit-cutoff college Test-optional 1180–1350 1265 Above midpoint; clears 1250 scholarship cutoff Submit (admission and money)

For College C, Priya weighs her record. Her 3.71 GPA sits inside College C's range, and her course rigor is strong, but her score is 25 points below the estimated midpoint. Her counselor points out that College C is test-optional, so its published range is probably inflated. Priya decides to submit if a retest raises her score and to withhold it otherwise. That leads straight to the next question, whether to retest. The planner below runs this kind of comparison for your whole list.

docs.title: The Retesting Decision
docs.text:
The retesting decision is the choice of whether to take the SAT or ACT again to try to raise your score. Retest when three things are true: your score is below the level that matters for at least one important college or scholarship; you have a specific way to improve, such as a weak section you can study for; and there's time for another test date before your deadlines. If all three hold, a retest is usually worth it. Most students improve somewhat on a second attempt, especially after focused prep.

Don't retest endlessly, though. Two sittings are enough for most students. A third makes sense only if something specific changed, like a new prep plan or a first test disrupted by illness. Beyond that, the gains shrink, and the time is usually better spent on essays and grades.

docs.title: Superscoring
docs.text: Superscoring is a college policy of combining your highest section scores from different test dates into a new, higher composite. If you took the SAT twice and scored higher in Math the second time but higher in Reading and Writing the first time, a college that superscores uses the best of each. For the ACT, superscoring averages your best English, Math, and Reading scores across dates. Many colleges superscore, but not all, so check each college's policy. Superscoring makes retesting more attractive, because you can focus prep on one section without worrying that another will slip.

docs.title: Worked Example: Priya's Retest and Superscore
docs.text:
Priya's June SAT was Reading and Writing 680, Math 600, for a total of 1280. She meets the three retest conditions. College C is a judgment call and College A requires a score. Her Math section is clearly weaker. And there's an October test date before her November and January deadlines. She spends eight weeks on math prep and retests in October:

Test date Reading and Writing Math Total June 680 600 1280 October 660 650 1310 Superscore 680 650 1330

Her October total, 1310, is a modest gain, because her Reading and Writing score dipped. But at colleges that superscore, her score is now 1330. That's above College C's estimated midpoint of 1305, so she'll submit there. College B's 25th percentile is 1350, still above her superscore, so she still won't submit there. The calculator below lets you try your own test dates.
