Implementation: Chart.js bubble chart with a custom plugin for the shaded depth zone.

docs.title: Measurable Impact
docs.text:
Measurable impact is a result of your activity that can be counted, described specifically, or seen, such as money raised, people served, members recruited, events run, products built, or problems solved. It answers the reader's most important question about any activity: What difference did you make?

Numbers are the clearest way to show impact, because they're specific and quick to read: "raised $3,000," "tutored 12 students weekly," "grew membership from 8 to 30." But not all impact is numerical. "Wrote the code that lets the robot navigate on its own" or "designed the poster now used for every school play" are specific and visible without a number.

Two cautions. First, impact must be honest. Don't take credit for a team's result as if it were yours alone. Say "led the team that..." or "helped raise..." when that's what happened. Second, don't force numbers where they don't fit. "Practiced piano 400 hours" is less meaningful than "performed a solo recital of Chopin for 80 people." Choose the detail that best shows what changed.

docs.title: Worked Example: From Vague to Measurable
docs.text:
Applicant B from Chapter 2 volunteers at a community bike shop. Here's how the description improves draft by draft:

  1. "Volunteer at bike shop." This says what, but not what they did or what difference it made.
  2. "Repair bikes for community members at local bike shop." Better, but there's no scale or result.
  3. "Repair and refurbish donated bikes; now help run Saturday shop; about 150 bikes given to kids each year." This one shows a growing role and a result anyone can picture.

The third version uses about the same space as the second, but a reader now knows the activity's scale and the applicant's role in it.

docs.title: Community Service
docs.text:
Community service is unpaid work that benefits other people or your community, such as tutoring, food banks, hospital volunteering, environmental cleanups, animal shelters, or helping at a place of worship. Colleges value it as evidence that you care about people beyond yourself.

What makes service strong on an application is the same as for any activity: commitment and impact, not the number of organizations or a large total of one-time hours. A student who volunteers at the same food pantry every Saturday for three years and now trains new volunteers shows more than one who logged a hundred hours across ten different one-day events. Service connected to your interests also reads well, such as a future nurse volunteering at a clinic or a future teacher tutoring younger students.

Be cautious about expensive "voluntourism" trips, short paid trips to volunteer abroad. Readers often see them as experiences purchased rather than commitments made. Service close to home, sustained over time, usually says more. If you did go on such a trip, describe what you actually did and learned, without exaggerating your impact.

docs.title: Worked Example: Describing Service
docs.text:
Ana helps at her church's food pantry most Saturdays. Her first draft says "Volunteer at food pantry." After thinking about what she actually does, she writes:

  • Organization: St. Luke's Community Food Pantry
  • Description: Sort donations and pack about 60 family boxes each Saturday; translate for Spanish-speaking families at intake; 3 years.

The translation detail matters. It's a skill she brings that other volunteers don't, and it connects to her family responsibilities, which reinforces a theme in her application.

docs.title: Part-Time Jobs
docs.text:
A part-time job is paid work you do during the school year, summers, or both, whether for a business, a family business, or yourself, such as babysitting, lawn care, or tutoring. Many students leave jobs off or list them last because a job doesn't seem as impressive as a club. That's a mistake. Readers know that a job means showing up on time, handling customers, being trusted with money or safety, and managing a schedule around school. Fifteen hours a week at a grocery store is real commitment, and readers recognize it.

Jobs matter even more when they're part of your family's finances. If you work to help pay bills or save for college, that's important context, and you can say so briefly in the description or in the additional information section. A reader who knows you work twenty hours a week to support your family reads the rest of your application differently. They don't expect a long list of clubs from a student who has no time for them.

When you describe a job, include the responsibilities that grew over time, such as training others, handling the register, opening or closing, or supervising. Those are your leadership.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Grocery Store Job
docs.text:
Sam works at a grocery store: 15 hours a week during the school year and 25 hours a week in summer. Sam's first draft says "Cashier at FreshMart." The revised entry reads:

  • Position: Cashier, then front-end trainer
  • Organization: FreshMart Grocery
  • Description: Promoted to trainer after 1 year; train new cashiers on register and customer service; close store 2 nights/wk; save earnings for college.

A reader now sees reliability, a promotion, responsibility for others, and a purpose. Together, those are more convincing evidence of maturity than many club titles.

docs.title: Family Responsibilities
docs.text:
Family responsibilities are regular duties you carry out for your family that take significant time, such as caring for younger siblings or a relative, cooking, translating for family members, managing household tasks, or working in a family business. They're legitimate, valuable activities, and the Common App includes "Family responsibilities" as an activity type. If they're part of your life, list them plainly and without apology.

Students often hesitate because family duties feel private, or because they don't seem like "achievements." But readers are trained to see them as exactly what they are: evidence of responsibility, maturity, and time commitment. They also explain things. A student who spends twenty hours a week caring for siblings can't also be in five clubs, and a reader who sees the family responsibility understands why the list is short.

Describe what you do, how often, and what it involves. You don't need to explain why your family needs your help unless you want to. If there's important context, such as a parent's illness or a family financial crisis, the additional information section is the place for a brief, factual note.

docs.title: Worked Example: Listing Family Duties
docs.text:
Ana lists her family responsibilities as two separate entries, because they're different kinds of work:

  1. Family responsibilities: sibling care. "Pick up 2 younger brothers daily; supervise homework; cook dinner 3 nights/wk while parents work." 15 hours a week, 40 weeks, grades 9–12.
  2. Family responsibilities: translation. "Translate for parents at medical, school, and bank appointments; help complete forms in English." 3 hours a week, 52 weeks, grades 9–12.

Together, these two entries account for eighteen hours of Ana's week and show four years of sustained responsibility. They're among the strongest entries on her list.

docs.title: Summer Experiences
docs.text:
Summer experiences are the ways you spend your summers, such as jobs, academic programs, internships, research, camps, travel, caring for family, independent projects, or simply working more hours at an activity you already do. Colleges look at summers because summers are mostly unstructured time. How you use them shows what you choose to do when no one is scheduling your day.

A common misconception is that impressive summers require expensive programs. Readers know that many prestigious-sounding summer programs simply admit anyone who can pay, and they don't weigh them heavily. A summer job, a free program at a local college, a self-directed project, or more time with family responsibilities can be just as meaningful. What matters is what you did and what came of it.

On the Common App, a summer activity can be its own entry, with the timing marked as "school break," or it can be folded into a year-round activity if it continues one you already do.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Low-Cost Summer
docs.text:
Marcus couldn't afford a paid summer coding camp. Instead, he spent the summer before senior year working more restaurant shifts and, in the evenings, building a small app that lets his family's restaurant take pickup orders by text. He used free online tutorials and spent about 8 hours a week on it for 10 weeks.

He lists it as its own activity: "Built text-message ordering app for family restaurant using free tutorials; now handles about 30 pickup orders a week." The entry is more distinctive than a camp certificate would have been, and it gives him a ready story for a supplemental essay about his interest in computer science.

docs.title: Personal Interests
docs.text:
Personal interests are activities you pursue on your own because you enjoy them, outside any organization: teaching yourself an instrument, writing fiction, building furniture, cooking, coding, running a YouTube channel, birdwatching, restoring a car. They count. The Common App doesn't require an activity to be school-sponsored, and some of the most memorable entries are things no one asked a student to do.

Personal interests are especially valuable because they're self-directed. Nobody signed you up or graded you, so they show genuine curiosity and initiative. A personal interest belongs on your list when you've spent real, regular time on it and can describe something specific: what you've made, learned, or done. "Like to read" is too thin. "Read and review about 40 books a year on my book blog, 200 subscribers" is an activity.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Hobby That Counts
docs.text:
Priya has baked bread since 9th grade. She thought of it as just a hobby until her counselor asked how much time she spends on it. The answer: about 4 hours a week, and she now bakes for her family, sells loaves at a farmers market stand once a month in summer, and has taught three friends to make sourdough.

Her entry reads: "Self-taught sourdough baker; sell loaves at monthly summer farmers market; taught 3 friends." It adds something her other activities don't. Her list is otherwise all reading and writing, and this entry shows she builds things with her hands, sticks with a craft, and shares it. It also gives her a possible essay topic.

docs.title: Honors and Awards
docs.text:
Honors and awards are formal recognitions you've received for achievement, such as academic awards, competition results, scholarships, honor societies, and athletic or artistic distinctions. On the Common App, they have their own section, separate from activities, with room for up to five entries. For each, you list the honor, the grade levels you received it, and its level of recognition.

Level Examples School Department award, honor roll, student of the month State or regional All-state orchestra, regional science fair placement, state writing award National National Merit recognition, national competition finalist, national scholarship recognition International International olympiad or competition placement

Choose the most significant honors first, and keep descriptions specific: "1st place, regional science fair (biology)" rather than "science fair." Don't worry if you have few or none. Many strong applicants have one or two school-level honors. An empty honors section isn't a red flag, especially for students whose time goes to work or family, and readers won't penalize you for it.

docs.title: Worked Example: Choosing Five Honors
docs.text:
Priya has seven possible honors. She ranks them by level and significance and lists five:

  1. State young writers award, poetry (grade 11), state level.
  2. Scholastic Art & Writing Awards Gold Key, short story (grade 11), regional level.
  3. National Honor Society (grades 11–12), school level.
  4. English Department Award (grade 10), school level.
  5. Honor roll, all semesters (grades 9–11), school level.

She leaves off a 9th-grade spelling bee and a perfect-attendance award, which add little. Her strongest recognitions appear first, so a reader who skims sees the state award immediately.

docs.title: The Activities List
docs.text:
The activities list is the section of your application where you record your extracurricular activities in a fixed, structured format. On the Common App, you can list up to 10 activities, and each entry has the same set of fields:

  • Activity type: chosen from a menu (for example, Work (paid), Family responsibilities, Community service, Athletics, Art, Research, Other club or activity).
  • Position or leadership description: up to 50 characters.
  • Organization name: up to 100 characters.
  • Description: up to 150 characters, about one or two short lines.
  • Grade levels: 9, 10, 11, 12, or post-graduate.
  • Timing: during the school year, during school breaks, or all year.
  • Hours per week and weeks per year.

Those limits are tight. A 150-character description is shorter than most text messages people write when they're explaining something. Every word has to work. The activities list rewards a writing style closer to a headline than a paragraph. That's why the next sections cover action verbs and description writing.

You don't need to fill all ten slots. Many strong applicants list six or seven. An empty slot is better than a weak entry that dilutes the strong ones.

docs.title: Action Verbs
docs.text:
Action verbs are specific verbs that describe what you actually did, such as founded, organized, trained, built, raised, taught, designed, or led. They replace vague, passive phrasing like "was involved in," "participated in," or "helped with." In a 150-character description, an action verb is the fastest way to show a reader your role.

Compare two openings:

  • "Was a member of the environmental club and participated in events." That's 66 characters, and the reader still doesn't know what you did.
  • "Organized 4 park cleanups; recruited 25 volunteers." That's 51 characters of specific action and results.

Strong action verbs fall into a few families, depending on what you want to show:

To show Verbs Starting something Founded, launched, created, established, initiated Leading people Led, trained, mentored, coached, recruited, supervised Organizing Organized, coordinated, planned, scheduled, managed Making things Built, designed, wrote, programmed, composed, produced Helping others Tutored, taught, translated, cared for, served, supported Improving things Raised, grew, increased, reduced, improved, expanded

Choose verbs that are true and precise. "Led" is wrong if you helped. "Founded" is wrong if you joined. Honesty matters more than sounding impressive. Readers, recommenders, and interviewers may all ask about your activities, and the details have to hold up.

docs.title: Worked Example: Upgrading Verbs
docs.text: Sam's tutoring entry starts as "Helped with tutoring at the middle school." Sam asks what "helped" really meant. Sam met weekly with the same three students, planned practice problems, and led a review session before their state math test. The revised entry: "Tutored 3 middle schoolers weekly in math; planned practice sets; led pre-test review for 20 students." Every verb now names an action, and the entry shows both one-on-one teaching and a moment of leadership.

docs.title: Activity Descriptions
docs.text:
An activity description is the short text, up to 150 characters on the Common App, that explains what you did in an activity and what came of it. It's where readers learn the substance behind a title. A strong description follows a simple pattern: action + specifics + result. Lead with your strongest action verb, add a number or concrete detail, and end with the result or scope.

A few techniques help you fit more into less space:

  • Skip "I" and full sentences. Write in clipped phrases, like a résumé: "Trained 2 new servers," not "I trained two new servers."
  • Use numerals and common abbreviations. "3 hrs/wk" saves space, and readers expect it.
  • Separate items with semicolons instead of using connecting words.
  • Don't repeat information from other fields. If your position says "Captain," don't open the description with "Team captain."
  • Draft long, then cut. Write everything you'd want a reader to know, then cut it down to the strongest details.

Write descriptions so they make sense to someone who has never seen your school. "Ran SGA spirit week" may be clear to you, but "Planned school-wide spirit week for 900 students" is clear to anyone.

The builder below lets you draft an entry with live character counts for every field, then checks it for action verbs and specifics.

docs.title: Diagram: Activity Entry Builder
docs.text:
Activity Entry Builder

Type: microsim sim-id: activity-entry-builder Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Let students draft a Common App-style activity entry within the real character limits and get feedback on action verbs, specifics, and measurable impact.

Bloom Level: Create (L6) Bloom Verb: compose, revise Learning Objective: Students will compose an activity entry within the Common App's character limits and revise its description to lead with an action verb and include specific, measurable detail.

Canvas layout: - Left: the entry form. - createSelect "Activity type" (Work (paid), Family responsibilities, Community service, Athletics, Arts, Club, Research, Independent project, Other). - createInput "Position or leadership description" with a live counter "x / 50." - createInput "Organization name" with a counter "x / 100." - createInput (multi-line style) "Description" with a counter "x / 150." The counter turns orange above 140 and red above 150; text beyond 150 is shown struck through in the preview. - Checkboxes for grade levels 9, 10, 11, 12; createSelect "Timing" (School year / School break / All year); createInput "Hours per week" and "Weeks per year." - Right: a "Reader's view" preview card styled like a compact application entry, plus a feedback panel.

Feedback checks (each shows a green check or an orange tip): 1. Starts with an action verb (checks the first word against a built-in list of about 80 action verbs, and flags weak openers such as "was," "member," "participated," "helped," "involved"). 2. Includes at least one number (digit or spelled number). 3. Avoids "I" and full-sentence filler (flags "I ", "my ", "was responsible for"). 4. Does not repeat the position text inside the description. 5. Hours make sense (flags hours per week above 40 or weeks per year above 52). 6. Shows total hours per year = hours per week × weeks per year.

Presets (createButton): "Marcus — restaurant" (from the chapter), "Sam — tutoring before" (weak draft) and "Sam — tutoring after" (revised), "Applicant B — bike shop."

Controls (all created in setup() before positioning): the inputs, selects, and checkboxes above; createButton presets; createButton "Copy entry text."

Responsive behavior: Call updateCanvasSize() first in setup(); the form and preview stack on narrow screens; controls reposition on resize.

Implementation: p5.js with createInput, createSelect, createCheckbox, and createButton; canvas parented to the main element.

docs.title: Worked Example: Cutting to 150 Characters
docs.text:
Priya's first draft for her literary magazine entry runs 217 characters:

"I am the editor-in-chief of our school's literary magazine, which publishes two issues each year. I am responsible for reading all the submissions and working with the staff on editing and on the layout of each issue."

She cuts it in three passes:

  1. Remove "I am," "which," and filler: "Editor-in-chief of school literary magazine; 2 issues/yr; read all submissions; work with staff on editing and layout of each issue." (132 characters)
  2. Move the title to the position field, since it doesn't need to be in both places, and add a result: "Read 200+ submissions/yr; lead staff of 8 in editing and layout; 2 issues/yr; started first online issue." (105 characters)
  3. Lead with the strongest verb: "Lead staff of 8; started first online issue; read 200+ submissions/yr; edit and lay out 2 print issues/yr." (106 characters)

The final version is about half the length of her first draft, and it says more: her leadership, an initiative she started, and the scale of the work.

docs.title: Activity Ordering
docs.text:
Activity ordering is the order in which you list your activities. On the Common App, readers see them in the order you enter them, so your order is itself a signal of what you consider most important. List your most significant activities first: the ones with the most time, the longest commitment, the most responsibility, or the deepest personal meaning.

Readers often spend only a short time on the activities section, so the first three or four entries do most of the work. Don't bury your best activity in slot seven because you joined it most recently or because it's not school-sponsored. A family responsibility or job that takes twenty hours a week usually belongs near the top, not at the bottom.

A useful way to decide is to rank your activities by three questions:

  1. Which ones matter most to me? Which would I be most sorry to give up?
  2. Which show the most commitment? Years, hours, and growing roles.
  3. Which show the most impact? What changed because of me?

Activities that rank high on all three go first. Then check the order against your application as a whole. If your essay is about your family responsibilities, those should appear near the top of your list as well, so the two parts of the application reinforce each other.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reordering Marcus's List
docs.text:
Marcus entered his activities in the order he thought of them: Computer Science Club, Intramural Basketball, Robotics Team, Restaurant Job, National Honor Society, the ordering app, and Math Tutoring. After ranking them by meaning, commitment, and impact, he reorders:

  1. Restaurant job (15 hrs/wk, 3 years, trained staff, inventory system)
  2. Ordering app (self-directed, real users, ties to his intended major)
  3. Robotics team (3 years, programming lead)
  4. Computer Science Club (2 years, member)
  5. Math tutoring (1 year)
  6. National Honor Society
  7. Intramural basketball

His first three entries now show work, initiative, and depth in computer science, which is the story he wants a reader to take away. Intramural basketball is still there, but at the end, where its light commitment fits.

docs.title: The Activities Resume
docs.text:
An activities resume is a one- to two-page document that lists your activities, jobs, family responsibilities, honors, and summer experiences in more detail than the application's activities list allows. It's not usually submitted with your application, though some colleges and scholarships accept or request one. Its real value is as a master document you use everywhere else:

  • For the Common App activities list: You write fuller descriptions on the resume, then cut each down to 150 characters.
  • For recommenders: Teachers and your counselor use it to write specific, detailed letters. Chapter 11 covers the brag sheet, which builds on it.
  • For essays: Reviewing your activities in one place often reveals essay topics and themes. Chapter 10 covers the activity essay.
  • For interviews and scholarships: It's a quick reference for the stories you'll be asked about.

A good activities resume is organized by section, most important first, with a few lines for each entry:

  • Heading: your name, school, graduation year, and contact information.
  • Activities and leadership: each with organization, your role, years, hours, and two or three bullet points of what you did and achieved.
  • Work experience: jobs with responsibilities and any promotions.
  • Family responsibilities: described plainly, with hours.
  • Community service.
  • Summer experiences.
  • Honors and awards.
  • Skills and interests: languages, technical skills, and personal interests.

Start your resume early. The five first steps in Chapter 5 included drafting it, and keep it updated as senior year goes on. Because it isn't limited by character counts, it's also the place to record details you'll want later: dates, numbers, names of supervisors, and specific moments that could become essay material.

docs.title: Worked Example: One Entry, Three Uses
docs.text:
Here's one entry from Ana's activities resume:

Sibling care and household support (family responsibility) — Grades 9–12, about 15 hours/week

  • Pick up two younger brothers from school daily and supervise homework until parents return from work.
  • Cook dinner three nights a week; plan weekly grocery list within family budget.
  • Helped my younger brother raise his reading level by two grades through nightly reading practice in 7th grade.

From this one entry, Ana gets three things. For the Common App, she cuts it to "Pick up 2 brothers daily; supervise homework; cook dinner 3 nights/wk; helped brother gain 2 reading levels." For her English teacher's recommendation, the reading detail gives the teacher a specific example of Ana's patience to mention. For her personal essay, the nightly reading sessions become her topic. One well-written resume entry feeds every part of her application.

The sorter below tests your sense of what counts as an activity. Try it before you build your own resume.

docs.title: Diagram: What Counts as an Activity?
docs.text:
What Counts as an Activity?

Type: microsim sim-id: what-counts-activity-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Challenge the assumption that only school-sponsored activities count, by having students classify real-life examples and see which activity type each would be listed under.

Bloom Level: Understand (L2) Bloom Verb: classify, explain Learning Objective: Students will classify everyday commitments as listable activities or not and explain which activity type each belongs to and why.

Canvas layout: - Top: a single scenario card showing one example. - Middle: two large buttons, "List it" and "Probably not." - After an answer: a feedback panel showing whether the answer matches the recommended one, the suggested Common App activity type, and a one-sentence reason, then a "Next" button. - Bottom: a running score and a tally of activity types discovered.

Scenario deck (shuffled, 14 cards), each with the recommended answer, type, and reason: 1. "Pick up younger siblings and supervise homework, 12 hrs/wk" — List it; Family responsibilities; "Real, regular responsibility that takes significant time." 2. "Bag groceries at a supermarket, 10 hrs/wk" — List it; Work (paid); "Jobs show reliability and time management." 3. "Taught yourself guitar; play at open mics monthly" — List it; Music (or Independent); "Self-directed and sustained, with something to show." 4. "Watched a lot of cooking videos" — Probably not; —; "Consuming isn't the same as doing. Cooking regularly for your family would count." 5. "Translate for parents at appointments, 2–3 hrs/wk" — List it; Family responsibilities; "A real skill and responsibility." 6. "Play video games" — Probably not, unless...; —; "Casual play isn't an activity. Competing, streaming, modding, or organizing a club could be." 12. "Youth group at your place of worship, leading the middle school group" — List it; Religious; "Leadership in a community." 14. Controls (all created in setup() before positioning): createButton "List it," "Probably not," "Next," and "Restart."

Interaction: Answers that differ from the recommendation aren't marked "wrong" for gray-area cards (9, 11, 14); the feedback reads "It depends" and explains the condition.

Color scheme: card in white; feedback green for match, orange for "it depends," gray for mismatch with an explanation.

Responsive behavior: Call updateCanvasSize() first in setup(); the card and buttons scale to the container; buttons stack on narrow screens.

Implementation: p5.js with createButton; canvas parented to the main element.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Extracurricular activities are anything outside class that takes real time and says something about you, including part-time jobs, family responsibilities, community service, summer experiences, and personal interests, not just school clubs.
  • The well-rounded applicant myth is wrong. Colleges build a well-rounded class from students with real depth.
  • Readers value leadership roles (titled or not), sustained commitment across years, depth over breadth, and measurable impact.
  • Report hours per week and weeks per year honestly. Readers multiply them.
  • The Common App activities list has 10 slots and a 150-character activity description for each. Lead with action verbs, add specifics, and end with a result.
  • Activity ordering is a signal. Put your most meaningful, committed, and impactful activities first.
  • List up to five honors and awards by significance. Few or none is fine.
  • An activities resume is your master document. It feeds your activities list, your recommenders, your essays, and your interviews.

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
A student volunteers 3 hours a week for 35 weeks a year. What total yearly hours does that imply?

3 × 35 = 105 hours per year.

Rewrite this description with an action verb and a specific detail: 'Was a member of the debate team.'

One possible answer: "Competed in 12 tournaments/yr; reached state quarterfinals; coach 4 novice debaters." Any revision that leads with a specific verb and includes concrete detail works, as long as it's true.

Why might a twenty-hour-a-week family responsibility belong at the top of an activities list?

Ordering signals importance. It represents the largest time commitment and strong evidence of responsibility, and it explains why the student has less time for other activities.

Is it a problem to leave three of the ten activity slots empty?

No. Many strong applicants list six or seven activities. An empty slot is better than a weak entry that dilutes the strong ones.

What's wrong with the idea that colleges want well-rounded applicants?

Colleges aim for a well-rounded class made of students with depth in a few areas. A shallow list of many activities usually reads as weaker than serious commitment to a few.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers writing the Common App personal essay from brainstorming and topic choice through structure, authentic voice, reflection, drafting, feedback, and revision. The personal essay is the one place the student's own voice comes through directly. This chapter takes students from a blank page to a revised, proofread draft.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 20 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score College Essay 620 Essay Drafts Folder 1 Personal Essay 462 Common App Essay Prompts 47 Essay Word Limit 15 Brainstorming 98 Essay Material List 47 Personal Story 50 Small Moment Essay 1 Overused Essay Topics 47 Essay Topic Selection 46 Show Don't Tell 15 Authentic Voice 15 Essay Structure 45 Opening Hook 15 Reflection and Insight 15 Drafting 14 Feedback on Essays 7 Revision 6 Editing and Proofreading 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: How Colleges Evaluate Applicants
  • Chapter 3: Finding Your Fit
  • Chapter 5: Getting Organized

docs.title: The Part of the Application in Your Own Voice
docs.text:
Every other part of your application describes you from the outside. Your transcript is a list of grades. Your activities list is 150-character summaries. Your recommendations are other people's words about you. The personal essay is the one place where a reader hears you directly, in your own voice, telling them something they couldn't learn anywhere else.

That's also why students dread it. It can feel like the essay has to be profound, a story of tragedy overcome or a life-changing moment, and most seventeen-year-olds haven't lived that kind of story. The good news is that it doesn't need one. The strongest essays are often about small, specific things, told honestly, with real thought about what they mean. A reader should finish your essay feeling they know one true, particular thing about you.

This chapter takes you from a blank page to a finished draft. You'll start with what college essays are and what the personal essay is for, then learn the prompts and the word limit. Next you'll brainstorm, collecting material and finding a personal story, while avoiding the topics readers see too often. Then come the writing techniques that make an essay work: showing instead of telling, an authentic voice, a clear structure, a strong opening, and real reflection. The chapter ends with the process of drafting, getting feedback, revising, and proofreading.

Throughout, you'll follow Ana as she writes her essay. Chapter 8 ended with her noticing a possible topic in her activities resume: the nightly reading sessions with her younger brother.

docs.title: College Essays
docs.text:
A college essay is any piece of writing a college asks you to submit as part of your application. There are two main kinds:

  • The personal essay, a longer essay about yourself, usually sent to every college through a shared platform like the Common App. This chapter covers it.
  • Supplemental essays, shorter essays that individual colleges add, often asking why you want to attend or about a specific interest. Chapter 10 covers them.

Colleges ask for essays because holistic review, as Chapter 2 described, tries to understand applicants as people, not just numbers. Essays give readers three things nothing else in the file can:

  1. Your voice. How you think, what you notice, and how you put things into words.
  2. Your reflection. Your ability to look at your own experience and understand what it means.
  3. What's missing. A part of your life, your values, or your thinking that the rest of the application doesn't show.

How much essays matter depends on the college. At formula-based public universities like Iowa, the essay may not be required for basic admission at all, though honors programs and scholarships may ask for one. At holistic colleges, the essay feeds a reader's personal rating. At the most selective colleges, where nearly every applicant has strong grades, essays often help decide among otherwise similar files. It's rare for an essay alone to win admission, but a strong one can tip a close decision, and a careless one can raise doubts.

Because you'll write many essays, one personal essay plus supplements for several colleges, organization matters. That's where your essay drafts folder comes in.

docs.title: The Essay Drafts Folder
docs.text: The essay drafts folder is the part of your filing system, from Chapter 5, where you keep every essay draft. Create a subfolder for your personal essay and one for each college's supplements. Save each significant version as a new file with a clear name and version number, such as "Personal_Essay_v3_2026-09-14," rather than overwriting the old one. You'll often want to recover a paragraph you cut, compare versions, or reuse a strong passage in a supplement. Keep a short "notes" file in the folder too, with the prompts, word limits, and feedback you've received.

docs.title: The Personal Essay
docs.text:
The personal essay, also called the personal statement or the Common App essay, is the main essay you submit with your application. You write it about yourself, in response to one of several broad prompts, and send it to every college that receives your Common App. It's typically the longest piece of writing in your application, and the only one most of your colleges will all read.

Its job is simple to state and hard to do: show the reader who you are through a story or idea that matters to you, told in your own voice, with honest reflection on what it means. A personal essay is not:

  • A résumé in paragraphs. Your activities list already covers what you've done.
  • An academic paper. You aren't proving a thesis with sources.
  • A list of virtues. Saying "I am hardworking and compassionate" proves nothing.
  • A story about someone else. Writing about a grandparent or a coach is fine, but the essay must ultimately reveal you.

The best way to understand the difference is to see two openings for the same topic.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Essays, One Topic
docs.text:
Two students write about working at a family restaurant.

Essay 1 opens: "Working at my family's restaurant has taught me many valuable lessons about hard work, responsibility, and customer service. These skills will help me succeed in college and beyond."

Essay 2 opens: "Every Friday at 6:15, the bell over the kitchen door rings eleven times in four minutes, and I've learned to hear in it which orders will go wrong."

Essay 1 tells the reader what to think, in words any student could have written. Essay 2 drops the reader into a specific moment only this student could describe, and it raises a question, how can a bell tell you which orders will go wrong?, that makes the reader want to continue. By the end, Essay 2 can reach the same lessons about responsibility. But the reader will believe them, because they've seen them happen. The rest of this chapter is about how to write the second kind of essay.

docs.title: The Common App Essay Prompts
docs.text:
The Common App essay prompts are the set of essay questions the Common App provides each year for the personal essay. You choose one. The prompts have stayed largely the same for several years. There are seven, and in summary they ask you to write about:

  1. A background, identity, interest, or talent so central to you that your application would feel incomplete without it.
  2. An obstacle, setback, or failure, and what you learned from it.
  3. A time you questioned or challenged a belief or idea.
  4. Something someone did for you that made you grateful in a surprising way.
  5. An accomplishment, event, or realization that sparked personal growth.
  6. A topic, idea, or concept so engaging that you lose track of time.
  7. Any topic of your choice.

Read the exact wording on the Common App website, since prompts are occasionally revised, but understand what they're for. The prompts are broad on purpose. They're doors into almost any story, not narrow assignments. Most good essays fit more than one prompt, and prompt 7 exists for stories that don't fit the others neatly. Readers care about what your essay reveals, not about how precisely it answers the literal question.

That leads to the most useful piece of advice about prompts: don't start with them. Start with your material. Once you know your story, find the prompt it fits. Students who start with a prompt often end up writing what they think the prompt wants instead of what's true about them.

docs.title: Worked Example: Finding the Prompt After the Story
docs.text:
Ana's essay idea is about reading with her younger brother every night in 7th grade, when he was struggling and she realized she was good at teaching. She checks it against the prompts:

  • Prompt 1 (background or identity): possible, since being the family's translator and helper is central to who she is.
  • Prompt 5 (growth): strong. Teaching her brother changed how she saw herself.
  • Prompt 2 (obstacle): possible, though the obstacle was her brother's, not hers.

Ana chooses prompt 5, because her story is really about a realization. But the choice barely matters. Her story would work under any of the three. That's typical, and it's why the story should come first.

docs.title: The Essay Word Limit
docs.text:
The essay word limit is the maximum length a college or platform allows for an essay. For the Common App personal essay, it's 650 words, with a minimum of 250. The application box enforces the maximum, so you can't go over.

650 words is shorter than it sounds, about a page and a third, double-spaced. That length shapes the essay in two ways. First, there's room for one story, told well, not three stories told briefly. Students who try to cover their whole life end up with an essay that's broad and thin. Second, every sentence has to earn its place. Long introductions, repeated points, and general statements about what you learned use up words that could go to specific detail and reflection.

Most strong essays use most of the space, roughly 550 to 650 words. An essay much shorter than that is usually missing reflection. It's also fine to draft long and cut later. Many students' first drafts run 900 words or more, and cutting them down is part of the revision process.

docs.title: Brainstorming
docs.text:
Brainstorming is the process of generating many possible essay ideas and details before choosing a topic. It works best when you resist the urge to find your "big story" right away and instead collect small, specific material. A few techniques work well:

  • Start with your running list. If you began a list of essay material as one of the five first steps in Chapter 5, read through it first. It's already full of raw material.
  • Ask people who know you. Ask a parent, a friend, a coach, or a sibling what they'd say makes you you. Their answers often surface qualities you take for granted.
  • Look for specific, not significant. A small, vivid detail, like the way your grandmother organizes her spices or the sound of a bell in your family's kitchen, is often better material than a large, vague event like a trip or a tournament. Specificity is what makes an essay feel true.
  • Work backward from a quality. Choose one trait you'd want a reader to know about you, such as curiosity, persistence, humor, or care for others. Then list three ordinary moments when that trait showed.
  • Mine your activities resume. Your resume from Chapter 8 lists where your time goes. The moments inside those activities are often essay material.
  • Use object and place prompts. List ten objects in your room that matter to you, or five places where you feel most like yourself. Write a sentence about why for each.

Brainstorming should feel loose. Write everything down, including ideas that seem silly. You're collecting, not judging.

docs.title: Worked Example: Ana's Brainstorm
docs.text:
Ana spends forty-five minutes brainstorming. She asks her mother and her best friend what makes her her. Her mother says "you notice when someone is confused before they say it." Her friend says "you explain things better than teachers." She lists objects (a worn copy of Charlotte's Web, her phone's translation app, a whiteboard in the kitchen) and moments:

  • Translating a doctor's explanation for her father and realizing she didn't understand it herself.
  • The food pantry family who came back to thank her in Spanish.
  • Reading Charlotte's Web with her brother night after night until he could read it alone.
  • Learning to edit videos from free tutorials for her church.
  • Burning dinner the first night she cooked alone.

She doesn't choose yet. But she notices that her mother's and friend's comments, and three of her five moments, are all about explaining things to people.

docs.title: The Essay Material List
docs.text: The essay material list is the running record you keep of possible essay material: moments, details, quotes, objects, and ideas, collected over weeks or months. It's different from a one-time brainstorm because it builds up. The best material rarely shows up when you sit down to write. It shows up in the shower, on the drive home, or in the middle of a shift. Keep the list on your phone so you can add to it right away, and save a copy in your essay drafts folder. When you're ready to choose a topic, you'll have far more to choose from than any single brainstorming session could produce. Write down specifics, not summaries: "Dad's face when the doctor said 'benign' and I had to look up the word," not "translating at the doctor."

docs.title: The Personal Story
docs.text:
A personal story is the specific experience, moment, or idea at the center of your essay, told from your own point of view and revealing something about who you are. It's the raw material the essay is built from, and its quality depends less on how dramatic it is than on how specific and meaningful it is to you.

A good personal story has three qualities:

  1. It's yours. Only you could tell it this way. It comes from your life, your perspective, and your details.
  2. It's specific. It's grounded in particular moments, places, and details, not a summary of a whole period.
  3. It reveals something. It shows a quality, a value, a way of thinking, or a change in you that the reader wouldn't otherwise know.

Notice what's not on the list: drama, achievement, or uniqueness of experience. Many students have worked at a restaurant or cared for a sibling. What makes a story distinctive is how you see it and what you make of it.

docs.title: Worked Example: Testing Three Stories
docs.text:
Ana tests her three strongest ideas against the three qualities:

Story Hers? Specific? Reveals something new? Translating at the doctor's office Yes Yes, one appointment Partly. Her activities list already shows she translates. Reading Charlotte's Web with her brother Yes Yes, nightly sessions, one book Yes. It shows how she learned to teach, which isn't on her list. Burning dinner the first night Yes Yes Not much. It's funny, but the meaning is thin.

The reading story passes all three tests and reveals something new: how she figured out, at twelve, that patience and noticing confusion are skills. It becomes her topic, and the translation story may appear briefly inside it.

docs.title: The Small Moment Essay
docs.text: A small moment essay is a personal essay built around one brief, specific experience, sometimes only a few minutes long, which the writer explores in detail and then reflects on. Instead of summarizing years of your life, it zooms in on a single scene, like a conversation, a mistake, or an ordinary afternoon, and uses it to reveal something larger. Small moment essays work well because 650 words is exactly enough to render one moment vividly and reflect on it, and because a small, true moment often stands out among essays about big events. The moment doesn't need to be dramatic. It needs to be one you can describe in detail and that genuinely means something to you.

docs.title: Overused Essay Topics
docs.text:
Overused essay topics are subjects that admissions readers see so often that essays about them tend to blend together. They're not forbidden. Any topic can work if it's told with specific detail and genuine reflection. But they make standing out harder, so if you choose one, you need a fresh angle.

The table below lists common overused topics, why they're risky, and how a strong essay on the same subject might work.

Topic Why it's risky How it can work The big game or performance Readers have seen thousands of winning shots and comeback stories Focus on an unexpected, specific moment, such as what you noticed on the bench, not the win The service trip Often reads as privileged or as "I helped them" Write about something you were wrong about, or skip the trip for service close to home A grandparent's death Common and often more about the grandparent than you Center a specific thing you learned or do differently because of them Immigrant or moving story told as summary Easy to fall into general statements Anchor it in one object, ritual, or conversation "I learned hard work from my job/sport" The lesson is predictable Show one specific skill or insight the reader wouldn't expect Résumé essay Repeats the activities list Choose one activity and go deep Trauma told for its own sake Can overwhelm the essay and leave little room for you If you write about hardship, focus on your response and reflection, and share only what you're comfortable sharing

A useful test: if a hundred students could write your essay with only the names changed, you need a more specific angle. If only you could have written it, you're fine, whatever the topic.

docs.title: Essay Topic Selection
docs.text:
Essay topic selection is the decision about which story or idea your personal essay will be about. It draws on everything above: your material list, the qualities of a good personal story, the prompts, and awareness of overused topics. Ask four questions of each candidate:

  1. Does it reveal something important about me that the rest of my application doesn't?
  2. Can I tell it with specific scenes and details?
  3. Do I have something to say about what it means, not just what happened?
  4. Do I want to write about it? Energy shows in the writing.

If two topics pass, try writing a quick, messy paragraph about each. The one that's easier to write about, the one where details keep coming, is usually the right choice. Don't agonize too long. A good topic written well beats a perfect topic chosen in late December.

The prompt matcher below helps you test a topic. Describe your story with a few choices, and it shows which prompts fit and flags risks.

docs.title: Diagram: Essay Topic and Prompt Matcher
docs.text:

Type: microsim sim-id: essay-prompt-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Help students test an essay topic against the qualities of a strong personal story and see which Common App prompts it fits, reinforcing that the story comes before the prompt.

Bloom Level: Evaluate (L5) Bloom Verb: assess, select Learning Objective: Students will assess a candidate essay topic against criteria for a strong personal story and select the Common App prompts it fits.

Canvas layout: - Left: a topic description panel with createInput "Your topic in a few words" and five createSelect questions: 1. "What is the story mostly about?" (A part of who I am / A setback or failure / Questioning a belief / Gratitude for someone / A moment of growth / Something I love to learn about / Something else) 2. "How specific is it?" (One moment or scene / A few connected moments / A long period summarized) 3. "Does it reveal something not elsewhere in my application?" (Yes / Partly / No) 4. "Can I say what it means to me?" (Yes, clearly / Somewhat / Not yet) 5. "Is it one of the common topics?" (No / Big game or performance / Service trip / Grandparent / Job or sport lesson / Résumé of activities) - Right: seven prompt cards (short paraphrased labels, numbered 1–7) that light up green (strong fit), yellow (possible fit), or stay gray. Prompt 7 always shows as a possible fit with the note "Any topic works here." - Bottom: a "Story strength" meter (Weak / Promising / Strong) based on questions 2–4, plus a tip line. If question 5 names a common topic, a tip appears with the matching "How it can work" advice from the chapter table.

Mapping (question 1 to prompts): part of who I am → 1 strong, 5 possible; setback → 2 strong, 5 possible; questioning a belief → 3 strong; gratitude → 4 strong; growth → 5 strong, 1 and 2 possible; love to learn → 6 strong, 1 possible; something else → 7 strong.

Presets (createButton): "Ana — reading with my brother" (growth; one moment; reveals new; yes → prompt 5 strong, 1 and 2 possible; Strong), "The big game" (performance; long period; partly; somewhat; common topic → Promising with tip), "Translating at the doctor" (part of who I am; one scene; partly; yes).

Controls (all created in setup() before positioning): createInput, five createSelect controls, createButton presets.

Implementation: p5.js with createInput, createSelect, and createButton; canvas parented to the main element.

docs.title: Show, Don't Tell
docs.text:
Show, don't tell is the writing principle of letting readers see a quality through specific actions, scenes, and details, instead of stating it directly. Telling names the quality: "I am patient." Showing puts it in front of the reader: "I read the same page of Charlotte's Web to my brother eleven nights in a row, until he stopped looking at the pictures and started looking at the words." The reader concludes that you're patient, and believes it, because they saw it.

Showing works because readers trust evidence more than claims. Every applicant claims to be hardworking, curious, and kind. Only you can show the specific moment when you were.

To show, use:

  • Specific actions: what you did, step by step.
  • Concrete details: what you saw, heard, or held.
  • Dialogue, in small doses: what someone actually said.
  • Numbers and particulars: "eleven nights," not "many nights."

The principle isn't absolute. A personal essay also needs reflection, where you step back and tell the reader what the experience meant. The common pattern is show first, then tell briefly. Ground the essay in scenes, then reflect on them. An essay that's all telling feels empty. An essay that's all showing feels unfinished.

docs.title: Worked Example: From Telling to Showing
docs.text:
Ana's first draft includes this sentence: "Helping my brother learn to read taught me that I am a patient and caring person who enjoys helping others."

She revises it by asking, what did that actually look like?

"Every night at 8:30, after the dishes, Mateo and I sat on the kitchen floor with Charlotte's Web. He'd guess at words from the pictures. I'd cover the pictures with my hand. He'd cry. We'd try again. On the eleventh night, he read the book's first line, the one about Papa and the ax, without looking up at me."

The revision never uses the words "patient" or "caring." It doesn't need to. The exercise below lets you practice the same move.

docs.title: Diagram: Show-Don't-Tell Practice
docs.text:
Show-Don't-Tell Practice

Type: microsim sim-id: show-dont-tell-practice Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Give students practice recognizing showing versus telling and choosing or writing the more specific version of a sentence.

Bloom Level: Apply (L3) Bloom Verb: distinguish, revise Learning Objective: Students will distinguish telling sentences from showing sentences and revise telling sentences into specific, concrete showing sentences.

Canvas layout: - Top: a "telling" sentence card, for example "I am a dedicated athlete." - Middle: three candidate revisions as buttons. One is strong showing, one is weak (still general), and one is overloaded (piles on adjectives without action). - After a choice: feedback explaining why the strong version works (specific action, concrete detail, numbers), what the weak one lacks, and why the overloaded one still tells. - Bottom: a "Write your own" mode with createInput for the student's telling sentence and a second createInput for their showing revision, plus a checklist that flags the revision for: concrete nouns (simple check for words not on a list of abstract virtues), numbers, an action verb, and absence of the original adjective.

Card deck (8 cards, shuffled), each with three options. Example cards: 1. "I am patient." Strong: "I read the same page to my brother eleven nights in a row." Weak: "I was very patient with my brother when he was learning." Overloaded: "I am an incredibly, deeply, endlessly patient and kind person." 2. "I love science." Strong: "I've kept a notebook of 62 questions about how our creek floods." Weak: "Science has always been my passion." 3. "Work taught me responsibility." Strong: "At 16, I was the one who counted the register at closing, and the one who called when it was $4 short." Weak: "My job made me very responsible." (Include five more cards for leadership, curiosity, resilience, humor, and kindness.)

Controls (all created in setup() before positioning): three createButton option controls, createButton "Next," createButton "Write your own," createInput fields for the write-your-own mode.

Interaction: Score tally across the deck; options are shuffled each round.

Responsive behavior: Call updateCanvasSize() first in setup(); option buttons stack on narrow screens.

Implementation: p5.js with createButton and createInput; canvas parented to the main element.

docs.title: Authentic Voice
docs.text:
Authentic voice means writing that sounds like you, with the words, rhythm, and personality of the way you actually think and talk, polished but not replaced. Readers spend much of their time trying to get a sense of the real person behind the application. An essay that sounds like a seventeen-year-old thinking carefully earns trust. An essay that sounds like a thesaurus or an adult editor makes them wonder who wrote it.

Voice is easy to lose in two ways. The first is trying to sound impressive: big words you wouldn't normally use, formal phrasing, sentences that perform intelligence rather than show it. "The pedagogical experience engendered within me a profound appreciation for literacy" is grammatically fine, and no one believes a student wrote it. The second is over-editing by others: when parents, tutors, or friends rewrite sentences in their own voice.

The best test of voice is simple: read your essay out loud. If a sentence sounds like something you'd never say, revise it until it does. Your voice can be serious, funny, quiet, or energetic. It just has to be yours. Humor is fine if it's natural for you. Don't force it if it isn't.

docs.title: Worked Example: Finding the Voice
docs.text:
Ana's second draft has a sentence she's proud of: "This formative experience profoundly illuminated my innate predisposition toward educational endeavors." When she reads it aloud to her father on Sunday morning, he laughs and says, "That's not you." She asks what would sound like her. He says, "You always say you like it when someone finally gets it."

Her revision: "I found out I like the exact second someone finally gets it, the way Mateo's whole face changed on the eleventh night." It uses ordinary words, sounds like her, and is more vivid than the original.

docs.title: Essay Structure
docs.text:
Essay structure is the way an essay's parts are arranged: where it begins, how it moves, and where it ends. A personal essay doesn't need the five-paragraph format from English class. It needs a shape that carries the reader through your story and into your reflection. Three structures work well for most personal essays:

  • Narrative arc: a single story told mostly in order, with an opening scene, a turning point, and reflection on what changed. It's the most common structure and the easiest to control.
  • Montage: several short scenes or images connected by a common thread, such as an object, a place, or a quality, with reflection tying them together. It works well when no single moment tells the whole story.
  • Idea-driven: an essay organized around a question or idea you care about, using examples from your life to explore it. It works well for prompt 6 and for intellectually curious writers.

Whichever you choose, most strong personal essays share an underlying pattern. They open in a specific moment, move through the story with concrete detail, reach a turn where something shifts or becomes clear, and close with reflection that reaches beyond the story. A rough word budget for a 650-word narrative might be: opening scene, 80–120 words; story and detail, 250–300; the turn, 80–120; reflection and ending, 150–200.

docs.title: Worked Example: Outlining Ana's Essay
docs.text:
Ana chooses a narrative arc and outlines her essay with a rough word budget:

  1. Opening scene (≈100 words): the kitchen floor, 8:30 p.m., Mateo guessing from pictures.
  2. The story (≈275 words): the nightly routine; her covering the pictures; his frustration and hers; noticing that he got stuck on the same kinds of words; making flash cards on the back of grocery receipts.
  3. The turn (≈100 words): the eleventh night, when he reads a line without looking up.
  4. Reflection (≈175 words): what she learned about noticing confusion; how that shows up now in translating for her parents and tutoring at church; why she wants to study education.

The outline adds up to about 650 words. It also shows her where the translation story fits, as a brief connection in the reflection rather than a competing topic. The explorer below shows how each part of a structure does its job.

docs.title: Diagram: Personal Essay Structure Explorer
docs.text:

Purpose: Show how the parts of a personal essay work together under three common structures, and let students plan their own essay with a word budget that totals 650.

docs.title: The Opening Hook
docs.text:
An opening hook is the first sentence or two of an essay, written to draw the reader in and make them want to keep reading. Readers often go through many essays in a sitting, so the opening shapes how attentively they read the rest.

The strongest hooks usually do one of three things:

  • Start in a scene: drop the reader into a specific moment. "Every night at 8:30, after the dishes, Mateo and I sat on the kitchen floor."
  • Raise a question: say something surprising enough that the reader needs to know more. "I've learned to hear in the kitchen bell which orders will go wrong."
  • Offer a striking detail: begin with an unexpected, concrete image. "My most important textbook is a grocery receipt covered in the word 'thought.'"

Avoid the openings readers see constantly: dictionary definitions ("Webster's defines courage as..."), famous quotations, sweeping statements ("Since the dawn of time, humans have..."), and summaries of what the essay will say ("In this essay, I will describe..."). A good hook doesn't have to be clever. It just has to be specific. And it's often easier to write last. Many writers find their best opening sentence somewhere in the middle of their first draft.

docs.title: Worked Example: Trying Three Openings
docs.text:
Ana drafts three openings for her essay:

  1. "Literacy is one of the most important skills a person can have." This is general, and could open any essay about reading.
  2. "Have you ever taught someone to read?" This asks a question, but a generic one. Many readers will simply answer "no" and move on.
  3. "On the eleventh night, my brother read a sentence about an ax without looking up at me." This starts in a specific, slightly strange moment, and raises questions: What ax? Why eleven nights?

She chooses the third, which means her essay now opens at the turning point and flashes back. That's a small structural change her outline can absorb. A strong hook sometimes reshapes the essay around it.

docs.title: Reflection and Insight
docs.text:
Reflection and insight are the parts of an essay where you step back from the story and explain what it means: what you learned, how you changed, what it shows about how you think, or why it still matters to you. Reflection is what turns a story into a personal essay. Without it, a reader knows what happened but not who you are.

Reflection is the part students most often leave thin, partly because it's hard. Good reflection avoids two traps. The first is the generic lesson: "This taught me that hard work pays off." Readers have seen it thousands of times, and it could follow any story. The second is the oversized claim: "This experience changed my life forever." It's rarely true, and readers know it.

Strong reflection is specific to your story and honest about its size. It might name a small realization, a question you still have, a way you act differently now, or a connection between this moment and other parts of your life. Ask yourself:

  • What did I understand afterward that I didn't before?
  • Where does that understanding show up in my life now?
  • What's still unresolved or surprising to me about it?
  • Why does this matter to who I want to be?

Reflection doesn't have to wait until the last paragraph. Brief moments of thought woven through the story often read better than one big lesson at the end.

docs.title: Worked Example: Deepening Reflection
docs.text:
Ana's first-draft reflection reads: "Teaching Mateo taught me that helping others is rewarding, and I want to keep helping people in the future."

She asks herself the four questions and revises:

"What I learned on the kitchen floor wasn't really about reading. It was that confusion has a look, a small pause before someone guesses, and that if you catch it in that pause, you can help before they give up. I notice that pause everywhere now: in my father's face when a doctor speaks too fast, in the families at the food pantry intake table, in my own face in the mirror before a chemistry test. I don't know yet whether I'll be a teacher. I do know I want to spend my life catching people in that pause."

The revision connects the story to her present life, names a specific insight, admits what's uncertain, and points to the future without overclaiming.

docs.title: Drafting
docs.text:
Drafting is the stage of writing where you get the whole essay down on the page for the first time. The most useful advice about drafting is to write the first draft fast and messy. Don't edit while you draft. Get the entire story down, even badly, from beginning to end, before you start refining anything. Students who try to make each sentence perfect before writing the next often stall for weeks.

A good drafting session looks like this:

  1. Start with your outline and word budget, if you have one.
  2. Set a timer for 45 to 60 minutes and write without stopping to fix things.
  3. Overwrite. Put in every detail you remember. It's easier to cut than to add.
  4. Mark gaps with brackets, such as [better word] or [what did he say?], instead of stopping to fill them.
  5. Stop and save as version 1 in your essay drafts folder.

Then step away for at least a day. Distance lets you see the draft the way a reader will. Plan for several drafts. Four or five versions are normal for a strong personal essay. The first draft finds the story, and later drafts find the voice and the meaning. That's why starting in summer, or at least early in senior fall, matters so much.

docs.title: Feedback on Essays
docs.text:
Feedback on essays is input from other readers, such as a teacher, counselor, parent, or friend, about what's working and what isn't in your draft. Good feedback helps you see your essay as a stranger would: where it's unclear, where it drags, where the voice slips, and where the meaning isn't coming through.

Feedback works best when you choose your readers and your questions deliberately:

Reader Good for Watch out for English teacher Clarity, structure, and writing quality Turning it into an academic essay School counselor What admissions readers look for; whether it adds to your application Limited time; ask early Parent or family member Whether it sounds like you; factual accuracy Rewriting in their voice; protectiveness about family details Friend Whether it's interesting and sounds like you Too much praise or too little honesty

Two or three readers are usually enough. More than that, and you'll get conflicting advice that pulls the essay in too many directions. Ask specific questions instead of "Is it good?": What do you think this essay says about me? Where did you lose interest? Is there a sentence that doesn't sound like me? What's one thing you want to know more about?

Above all, stay the author. Take feedback as information, not instructions. If someone's suggested edits start to sound like their writing instead of yours, that's a signal to pull back. Admissions readers can tell when an essay sounds adult-polished rather than teenager-honest, and it costs you their trust. Having someone else write or substantially rewrite your essay isn't just unwise. It's dishonest, and the Common App asks you to certify that your application is your own work.

docs.title: Revision
docs.text:
Revision is the process of rethinking and reworking a draft: changing its content, structure, focus, or meaning, not just fixing sentences. It's where most of an essay's quality comes from. Revision is different from editing. Editing makes sentences correct. Revision makes the essay better.

Revise in passes, from big to small:

  1. Big picture: Does the essay reveal what I want it to? Is the story the right one? Is there enough reflection?
  2. Structure: Does the order work? Does the opening hook? Is there a clear turn? Does the ending land?
  3. Scenes and detail: Where am I telling instead of showing? Where do I need a specific detail?
  4. Voice: Read it aloud. Which sentences don't sound like me?
  5. Length: Cut to 650 words, starting with general statements, repeated points, and long setup.

When cutting, a useful rule is to remove anything the reader already knows or could guess. Cut sentences that restate the previous one, introductions that warm up before the essay starts, and lessons the reader already understood from the scene.

docs.title: Worked Example: Ana's Five Drafts
docs.text:
Ana's essay goes through five versions over seven weeks:

  • Draft 1 (August 10, 910 words): the whole story in order, with a long introduction about her family and a one-sentence lesson at the end.
  • Draft 2 (August 24, 820 words): she cuts the introduction and starts on the kitchen floor. Her English teacher says the reflection is too general.
  • Draft 3 (September 7, 760 words): a new reflection about "the pause." Her father points out the sentence that doesn't sound like her.
  • Draft 4 (September 21, 690 words): a new hook that opens on the eleventh night, plus voice fixes. Her counselor says the essay adds something her application didn't show.
  • Draft 5 (October 1, 642 words): she cuts 48 words of repetition and tightens the ending.

The story never changed after Draft 1. What changed was where it started, what it meant, and how it sounded. That's what revision is.

docs.title: Editing and Proofreading
docs.text:
Editing and proofreading are the final checks of an essay, after revision is done, for errors in grammar, spelling, punctuation, word choice, and formatting. Editing looks at sentences: clarity, wordiness, and word choice. Proofreading is the last pass for typos and mechanical mistakes. Errors don't usually sink an essay, but they can distract a reader and suggest carelessness.

Proofread in ways that make you see the words fresh. Read the essay aloud, slowly. Read it on paper or in a different font. Read it backward, sentence by sentence, to catch typos your brain auto-corrects. Have one careful reader do a final proofread. Then paste the essay into the Common App box and read it there, since formatting such as italics, paragraph breaks, and special characters sometimes changes when you paste. Check the word count in the box itself. Finally, save the exact submitted version in your essay drafts folder, labeled "FINAL — submitted."

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A college essay is any essay a college asks for. The personal essay is the main one, sent to every Common App college, and its job is to show the reader who you are in your own voice. Keep every version in an essay drafts folder.
  • The Common App essay prompts are broad on purpose. Choose your story first, then the prompt. The essay word limit is 650 words, enough for one story told well.
  • Brainstorming and a running essay material list collect specific moments. A good personal story is yours, specific, and revealing. A small moment essay can be the strongest kind.
  • Overused essay topics can work with a fresh, specific angle. Essay topic selection asks whether a story reveals something new, has scenes, has meaning, and makes you want to write.
  • Show, don't tell: let scenes prove your qualities, then reflect briefly. Keep an authentic voice by reading aloud.
  • Choose an essay structure (narrative arc, montage, or idea-driven), open with a specific opening hook, and give real space to reflection and insight.
  • Drafting fast and messy, feedback from two or three chosen readers, revision in passes from big to small, and careful editing and proofreading take an essay from blank page to final.

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
Why is it usually better to choose your story before choosing a Common App prompt?

The prompts are broad on purpose, and most good stories fit more than one. Starting with the prompt tempts you to write what you think it wants instead of what's true about you. Prompt 7 accepts any topic anyway.

Rewrite this as showing: 'I am curious about how things work.'

One possible answer: "By age ten, I had taken apart three toasters, two remote controls, and, by accident, my mom's hair dryer." Any revision that uses specific actions and details instead of naming the quality works.

An essay's reflection reads: 'This experience taught me that hard work pays off.' What's wrong with it, and how would you improve it?

It's a generic lesson that could follow any story. Improve it by naming a specific insight tied to this story, where it shows up in your life now, and anything still unresolved.

Your draft is 890 words. What should you cut first?

Start with general statements, long setup, and repeated points, including sentences that restate what the scene already showed. Protect the specific scenes and the reflection.

A parent rewrites several of your sentences so they sound more polished. What's the risk?

The essay may lose your authentic voice and sound adult-written, which costs readers' trust. Substantial rewriting by someone else is also dishonest. Take feedback as information, and keep the writing yours.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers researching each school to write specific Why Us, major, community, and activity essays and short answers, and adapting material without falling into the recycled-essay trap. It builds on the personal essay and the school research from earlier chapters. Students finish with a plan for every supplement on their list.
