docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: Finding Your Fit
  • Chapter 4: Researching and Narrowing Your College List
  • Chapter 5: Getting Organized
  • Chapter 8: Activities and Resume
  • Chapter 9: The Personal Essay

docs.title: You and This College
docs.text:
The personal essay is about you. Supplemental essays are about you and a particular college. They're also where applications most often go wrong quietly, because they're written last, under deadline pressure, ten at a time, and treated as an afterthought. A strong personal essay followed by a generic "Why us?" essay leaves a reader wondering whether you actually want to be there.

The fix isn't more talent. It's more specificity, and specificity comes from research and planning. This chapter starts with what supplemental essays are, then covers the research that makes them work. Next it walks through the most common types: the Why Us essay, the major essay, the community essay, the activity essay, short answers, and optional essays. It ends with the two skills that make a long list manageable: adapting material without falling into the recycled-essay trap, and planning every supplement before you start.

docs.title: Supplemental Essays
docs.text:
Supplemental essays are the additional essays and short-answer questions that individual colleges require or invite beyond the personal essay. They appear in each college's section of the Common App, or in its own institutional application, and they vary widely. Some colleges ask for none. Others ask for one short essay, and the most selective colleges may ask for three, four, or more, with word limits from 25 to 650 words.

Colleges use supplements to learn things the personal essay and the rest of the shared application can't tell them:

  • Fit: Do you know what this college offers, and does it match what you want? This is the purpose of the Why Us essay.
  • Academic interest: Why your intended major, and why here?
  • Community: How would you contribute to and experience campus life?
  • Depth: More on an activity, an idea, or an experience your application mentions only briefly.
  • Interest: At colleges that track demonstrated interest, as Chapter 2 described, a specific, well-researched supplement is one of the clearest signals that you'd enroll if admitted.

That last point is why supplements reward effort. At a college that weighs demonstrated interest, a generic supplement doesn't just miss a chance. It signals the opposite of interest.

Because supplements are short, students often assume they matter less than the personal essay. That's not quite right. A 250-word Why Us essay can carry as much weight in a reader's judgment of fit as the personal essay carries for character, and it's usually easier to make strong, because the main ingredient is research, not inspiration.

docs.title: Worked Example: Counting the Real Workload
docs.text:
Priya's requirements matrix from Chapter 5 shows that her ten colleges ask for:

  • Two colleges: no supplements.
  • Her state flagship: one 250-word short answer about her intended major.
  • Four colleges: one Why Us essay each (150–300 words).
  • One college: a Why Us essay plus a 250-word community essay.
  • One college: a 200-word major essay and three short answers (50 words each).
  • College A, her top reach: a 250-word activity essay, a 250-word community essay, and five short answers (100 words or less).

That's 18 separate pieces of writing, about 3,000 words in total, more than four times the length of her personal essay. Seeing the total in August, rather than discovering it one college at a time in October, changes how she schedules her fall.

docs.title: School-Specific Research
docs.text:
School-specific research is the targeted research you do on one college to find concrete details for its supplemental essays: particular programs, courses, professors, research opportunities, traditions, student organizations, and resources that connect to your goals. It goes deeper than the research in Chapter 4, which was about deciding whether a college fits. This research is about showing how it fits.

Good sources, roughly in order of usefulness:

  1. Department pages for your intended major: course listings, special tracks, research centers, and faculty interests.
  2. The course catalog: specific course titles and descriptions you'd actually take.
  3. Student organization directories: clubs and groups you'd join.
  4. Your own notes from visits, virtual tours, and information sessions.
  5. Conversations with current students, which often give the most specific and believable details.
  6. The college's student newspaper and social media: current events, traditions, and campus life.

Avoid relying on the admissions homepage and brochures. They describe the college in the same terms every college uses, such as "vibrant community," "world-class faculty," and "beautiful campus," and those phrases are exactly what readers don't want to see repeated back to them.

As you research, collect details in a note for each college, and next to each one, write why it matters to you. A detail with no connection to you is just a fact.

docs.title: Worked Example: Twenty Minutes of Research
docs.text:
Marcus has twenty minutes to research Lakeshore University's computer science program for its Why Us essay. He finds:

  • A course called Software for Social Good, where students build apps for local nonprofits. Matters because: his restaurant ordering app was his favorite project.
  • A peer-mentoring program where upper-level students tutor intro CS students. Matters because: he saw teaching assistants helping in the lecture he visited, and he tutors math.
  • A student hackathon club that runs a 24-hour event each spring. Matters because: he's never built anything in a team under time pressure and wants to.
  • A professor who studies small-business software. Matters because: his family's restaurant runs on spreadsheets.

Each detail is specific to Lakeshore, and each one connects to something real about Marcus. He now has more material than a 250-word essay can hold.

docs.title: Common Types of Supplemental Essays
docs.text:
Most supplemental prompts, however they're worded, fall into a handful of types. Recognizing the type tells you what the college is really asking and lets you reuse your thinking across colleges, though not your exact sentences. The table below previews the types covered in this section.

Type What the college is really asking Typical length Why Us Do you know us, and do we fit you? 100–400 words Why This Major Why this field, and why study it here? 150–400 words Community What communities shape you, and what would you bring? 150–400 words Activity Tell us more about something you care about. 150–250 words Short answers Quick glimpses of personality and interests 25–100 words Optional Anything else we should know, if there is anything Varies

docs.title: The Why Us Essay
docs.text:
The Why Us essay asks why you want to attend a particular college. It's the most common supplement, and the most commonly done badly. Weak versions repeat the college's marketing language, such as "your beautiful campus," "world-class faculty," or "strong sense of community," which could describe almost any college and tell the reader nothing.

A strong Why Us essay is specific and two-directional. It names concrete things about the college, such as a program, course, research opportunity, professor, tradition, or organization, and it connects each one to something concrete about you: a goal, an experience, an interest. The essay should read as if it could only have been written by this applicant for this college.

The simplest check is the swap test. Replace the college's name with another college's name. If the essay still makes sense, it isn't specific enough. A good structure for a short Why Us essay is two or three specific details, each paired with a sentence about why it matters to you, wrapped in a brief opening and closing that state what you're looking for.

docs.title: Worked Example: Passing the Swap Test
docs.text:
Priya's first draft of her 300-word "Why Hillcrest" essay begins:

"I want to attend Hillcrest College because of its excellent English program, small class sizes, and welcoming community. I know that at Hillcrest I will be challenged academically and grow as a person."

She runs the swap test, replacing "Hillcrest" with "College C." It still works perfectly, which means it fails. She returns to her research notes and revises:

"On my visit, I sat in on Professor Lin's seminar on the novel and memory, where eleven students argued for forty minutes about one paragraph of Mrs. Dalloway and nobody checked their phone. I want four years of that. Hillcrest's writing-intensive first-year seminar and its student-run literary review, the Hillcrest Quarterly, would let me keep doing what I love most about editing my school's magazine: arguing over a single sentence until it's right."

Now the swap test fails in the right way. The essay names a specific class, a seminar requirement, and a student publication, and it ties each one to Priya's experience.

The tool below runs the swap test for you and flags generic phrases.

docs.text:

docs.title: The Why This Major Essay
docs.text: The Why This Major essay asks why you want to study your intended field and, often, why at this college. A strong one does two things. First, it shows where your interest came from, with a specific experience rather than a declaration like "I have always been passionate about biology." Second, it shows what you'd do with the major here, naming courses, research, or programs at this college, as in a Why Us essay. If you're undecided, many colleges invite you to write about two or three interests instead. Exploring honestly reads far better than inventing certainty. And if you're applying to a capped major, as Chapter 3 described, this essay is especially important. It may be read by the department deciding on your admission.

docs.title: The Community Essay
docs.text: The community essay asks about a community you belong to, such as a family, neighborhood, culture, faith, team, or online group, and what you've contributed to it or learned from it. Some versions ask how you'd contribute to the college's community. Colleges ask because they're building a class, as Chapter 2 described, and want to understand what you'd bring to campus life. A strong community essay is specific about what you actually do in the community and what it has taught you, rather than describing the community in general. Ana, for example, might write about the food pantry's Saturday intake table, where she translates, and what she's learned about how people ask for help.

docs.title: The Activity Essay
docs.text: The activity essay asks you to describe one of your extracurricular activities, work experiences, or responsibilities in more depth, usually in 150 to 250 words. It's your chance to go beyond the 150-character description on your activities list. Choose an activity that matters to you and that your personal essay doesn't already cover. Then use a specific moment or detail to show what you do and why it matters, drawing on your activities resume from Chapter 8. Marcus, whose personal essay is about his family, might use his activity essay for the restaurant ordering app: one scene of the first text order coming in, and what building it taught him.

docs.title: Short-Answer Questions
docs.text: Short-answer questions are brief supplemental prompts, often 25 to 100 words, that ask for quick, direct responses: a favorite book, a word that describes you, what you'd do with a free afternoon, the best advice you've received. They feel low-stakes, but readers often get their clearest sense of your personality from them, because there's no room to hide behind elaborate sentences. Be direct and concrete. A specific, vivid answer beats a vague, safe one at this length. Let personality or humor through where the prompt allows. Don't cram in "impressive" content the space can't hold. A clean answer that reveals one true thing reads best.

docs.title: Worked Example: A 50-Word Answer
docs.text:
College A asks: "What is something you love to do that most people would find boring? (50 words)"

Safe draft: "I love reading, which many people find boring, but I find it exciting because books let me learn about new worlds and perspectives." (24 words, could be anyone)

Revised: "Proofreading. I read our school literary magazine's final proofs aloud, every word, the night before it goes to print. Last spring I caught a poet's name misspelled on the cover. I still think about it." (35 words)

The revision is specific, a little funny, and shows a trait, care with details, that matches the rest of Priya's application.

docs.title: Optional Essays
docs.text: Optional essays are supplemental prompts a college invites but doesn't require. They're sometimes labeled "optional," and sometimes they're an open "anything else you'd like us to know" box. Treat them according to what they ask. If an optional prompt asks a real question, such as "Why us?" or "Tell us about an intellectual interest," it's usually wise to answer it. Skipping it can signal less interest, especially at colleges that track it. If the prompt is an open "additional information" box, use it only when there's something important the rest of your application doesn't explain, such as a gap in your schooling, a family circumstance, or a sharp change in grades. An empty additional-information box is completely normal, and filling it with more of the same doesn't help.

docs.title: The Recycled Essay Trap
docs.text: The recycled essay trap is the mistake of writing one supplemental essay, usually a Why Us essay, and sending it to several colleges with only the name changed. With a long list, it's tempting. Readers can usually tell, and it undercuts an otherwise strong application. A generic essay signals low genuine interest, which matters at colleges that track demonstrated interest. Worse, recycled essays sometimes keep the wrong college's name or details, which readers notice every year. Reusing your thinking and material across colleges is fine, and smart. Reusing your sentences unchanged is the trap.

docs.title: Essay Adaptation
docs.text:
Essay adaptation is the careful reuse of material from one essay in another: taking a story, theme, or paragraph that works and revising it to fit a new prompt, length, and college. It's how students with long lists write strong supplements without starting from scratch every time. Adaptation works because many prompts overlap. A community essay for one college can become a different college's "how would you contribute" essay, and a core paragraph about your academic interest can anchor several major essays.

The method that works:

  1. Write one strong core version of each recurring type, especially the major essay and the community essay.
  2. For each college, rewrite at least 30–40% with specific, researched details for that college. For Why Us essays, nearly everything except your personal goals should be new.
  3. Re-fit to the prompt and length. Answer the exact question asked, within the limit.
  4. Run the swap test and check every college name and detail before submitting.

docs.title: Supplement Planning
docs.text: Supplement planning is mapping every supplemental prompt across your whole list before you write, grouping prompts by type, deciding where material can be adapted, and scheduling each piece by deadline. Without a plan, students write supplements one college at a time, in deadline order, and run out of time for the last ones. With a plan, you write each core essay once and adapt it efficiently. You'll also see which prompts need fresh research and which are short. Copy every prompt into your tracker in August, when the Common App opens and colleges post their prompts, then group them by type and schedule the work backward from your early deadlines.

docs.title: Worked Example: Priya's Supplement Plan
docs.text:
Priya groups her 18 pieces by type:

Type Colleges Plan Why Us 5 colleges Fresh research for each; shared opening idea about discussion-based classes Community 2 colleges One core essay on the literary magazine staff, adapted to each prompt Major (English) 2 colleges One core paragraph on why English, adapted for the flagship's short answer and the 200-word essay Activity College A Sourdough baking, not covered elsewhere Short answers 2 colleges, 8 total Brainstorm in one sitting; draft in two

She schedules the Early Action Why Us essays first, in early October. Then come College A's activity and community essays, then the regular-round Why Us essays in November and December. Writing the community essay once and adapting it saves her about a week. Grouping the eight short answers into two sittings keeps them from being written in a rush on deadline nights. The planner below builds this kind of map for your list.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Supplemental essays show fit and interest. Across a full list, they can add up to several times the length of your personal essay.
  • School-specific research in department pages, course catalogs, organization lists, and student conversations supplies the details. Write down why each detail matters to you.
  • A Why Us essay must be specific and two-directional: college details tied to your goals. Run the swap test.
  • A Why This Major essay shows where your interest came from and what you'd do with it here. A community essay shows what you do and learn in a community. An activity essay goes deeper on something your personal essay doesn't cover.
  • Short-answer questions reward directness and personality. Answer optional essays that ask real questions, and use additional-information boxes only when needed.
  • Avoid the recycled essay trap. Use essay adaptation instead: reuse material, rewrite 30–40% or more for each college, and check every name.
  • Supplement planning maps every prompt by type and deadline before you start.

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
What is the swap test, and what does it mean if your essay passes it?

Replace the college's name with another college's name. If the essay still makes sense, it isn't specific enough. A strong Why Us essay should stop making sense when another name is swapped in.

A Why Us essay praises 'world-class faculty and a vibrant campus community.' What's wrong, and how would you fix it?

The phrases are generic marketing language that fits any college. Replace them with specific courses, programs, professors, or organizations, and connect each one to something true about you.

Should you answer an optional prompt that asks 'Why are you interested in our college?'

Usually yes. It asks a real question, and skipping it can signal low interest, especially at colleges that track demonstrated interest.

What's the difference between essay adaptation and the recycled essay trap?

Adaptation reuses material but rewrites a substantial share for each college's prompt and details. The recycled essay trap sends the same essay with only the name changed.

Why plan all your supplements in August rather than writing them in deadline order?

Planning reveals the total workload, groups prompts so core essays are written once and adapted, and schedules work before deadlines pile up, rather than leaving the last supplements to be rushed.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers choosing and asking teacher and counselor recommenders, preparing a brag sheet and recommender packet, the FERPA waiver, and following up with thanks. It shows students how to make it easy for recommenders to write a strong letter. After this chapter, students can choose recommenders, ask at the right time, and hand over everything a writer needs.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
  • Chapter 2: How Colleges Evaluate Applicants
  • Chapter 5: Getting Organized
  • Chapter 8: Activities and Resume

docs.title: Someone Else's Words About You
docs.text:
Almost everything in your application comes from you: your activities list, your essays, your self-reported courses. Recommendation letters are different. They're other people's words about you, written by adults who have watched you learn and work. That's what makes them valuable to readers, and also what makes them feel out of your control.

You can't write your own letters, and you shouldn't try to see them. But you have far more influence over them than most students realize. You choose who writes them. You choose when to ask and how. You also give your recommenders the material they need, so they can write a specific, vivid letter instead of a generic one.

This chapter covers what recommendation letters are and the two kinds most colleges ask for, teacher and counselor letters. Then it walks through the process step by step: choosing recommenders, timing your request, asking well, preparing a brag sheet and recommender packet, tracking deadlines, signing the FERPA waiver, and saying thank you. It ends with the optional additional recommendation, and when one helps.

docs.title: Letters of Recommendation
docs.text:
Letters of recommendation are written evaluations of you from teachers, your school counselor, and sometimes other adults, submitted directly to colleges as part of your application. Most selective colleges ask for one or two teacher letters plus a counselor letter. Many less selective and formula-based colleges ask for none. Iowa, for example, doesn't require letters for general admission. Check each college's requirements and record them in your tracker, as Chapter 5 described.

Letters matter because they give readers outside confirmation of who you are. Your transcript says you earned an A in chemistry. A teacher's letter can say that you were the student who asked why the textbook's explanation didn't match the lab results, then stayed after class to work it out. Holistic readers, as Chapter 2 described, often use letters to inform the "personal qualities" part of their rating.

The strongest letters share one trait: specificity. They describe particular moments, projects, and habits that only someone who knows you could describe. A letter that says "Priya is a hardworking, intelligent student" tells a reader almost nothing, since nearly every letter says something similar. A letter that describes how Priya rewrote a classmate's struggling thesis statement in a peer workshop without taking it over tells them a lot.

You can't control what a recommender writes. But you can make specificity much more likely by choosing someone who knows you well and giving them concrete material to work with. That's the strategy behind everything in this chapter.

docs.title: Worked Example: Generic and Specific Letters
docs.text:
Here are two passages a reader might see about the same student.

Generic: "Marcus is one of the most talented students I have taught. He is diligent, intelligent, and a pleasure to have in class. I recommend him without reservation."

Specific: "When our robotics team's navigation code failed two days before regionals, Marcus didn't rewrite it himself. He sat with the two sophomores who'd written it and asked them questions until they found the bug on their own. Then he stayed until 9 p.m. to help them test it."

Both passages are positive. Only the second shows the reader something they'll remember: leadership that builds other people up. Notice that the specific letter depends on the teacher having seen that moment, or having been reminded of it. That's what a brag sheet is for.

docs.title: Teacher Recommendations
docs.text:
A teacher recommendation is a letter from a teacher who has taught you, usually in a core academic subject, describing you as a student and classmate. Teachers can speak to things no other part of your application shows: how you think in discussion, how you handle difficulty, how you treat classmates, and how you grew over a year.

Most colleges that require teacher letters ask for one or two, and many prefer teachers from core academic subjects, which are English, math, science, social studies, and world languages, from 11th or 12th grade. Some colleges, especially for engineering or arts programs, ask that one letter come from a teacher in a related subject. On the Common App, teachers complete a short form rating you on several qualities and then upload a letter. You'll invite them through the application, as Chapter 12 explains.

docs.title: Worked Example: What a Teacher Can See
docs.text:
Ana's English teacher, Ms. Ortiz, taught her in 11th grade. In her letter, Ms. Ortiz can describe things that don't appear anywhere else in Ana's application:

  • In a unit on Their Eyes Were Watching God, Ana noticed that three quieter classmates hadn't spoken all week and asked whether the class could try small-group discussions.
  • Ana's essays improved sharply between September and March, and her revision notes showed she read every comment.
  • Ana translated a permission form for a classmate's parents without being asked.

Each of those details confirms a theme of Ana's application, noticing confusion and helping people understand. That's why a letter from a teacher who knows her well is so valuable.

docs.title: The Counselor Recommendation
docs.text:
The counselor recommendation is a letter from your school counselor that places you in the context of your school and your life, usually submitted along with the school report and your transcript. Colleges that require letters almost always require it. Unlike teachers, counselors see your whole high school record: your course choices compared with what the school offers (including the course-rigor rating from Chapter 2), your activities, and any circumstances at home or at school that affected your path.

The counselor letter is especially important for explaining context: a family responsibility, a move, an illness, a change in grades, or the fact that you're the first in your family to apply to college. Counselors who work with hundreds of students, as many do, need your help to write a personal letter. Meet with your counselor (Chapter 5), complete any questionnaire or brag sheet they provide, and tell them anything you'd like colleges to understand.

docs.title: Choosing Recommenders
docs.text:
Choosing recommenders means deciding which teachers, and occasionally which other adults, you'll ask to write letters. The most important rule is simple: choose the teacher who knows you best, not the one who gave you the highest grade. A B+ student a teacher can describe in vivid detail gets a stronger letter than an A student the teacher barely remembers.

Weigh these factors:

  • How well they know you. Have you talked with them outside class, sought their help, or worked on a project with them?
  • Recency. A junior-year teacher has seen your most recent and mature work. A teacher from earlier can work if they know you exceptionally well, especially if they taught you again later.
  • Subject variety. If you need two letters, choose teachers from different areas, such as one humanities and one STEM, so the letters show different sides of you.
  • Relevance to your goals. If you're applying to engineering, a math or science letter makes sense. If you're applying undecided, choose the two who know you best.
  • Their reliability. A teacher known for meeting deadlines and writing thoughtful letters is worth a lot. Your counselor or older students can tell you who they are.

docs.title: Worked Example: Priya Chooses Two Teachers
docs.text:
Priya considers four teachers:

Teacher Subject and year Grade Knows her well? Notes Mr. Okafor AP U.S. History, 11th A Yes. She went to his office hours weekly and he advised her research paper. Taught the paper she's submitting to one college Ms. Chen AP English Language, 11th A Somewhat. Large class, few one-on-one talks. Also the literary magazine's faculty advisor Mr. Grant AP Chemistry, 11th B Yes. She struggled, came for help often, and improved a lot. Can speak to persistence Mrs. Diaz Spanish III, 11th A Somewhat Good relationship, little depth

Priya's instinct is to ask Ms. Chen, since English is her intended major. But Mr. Okafor knows her work best, and Mr. Grant can describe her persistence in her hardest class, which shows a side of her that her A's don't. She asks Mr. Okafor and Mr. Grant. Ms. Chen still knows her through the literary magazine, so Priya keeps her in mind as a possible additional recommender. The interactive below lets you compare your own options the same way.

docs.title: Diagram: Recommender Comparison Tool
docs.text:
Recommender Comparison Tool

Type: microsim sim-id: recommender-comparison Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Help students compare possible teacher recommenders on the factors that predict a strong letter, and see why "knows me well" outweighs "gave me the highest grade."

Bloom Level: Evaluate (L5) Bloom Verb: compare, choose Learning Objective: Students will compare potential recommenders on how well they know the student, recency, subject, and reliability, and choose two teachers whose letters will be specific and complementary.

Canvas layout: - Top: an entry row for up to 5 teachers with createInput "Teacher name," createSelect "Subject area" (English, Math, Science, Social studies, World language, Arts, Other), createSelect "Grade taught" (9, 10, 11, 12), createSelect "Your grade" (A, B, C), and createSlider "How well they know you" (1–5), plus createCheckbox "Known for thoughtful, on-time letters." - Middle: one horizontal card per teacher with a "letter strength" bar. Strength is computed as: knows-you (weight 50%), recency (12th or 11th = full, 10th = half, 9th = low; weight 20%), core subject (weight 15%), reliability checkbox (weight 15%). The grade earned is shown on the card but given no weight, with a note: "Your grade isn't part of the score — readers care more about what the teacher can describe." - Bottom: "Best pair" panel that picks the two highest-scoring teachers, preferring different subject areas when scores are close (within 10%). It explains its choice in one sentence.

Presets (createButton): "Priya's four teachers" (from the chapter table), "Two English teachers" (shows the variety preference), and "Clear."

Controls (all created in setup() before positioning): the inputs above and createButton presets.

Interaction: Changing any input updates the bars and best pair immediately. Hovering a bar shows the contribution of each factor.

Responsive behavior: Call updateCanvasSize() first in setup(); cards stack and inputs wrap on narrow screens; controls reposition on resize.

Implementation: p5.js with createInput, createSelect, createSlider, createCheckbox, and createButton; canvas parented to the main element.

docs.title: Recommendation Request Timing
docs.text: Recommendation request timing is when you ask teachers to write your letters. Ask in the spring of junior year or at the very start of senior year, well before fall deadlines. Teachers who write letters often receive many requests, and some limit how many they accept. The earliest askers get the most time and attention, and asking in spring also gives teachers the summer to think. A good rule is to ask at least six to eight weeks before your first deadline. For a November 1 Early Action application, that means mid-September at the latest. Chapter 1's worked example on planning backward from a deadline showed exactly this. If your school has its own timeline for requests, such as a counselor's form due in May, follow it.

docs.title: Asking for a Recommendation
docs.text: Asking for a recommendation is the conversation, ideally in person, in which you request a letter from a teacher. Keep it simple and direct. Say you'd value their recommendation, and explain why them in a specific sentence: what you think they can speak to. Then give them an easy way to decline. Ask, "Would you feel comfortable writing me a strong recommendation?" That gives a teacher who doesn't know you well enough room to say so gracefully. You want a letter from someone who says yes with enthusiasm, not one who feels obligated. Follow up the same day with a short email confirming the request and saying when you'll send your materials.

docs.title: Worked Example: Priya Asks Mr. Grant
docs.text:
In May of junior year, Priya stops by Mr. Grant's room after class:

"Mr. Grant, I'm applying to colleges this fall, and I'd really value a recommendation from you. AP Chem was my hardest class, and you saw me work through it, especially stoichiometry, where I came in four or five times. I think you could speak to how I handle things that don't come easily. Would you feel comfortable writing me a strong recommendation?"

Mr. Grant says yes. That evening, Priya sends a short email thanking him, saying her first deadline is November 1, and telling him she'll send a brag sheet and list of colleges by the end of August.

docs.title: The Brag Sheet
docs.text:
A brag sheet is a short document, usually one or two pages, that you give a recommender to remind them of your accomplishments, your goals, and specific moments from their class or activity that they might mention. It builds on your activities resume from Chapter 8, but it's tailored to each recommender. Many counselors provide a brag sheet template. If yours doesn't, you can write your own.

A useful brag sheet for a teacher includes:

  • Two or three specific moments from their class you're proud of, such as a project, a breakthrough, a discussion, or a time you helped someone.
  • What you learned or how you grew in the class.
  • Your goals: intended major, kinds of colleges, and what you hope to study.
  • Anything you'd like them to know that might help them connect their letter to the rest of your application, such as a theme from your essay.

Write it in plain language, and keep it brief. Teachers are busy, and the goal is to jog their memory with specifics, not to write the letter for them.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Brag Sheet Entry
docs.text:
Here's the "moments" section of Priya's brag sheet for Mr. Grant:

Moments from AP Chemistry I'm proud of:

  • Stoichiometry, October. I failed the first quiz (58%). I came to your room four mornings that month, and you had me explain each step out loud. I got an 89 on the unit test.
  • Lab report on reaction rates, February. My group's results didn't match the expected curve. Instead of adjusting the numbers, I suggested we write about why: our water bath temperature drifted. You read part of our discussion section to the class.
  • Study group, spring. I started a Thursday study group for the AP exam, with six classmates.

Each entry gives Mr. Grant a specific, accurate detail he can use, and a reason to remember Priya as more than a B on a gradebook.

docs.title: Recommender Deadlines
docs.text: Recommender deadlines are the dates by which your recommenders must submit their letters for each college. They're usually the college's supporting document deadline, as Chapter 5 described, which can be a week or two after the application deadline. Give each recommender a list of your colleges with each deadline, and ask them to submit by your earliest deadline whenever possible. Most letters submitted through the Common App go to all the colleges you've assigned at once, so one early submission covers everything. Track each letter's status in your tracker, and send a polite check-in a week or two before each deadline if it hasn't been submitted. Teachers manage dozens of letters, so a gentle reminder is helpful, not rude.

docs.title: The Recommender Packet
docs.text: The recommender packet is the complete set of materials you give each recommender at once: a short cover note thanking them, your brag sheet for them, your activities resume, a list of your colleges with deadlines and how letters will be submitted, and any school-specific forms. Packaging everything together saves recommenders from having to search through separate emails and makes it far more likely they'll write a strong letter on time. Send it as one email with attachments, or as one shared folder, by the date you promised when you asked, ideally at least four to six weeks before your first deadline. Keep a copy in your filing system's Recommendations folder (Chapter 5).

docs.title: Worked Example: Priya's Packet for Mr. Grant
docs.text:
On August 28, Priya emails Mr. Grant one message, "Recommendation materials — Priya Raman," with:

  1. A three-sentence note thanking him again.
  2. Her brag sheet for AP Chemistry (one page).
  3. Her activities resume (one page).
  4. A table of the six colleges that require teacher letters, each with its deadline, starting with the earliest (November 1).
  5. A note that letters are submitted through the Common App, and that he'll get an invitation email in early September.

She records "Packet sent Aug 28" in her tracker and sets a reminder for October 18 to check whether his letter appears in the Common App as submitted.

docs.title: The FERPA Waiver
docs.text:
The FERPA waiver is a choice you make on your application about whether to give up your right to see your recommendation letters in the future. FERPA, the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, is a federal law that gives students the right to view their education records after they enroll at a college. On the Common App, you complete the FERPA release before you can invite recommenders, and you decide whether to waive your right to see the letters.

Most counselors advise waiving it. When you waive your right, colleges know your recommenders wrote freely, knowing you'd never read the letter. That makes the letters more credible. Some teachers also prefer to write only for students who have waived. Not waiving doesn't disqualify you, but it can make a reader wonder about the letter. Your decision is shared with your recommenders and colleges, applies to every college on your list, and can't be changed once you've invited your first recommender, so make it carefully before you invite anyone.

docs.title: Thank-You Notes
docs.text: Thank-you notes are short, sincere messages you send your recommenders after they submit your letters, and again when you hear your decisions. Writing a letter takes a teacher real time, often an evening or more, and is usually done on top of their regular work. A handwritten note, or at least a personal email, thanking them for their time and telling them where you're applying is the right thing to do. Then follow up in the spring to tell them where you were admitted and where you've decided to go. Teachers rarely hear how things turned out, and they genuinely want to know.

docs.title: The Additional Recommendation
docs.text:
An additional recommendation is an optional letter beyond what a college requires, often from a coach, employer, activity advisor, religious leader, or mentor who knows you outside the classroom. Some colleges invite one, some limit them, and some don't accept them at all. Check each college's policy.

The rule is simple: send one only if it adds something new. A letter from your employer describing how you trained new staff, or from a coach describing how you led younger teammates, can show a side of you that teacher letters can't. A third teacher letter that repeats the first two adds nothing and adds to the reader's workload. When in doubt, don't send it. More letters aren't better. Different letters are.

docs.title: Worked Example: Is a Third Letter Worth It?
docs.text:
Marcus's two teacher letters come from his junior-year math and chemistry teachers. He's considering two possible additional letters:

  • His robotics coach, who saw him mentor sophomores on the navigation code and lead the programming team for two years.
  • His English teacher, who gave him an A and likes him.

The robotics coach can describe leadership and teamwork that neither classroom teacher saw. That letter adds something new. The English teacher's letter would mostly repeat what his other teachers say. Marcus asks the coach and only sends the letter to the colleges that invite an additional recommendation.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Letters of recommendation give readers outside confirmation of who you are. The strongest are specific, and you can make specificity more likely.
  • Most selective colleges want one or two teacher recommendations, usually from 11th- or 12th-grade core subjects, plus a counselor recommendation that explains your context.
  • Choosing recommenders: pick teachers who know you well, ideally recent and from different subjects. The highest grade doesn't matter as much as how well they know you.
  • Request timing: ask in spring of junior year or the very start of senior year, at least six to eight weeks before your first deadline.
  • Asking: ask in person, say why you're asking them, and give them an easy way to decline.
  • Give each recommender a recommender packet: a brag sheet with specific moments, your resume, and your colleges with recommender deadlines. Check in politely before deadlines.
  • Sign the FERPA waiver to waive access. It makes letters more credible.
  • Send thank-you notes, and tell recommenders how things turned out.
  • An additional recommendation is worth sending only if it adds something new.

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
You earned an A in a large lecture-style class where the teacher barely knows you, and a B+ in a smaller class where the teacher has seen you struggle and improve. Who should you ask?

The B+ teacher who knows you well. They can write a specific, vivid letter. The A teacher can only confirm your grade, which your transcript already shows.

Your first application deadline is November 1. When should you ask your teachers, and when should they have your packet?

Ask by spring of junior year, and no later than mid-September. Send the recommender packet by late August or early September, at least four to six weeks before the deadline.

Why do most counselors recommend waiving your FERPA right to see your letters?

Waiving tells colleges your recommenders wrote freely, which makes the letters more credible to readers. Some teachers also prefer to write only for students who waive.

What should a brag sheet include?

Two or three specific moments from the class or activity, what you learned or how you grew, your goals, and anything that helps the recommender connect their letter to your application.

A college accepts optional additional letters. You could ask a third teacher who'd say similar things, or your manager at work. Which is better, and why?

The manager, because that letter shows a side of you (responsibility, work ethic, leadership at work) that teacher letters can't. An additional letter should add something new, not repeat the others.

docs.title: Filling Out the Common App and Coalition App
Summary
docs.text: This chapter walks section by section through the Common App and Coalition App, from profile to supplements, plus fees and waivers, submission, and sending transcripts and scores. This is where all the earlier work comes together in the application itself. Students finish able to complete, preview, and submit an application with transcripts and scores sent correctly.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 24 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Application Fee 2 Fee Waiver 1 Self-Reported Scores 128 Coalition App 126 Common App Dashboard 135 Adding Colleges 134 Profile Section 639 Family Section 127 Education Section 511 Testing Section 127 Activities Section 255 Writing Section 254 Additional Information Section 127 Self-Reported Academic Record 128 Courses and Grades Section 127 Member Questions 128 Writing Supplements 127 Assigning Recommenders 1 Application Preview 126 Application Submission 125 Submission Confirmation 124 Institution Codes 4 Sending Official Transcripts 1 Sending Test Scores 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: How Colleges Evaluate Applicants
  • Chapter 4: Researching and Narrowing Your College List
  • Chapter 5: Getting Organized
  • Chapter 6: The SAT and ACT Question
  • Chapter 8: Activities and Resume
  • Chapter 9: The Personal Essay
  • Chapter 10: Supplemental Essays
  • Chapter 11: Letters of Recommendation

docs.title: Where Everything Comes Together
docs.text:
Every earlier chapter built a piece of your application: your list, your test plan, your activities, your essays, your recommenders. This chapter is where those pieces go into the form itself. Most of the Common App is straightforward. But a few spots trip up nearly every applicant, such as a misspelled name, a missing dual-enrollment course, a self-reported grade that doesn't match the transcript, or a recommender never assigned to a college. Mistakes like these can delay or derail an application that's otherwise strong.

This chapter walks through the application in the order you'll meet it. It starts with the two shared platforms, the Common App and the Coalition App, and the Common App's dashboard, where you add colleges. Then it goes section by section through the core application: profile, family, education, testing, activities, and writing, plus the courses-and-grades section some colleges require. Next come each college's own questions and writing supplements, and assigning recommenders. The chapter ends with fees and waivers, previewing and submitting, confirming submission, and sending official transcripts and test scores.

Platforms update their layouts every year, so section names and the order of questions may differ slightly from what's described here. The logic stays the same.

docs.title: The Common App Dashboard
docs.text:
The Common App dashboard is the home screen of your Common App account. It lists every college you've added, along with each college's deadlines and the status of each part of your application for that college. Chapter 5 covered creating the account. The dashboard is where you'll manage it.

The Common App is organized into a few main areas, usually shown as tabs:

  • Dashboard: your colleges, deadlines, and a checklist of what's complete and what's missing for each.
  • My Colleges: each college's own questions, writing supplements, recommenders, and submission steps.
  • Common App: the core sections that go to every college, including profile, family, education, testing, activities, and writing.
  • College Search: where you find colleges and add them to your list.

The dashboard's job is to show you, at a glance, what's left. Each college has a status for every required component, such as the core application, the college's questions, the writing supplement, recommendations, and payment. A green check means complete. Anything else needs your attention. Look at the dashboard each time you log in, and compare it with your own tracker from Chapter 5. When the two disagree, the dashboard is usually showing you something you've missed.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading the Dashboard
docs.text:
In mid-October, Priya's dashboard shows her eight Common App colleges. (Her state flagship isn't there, since it uses its own application.) For College C, her Early Action target, every item has a green check. For Hillcrest College, her Regular Decision target, she sees "Writing supplement: in progress" and "Recommenders: not invited."

The first is expected, because her Why Hillcrest essay isn't finished yet. The second is a surprise. She'd invited her teachers through the Common App in September, but she'd added Hillcrest after assigning them, so they were never assigned to Hillcrest. She fixes it in My Colleges in two minutes. Without the dashboard, she'd have learned about it in January from a missing-documents email.

docs.title: Adding Colleges
docs.text:
Adding colleges means putting each college from your final list into your Common App account, so its questions, supplements, and deadlines appear in your application. You add colleges through the College Search tab, up to 20, as Chapter 5 noted. When you add a college, you'll choose your application round (such as Early Action or Regular Decision) and your term of entry, and some colleges ask you to choose a program or campus right away.

Adding a college early has two benefits. First, you see that college's requirements: its deadlines, its member questions, its writing supplements, and how many recommendations it requires. That's how you build the supplement plan from Chapter 10. Second, it lets you assign recommenders to that college, which you'll need to do for every college on your list. You can remove a college you decide not to apply to, though once you've submitted an application, it stays on your record. Double-check the application round for each college as you add it. Choosing Early Decision by mistake, or missing an Early Action option, is an easy error that's hard to undo once submitted.

docs.title: Worked Example: Choosing the Round
docs.text: Marcus adds ten colleges to his Common App. For eight of them, the round is simple: Regular Decision, the only round he's using. For Lakeshore University, the menu offers Early Decision I, Early Decision II, Early Action, and Regular Decision. He has no plans to commit before comparing aid offers, which Chapter 1 explained Early Decision would require, so he selects Early Action. He then checks the dashboard, which now shows Lakeshore's November 1 deadline in place of the January date. He updates his tracker to match.

docs.title: The Coalition App
docs.text:
The Coalition App is a second shared application platform, now run on the Scoir platform, that a smaller group of colleges accepts. Some colleges accept both the Common App and the Coalition App, and a few accept only the Coalition App alongside their own institutional application. Like the Common App, it has core sections that go to every college, plus college-specific questions and essays, and a set of essay prompts for its personal statement.

For most students, the Common App covers most or all of their list, and there's no reason to complete both platforms for the same college. Colleges that accept both treat them equally. Use the Coalition App when a college on your list accepts it but not the Common App, or when you're already using it for other colleges. Check each college's admissions page for the platforms it accepts, and record your choice in your tracker. Everything this chapter says about accuracy, previewing, and confirming submission applies equally to the Coalition App.

docs.title: Worked Example: Deciding Between Platforms
docs.text: Ana's list includes one college that accepts the Common App, the Coalition App, and its own application. The other seven accept the Common App. Since her Common App is already complete for seven colleges, adding the eighth there takes minutes, while the Coalition App would mean entering her profile, activities, and essay all over again. She uses the Common App. If one of her colleges had accepted only the Coalition App, she would have used it for that one college, copying her activities and essay from her saved documents.

docs.title: The Core Common App Sections
docs.text:
The core sections of the Common App are filled out once and sent to every college. The table below previews them in the order they usually appear. Each gets its own short section after the table.

Section What it covers What to watch for Profile Your name, address, contact information, demographics, citizenship, and fee waiver eligibility Your legal name exactly as on school records Family Household, parents' or guardians' education and jobs, siblings Complete parent education; it affects first-generation status Education Your high school, other schools, college courses, grades, current courses, honors Every school and college course you've taken Testing Self-reported SAT, ACT, AP, IB, and other scores Report only where you've decided to submit Activities Up to 10 activities The 150-character descriptions (Chapter 8) Writing Personal essay and optional additional information Paste and preview carefully Courses and Grades A full self-reported transcript, for colleges that require it Enter exactly what's on your transcript

docs.title: The Profile Section
docs.text:
The profile section is the first section of the Common App, covering your personal information: legal name and any preferred name, birthdate, address, phone, email, citizenship, language, and optional demographic questions. It also includes fee waiver questions, covered later in this chapter. Everything you enter here is copied into every application you send, so a typo here becomes a typo everywhere.

The most important detail is your legal name. It must match your official documents, including your transcript, test registrations, and eventually your financial aid forms, exactly. Colleges match incoming documents to your file partly by name. A mismatch, such as "Priya S. Raman" on the Common App and "Priya Sunita Raman" on the transcript, can leave documents unmatched and your file "incomplete." You can enter a preferred name separately. Use the email address from Chapter 5, and double-check your phone number and address. Demographic questions are optional, so answer what you're comfortable answering.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Unmatched Transcript
docs.text:
Casey's legal name is "Casey Lin Nguyen-Park," but Casey filled out the profile as "Casey Park" from habit. Casey's high school sent the transcript under the legal name. Three weeks later, one college's portal still showed "Transcript: not received," even though the counselor had sent it. The college's operations staff, as Chapter 1 described, had received a transcript for a "Casey Nguyen-Park" that didn't match any applicant.

A short email to admissions fixed it. But Casey updated the profile to the legal name immediately, before submitting to the remaining colleges, and added "Casey" as the preferred name.

docs.title: The Family Section
docs.text:
The family section asks about your household: who you live with, your parents' or guardians' names, education, and occupations, and your siblings. It may seem routine, but colleges use it in several ways. It's how they learn whether you're a first-generation student (Chapter 2), whether you have legacy connections at their college, and something about your family's circumstances.

Answer completely and accurately. For each parent or guardian, report the highest level of education they actually completed, such as high school, some college, an associate degree, or a bachelor's degree, and list any colleges they attended. Don't decide for yourself whether you "count" as first-generation. Each college applies its own definition to your answers. If your family situation doesn't fit the form neatly, for example a guardian who isn't a parent, a parent you have no contact with, or a blended family, the form usually allows for it. You can also add a brief explanation in the additional information section.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reporting Parent Education
docs.text: Ana enters her mother's education as "Associate degree" and lists the community college she attended. She enters her father's education as "High school." She doesn't add any note about being first-generation. Her colleges will see from these answers that neither parent completed a bachelor's degree. In her counselor meeting, Ana confirmed that this is what most of her colleges use to identify first-generation applicants, and that her counselor will also mention it in the counselor letter.

docs.title: The Education Section
docs.text:
The education section covers your schooling: your current high school (identified by its CEEB code, a six-digit code your counselor can confirm), any other high schools you've attended, any college courses you've taken, your grades and GPA, your current-year courses, your honors, and your future plans. This is also where you connect your counselor to your application, as Chapter 5 described.

Two rules matter most. First, list everything. That includes every high school you've attended, even briefly, and every college course you've taken, including dual enrollment and summer programs at a college. A college that later finds an unlisted course on a college transcript may treat it as an omission. Second, enter your grade information exactly as your school reports it. That means your GPA, its scale, whether it's weighted, and your class rank, if your school reports one. Your school profile will show the same information, and the two should match.

The current courses list matters too. It's how colleges see your senior schedule, which Chapter 7 explained they read closely. Enter every course you're taking this year with its full name and level, such as "AP Calculus AB," not "Calc."

docs.title: Worked Example: The Dual-Enrollment Courses
docs.text: Marcus fills out the Education section and almost skips "Colleges and universities." Then he remembers his two community college courses from Chapter 7. He adds the community college, the dates, and both courses, Introduction to Programming and Discrete Mathematics. He also checks that his counselor knows to send the community college transcript separately, and adds a line to his tracker. Leaving them off would have hidden two of his strongest rigor signals. It would also have created a discrepancy when the college transcript arrived later.

docs.title: The Testing Section
docs.text:
The testing section is where you report your scores on the SAT, ACT, AP exams, IB exams, and English proficiency tests such as the TOEFL, if you choose to. The scores you enter here are self-reported scores, covered next. Because the section goes to every college, but your submission decision differs by college (Chapter 6), most applications also ask, in each college's own questions, whether you want that college to consider your scores. Use that question to carry out your college-by-college decision.

Report scores exactly as they appear on your official score reports, including section scores and test dates. If you're superscoring, enter each test date's section scores as the form asks, and let colleges that superscore combine them. Report AP and IB scores selectively, as Chapter 7 suggested. Strong ones help, and leaving off weaker ones is usually fine.

docs.title: Self-Reported Scores
docs.text:
Self-reported scores are test scores you enter yourself on an application, rather than having them sent officially by the College Board or ACT. Many colleges accept them for admission review and require an official score report (Chapter 6) only if you enroll. That saves you the cost of sending official reports to every college.

Self-reporting comes with one firm rule: accuracy. If you're admitted and enroll, the college will compare your official report with what you reported, and a discrepancy can lead to a rescinded offer. Enter scores straight from your College Board or ACT account, not from memory.

docs.title: Worked Example: Following Each College's Rule
docs.text:
Priya, from Chapter 6, enters both of her SAT test dates in the Testing section: June (680 Reading and Writing, 600 Math) and October (660 and 650). Then she uses each college's own testing question to carry out her decisions:

  • College A (test-required): she answers "Yes, consider my scores" and sends official reports from her College Board account.
  • College C (test-optional, superscores): "Yes." She self-reports only for now.
  • College B (test-optional): "No, do not consider my scores." College B will review her application without them.

One Testing section, filled out once, supports three different decisions, because the per-college question controls what each college sees.

docs.title: The Activities Section
docs.text:
The activities section is where you list up to 10 extracurricular activities in the format Chapter 8 described: activity type, position, organization, a 150-character description, grade levels, timing, and hours. By this point, you've already done the hard part, which is writing and ordering your entries. Your job here is to transfer them accurately.

Copy your entries from your activities resume into the form, then check three things. First, fit: the form counts characters strictly, and some symbols count differently than you expect, so check that nothing is cut off. Second, order: you can rearrange entries, so make sure the order matches what you decided in Chapter 8. Third, consistency: your hours and grade levels should match what your recommenders and essays say. A reader who sees "4 years" in your activity entry and "since junior year" in your essay will notice.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Truncated Description
docs.text: Priya pastes her literary magazine description into the activities form: "Lead staff of 8; started first online issue; read 200+ submissions/yr; edit and lay out 2 print issues/yr." That's 106 characters in her document. The form shows the full text, but in the preview, the "+" displays oddly. She changes "200+" to "over 200," which reads clearly at the same length. The issue is small, but this is exactly what the preview step later in this chapter is designed to catch.

docs.title: The Writing Section
docs.text:
The writing section holds your personal essay, from Chapter 9, and an optional additional information box. You'll choose your prompt and paste your essay into a text box with a 650-word limit.

Paste carefully. Formatting such as italics, bold, and special characters may not carry over from a word processor. Paragraph breaks sometimes disappear or double. After pasting, read the essay in the box itself and in the application preview, and fix anything that changed. Check the word count in the box, which is the one colleges see. Keep the final version in your essay drafts folder.

You may have heard that the Common App asks about disciplinary history. It used to. The Common App dropped its criminal history question in 2018 and its school discipline question starting with the 2021–22 application, but individual colleges can still ask either one in their own member questions. If a college asks, answer honestly. A brief explanation that shows what you learned is far better than an omission discovered later.

docs.title: The Additional Information Section
docs.text:
The additional information section is an optional space, up to 650 words, within the Writing section, for context that the rest of your application doesn't explain. It's not a second personal essay. Use it only when you have something important to clarify, such as:

  • A gap in your schooling, or a semester with unusual grades.
  • A family circumstance, such as caring for a family member, a parent's illness or job loss, or homelessness.
  • A health issue or disability that affected your record, if you choose to share it.
  • A school situation, such as a change in grading policy, a school closure, or a course you couldn't take because it wasn't offered.
  • A brief clarification, such as an activity that needed more than 150 characters to make sense.

Write it plainly and briefly, in factual sentences rather than essay style. A few sentences is often enough. An empty additional information section is completely normal and not a red flag. Filling it with more accomplishments, or a second essay, doesn't help and can dilute the rest of your file.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Brief, Factual Note
docs.text:
Jordan's sophomore spring grades dropped from A's and B's to C's, then recovered by junior year. The reason was a family move mid-semester, which meant switching to a school with a different curriculum. Jordan writes three sentences in the additional information section:

"In March of my sophomore year, my family moved from Ohio to Iowa for my mother's job. I finished the semester at a new school with a different math and science sequence, which explains my lower grades that spring. My grades returned to A's and B's the following fall."

It's factual, brief, and explains a pattern a reader would otherwise wonder about. Jordan doesn't need to say more.

docs.title: Self-Reported Academic Records
docs.text: A self-reported academic record is a transcript you enter yourself, listing every high school course and grade, which some colleges require in place of, or in addition to, an official transcript at the time you apply. Colleges use self-reported records because they're faster to review and easier to compare than official transcripts in many different formats. Some colleges collect them through the Common App's Courses and Grades section. Others use a separate system, which they'll link to after you apply. If you're admitted, the college checks your self-report against your official transcript, so the two must match. Check each college's requirements, and record which ones require a self-report in your tracker.

docs.title: The Courses and Grades Section
docs.text:
The courses and grades section is the Common App's version of a self-reported academic record. It appears in your application only if at least one of your colleges requires it. You enter every course you took from 9th grade on, with its level (such as honors or AP), credits, and the grade for each term, exactly as your transcript reports them.

This section is tedious, often an hour or two of careful typing, and accuracy matters more than speed. Do it with your unofficial transcript (Chapter 5) open next to you, not from memory. Enter courses with the names and grades on your transcript, even if you think a grade was unfair or a course name is odd. Don't round grades, convert them, or calculate your own GPA here unless the form asks you to. Discrepancies between your self-report and your official transcript can raise questions, and in serious cases can lead to a rescinded offer.

docs.title: Worked Example: Checking Against the Transcript
docs.text: Marcus finishes his Courses and Grades section, then checks every entry against his unofficial transcript, line by line. He finds two errors. He'd entered his sophomore chemistry grade as B+, but his transcript says B. And he'd listed "Intro to Computer Science" in 9th grade, but the transcript calls it "Computer Applications I." He fixes both. Neither would have changed his admission decision. But if they'd been discovered after admission, both would have looked like attempts to make his record look better than it was.

docs.title: Member Questions
docs.text:
Member questions are the questions each college adds to the Common App for its own applicants, beyond the core sections. They appear under each college in the My Colleges tab. They cover things like your intended major and program, your interest in financial aid or specific scholarships, whether you want your test scores considered, how you heard about the college, family connections to the college, residency, and sometimes short-answer questions.

Answer them as carefully as the core sections, because they often control important things: which program you're applying to, whether you're considered for merit scholarships, and whether your scores are seen. Some questions can't be changed after submission, especially major and program choices at colleges with capped majors (Chapter 3). Read each one, and if you're unsure what a question means, check the college's admissions website or email the admissions office before submitting.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Question That Mattered
docs.text:
For one public university, Marcus's member questions ask him to choose a first-choice major and an optional second-choice major. The university's CS program is capped, so in Chapter 3 he decided it was a reach for him. If he lists only CS and isn't admitted to the program, the university may deny him entirely. If he lists a second choice, such as Mathematics, the university can admit him to the second program instead.

He lists Computer Science first and Mathematics second, after confirming on the university's website how second choices are handled. One member question made the difference between a possible denial and a possible admission in a related field.

docs.title: Writing Supplements
docs.text:
Writing supplements are the supplemental essays and short-answer questions each college adds to its section of the Common App, which you planned and wrote in Chapter 10. They appear under each college in My Colleges.

Paste each supplement from your drafts folder, and check three things before moving on: that you're answering the right prompt (some colleges offer a choice), that you're within the word limit shown in the box, and that every college name and detail is correct. That last check is the recycled-essay trap from Chapter 10. It's worth one more careful read for every college, especially when you've adapted essays across colleges. Work through supplements one college at a time, so you stay in the right frame of mind for each college's details.

docs.title: Assigning Recommenders
docs.text: Assigning recommenders is the step of inviting your teachers and counselor through the Common App and connecting them to each college that needs their letters. It happens in My Colleges, under each college's recommenders section, after you've completed the FERPA release from Chapter 11. You invite each recommender once by email, then assign them to each college individually. Recommenders you invite aren't automatically assigned to colleges you add later, which is what happened to Priya with Hillcrest. Check every college's recommender status on the dashboard after adding a new college, and don't invite teachers until you've asked them in person, as Chapter 11 described.

docs.title: Application Fees
docs.text: An application fee is the charge a college sets for processing your application, paid when you submit. Fees typically range from nothing to around $90, and some colleges charge nothing at all. On the Common App, you pay each college's fee separately when you submit to that college. Across a list of eight to twelve colleges, fees can add up to several hundred dollars, so include them in your family's budget conversation from Chapter 3. If cost is a concern, fee waivers can help.

docs.title: Fee Waivers
docs.text: A fee waiver is a request to have an application fee waived because paying it would be a financial hardship. On the Common App, you answer fee waiver eligibility questions in the profile section. Students who meet the criteria, such as qualifying for free or reduced-price school lunch, receiving certain public benefits, or having a household income within the platform's guidelines, can have fees waived at member colleges, and your counselor may be asked to confirm eligibility. Students who received an SAT or ACT fee waiver can also use them for college application fees at many colleges. And many colleges waive fees for first-generation students, for students who visit, or during certain periods. Check each college's website and ask your counselor. Fee waivers are confidential, and using one has no effect on your admission.

docs.title: Application Preview
docs.text:
The application preview is the PDF of your completed application, exactly as a college will see it, which the Common App generates before you submit. Preview your application for every college before submitting, even if you've already submitted to others. Each college's version includes its own questions and supplements, and formatting can shift between the entry form and the PDF. Line breaks, special characters, and essay paragraphs sometimes display differently.

Read the preview slowly, top to bottom. Check your name, contact information, and every date. Read your activities and essay as a reader would. Confirm that every section you expected is present. The preview is your last chance to catch errors before a reader does. The checklist below walks you through a full pre-submission review.

docs.title: Diagram: Pre-Submission Checklist
docs.text:
Pre-Submission Checklist

Type: microsim sim-id: pre-submission-checklist Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Walk students through a complete, college-specific pre-submission review so that common errors (name mismatches, missing courses, wrong round, unassigned recommenders, truncated essays) are caught before submission.

Bloom Level: Apply (L3) Bloom Verb: execute, check Learning Objective: Students will execute a structured pre-submission review of a Common App application for one college, checking every section and college-specific requirement before submitting.

Canvas layout: - Top: createInput "College name" and createSelect "Round" (ED, EA, REA, RD, Rolling). - Middle: grouped checklist with createCheckbox for each item: - Core application: Legal name matches transcript; Address, phone, and dedicated email correct; Parent education complete; Every school and college course listed; Current-year courses listed with full names; Scores entered exactly as on reports; Activities in chosen order, none cut off; Essay pasted and paragraphs intact; Additional information used only if needed. - Courses and Grades (shown only if a "This college requires Courses and Grades" checkbox is checked): Checked line by line against unofficial transcript. - This college: Correct round selected; Major/program choices confirmed; Testing question answered per my decision; All member questions answered; Supplements pasted, within limits, correct prompt; College name and details correct in every supplement. - Recommenders: FERPA release complete; Counselor assigned; Required teachers assigned to this college. - Final: PDF preview read in full; Fee paid or waiver applied. - Right side (below on narrow screens): a progress ring and a "Why this matters" infobox that shows a one-sentence explanation and a chapter reference for the most recently hovered item (e.g., "Name mismatch: documents may not match your file — see Profile Section").

Controls (all created in setup() before positioning): createInput, createSelect, createCheckbox for each item, createButton "Reset," and createButton "Show only unchecked."

Completion behavior: When every visible item is checked, the ring turns green and the message reads "Ready to submit [college]. After submitting, look for the confirmation email and the dashboard check."

Interaction: Items can be checked in any order. "Show only unchecked" hides completed items.

Persistence: Use localStorage (wrapped in try/catch) keyed by college name so a student can keep separate checklists for each college; the sim must render correctly if storage is unavailable.

Responsive behavior: Call updateCanvasSize() first in setup(); groups stack on narrow screens and controls reposition on resize.

Implementation: p5.js with createInput, createSelect, createCheckbox, and createButton; canvas parented to the main element.

docs.title: Application Submission
docs.text:
Application submission is the final step of sending your completed application to a college. On the Common App, you submit to each college separately. You'll review the preview, answer a short set of certification questions affirming that your application is your own work and accurate, pay the fee or apply a waiver, and click submit. Afterward, check the dashboard to make sure every part for that college, including any writing supplement, shows as complete.

Submit early, ideally a few days before your personal due date from Chapter 5, not on deadline night. Servers slow down near major deadlines, payment systems sometimes fail, and you may discover a last-minute problem. Submitting a few days ahead turns any of those into a minor annoyance. Once you submit, you generally can't change your submitted application for that college, though you can usually update your core application for colleges you haven't submitted to yet.

docs.title: Worked Example: Submitting Early
docs.text: Priya's personal due date for College C's November 1 Early Action deadline is October 27. She finishes on October 25, previews the PDF, and submits that evening. On October 31, a classmate tells her the Common App is running slowly and a friend's payment failed twice. Priya isn't affected. She'd already received her confirmation and, on October 29, an email from the college with her applicant portal login.

docs.title: Submission Confirmation
docs.text: Submission confirmation is the evidence that a college received your application: a confirmation on your dashboard, a confirmation email from the Common App, and usually, within days to a couple of weeks, an email from the college with instructions for its applicant portal (Chapter 5). Confirmations can take a few minutes to a few hours to appear, so don't panic if one isn't instant. Do check back, and don't consider an application done until you have confirmation. Save each confirmation email and a screenshot of the dashboard in that college's folder, update your tracker, and set a reminder to check the college's portal about a week later for missing documents.

docs.title: Institution Codes
docs.text:
Institution codes are the identification numbers testing agencies, financial aid systems, and application platforms use to send your documents to the right college. Each college has several, one for each system:

Code Used for Example: University of Iowa SAT code (College Board) Sending official SAT and AP scores 6681 ACT code Sending official ACT scores 1356 Federal School Code Sending your FAFSA to the college (Chapter 14) 001892 CEEB code (your high school) Identifying your high school on applications Your counselor can confirm it

Find each college's codes on its admissions website, usually on a "how to send scores" page, or by searching in your College Board, ACT, or FAFSA account. Record them in your tracker. A score report sent with the wrong code goes to the wrong college and can't easily be redirected.

docs.title: Sending Official Transcripts
docs.text: Sending official transcripts is the step of having your high school send your official transcript to each college, along with the school report and counselor letter. You don't send it yourself. You request it, following your school's process. Many schools send transcripts electronically through the Common App or through services such as Naviance, Scoir, or Parchment, once you've added colleges and connected your counselor. Others use a request form. Ask your counselor in early fall how your school handles requests and how much lead time it needs, then make the request well before each supporting document deadline. Remember that dual-enrollment courses need a separate transcript from the college that granted the credit (Chapter 7). After each deadline, check each college's portal to confirm the transcript arrived and was matched to your file.

docs.title: Sending Test Scores
docs.text: Sending test scores means ordering official score reports from the College Board or ACT for the colleges that require them, as Chapter 6 described. Log in to your testing account, choose the test dates to send (using Score Choice where allowed), enter each college's code, and pay the fee or apply a fee waiver. Order reports at least two to three weeks before each college's supporting document deadline, since they take time to be delivered and matched to your file. For colleges that accept self-reported scores, wait. You'll send an official report only to the college where you enroll. Record each order in your tracker.
