docs.title: Worked Example: Casey Sends Scores to Iowa
docs.text: Casey, an Iowa resident applying Early Action to the University of Iowa, plans to submit an ACT score. From Iowa's admissions website, Casey learns that Iowa's supporting documents deadline for Early Action is November 9, and finds Iowa's ACT code, 1356. On October 15, Casey logs in to MyACT, selects the September test date, enters code 1356, and pays for the report. Casey records "ACT sent Oct 15, code 1356" in the tracker and sets a reminder for November 1 to check Iowa's applicant portal. On October 28, the portal shows the score as received.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The Common App dashboard shows each college's status. Check it every time you log in. Adding colleges brings in each college's requirements, so double-check the application round.
  • The Coalition App is a second shared platform. Use whichever platform covers your list. Colleges treat them equally.
  • In the profile section, use your legal name exactly as on school records. The family section determines first-generation and legacy information. The education section must list every school and college course.
  • The testing section holds self-reported scores. Use each college's own question to carry out your submission decision. Self-reported scores must be exact.
  • The activities section and writing section hold the work from Chapters 8 and 9. Paste carefully and check formatting. The additional information section is for brief, factual context, and leaving it empty is normal.
  • A self-reported academic record, including the Common App's courses and grades section, must match your transcript line by line.
  • Member questions can control your program and scholarship consideration. Writing supplements need a final check for the right prompt, length, and college name. Assigning recommenders must be done for every college.
  • Application fees add up. Fee waivers are available and confidential.
  • Read every application preview, complete application submission days early, and save each submission confirmation.
  • Use the right institution codes. Request official transcripts through your school, and send test scores only where required.

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
Your Common App profile says 'Taylor Kim,' but your transcript says 'Taylor A. Kim-Morales.' What could happen, and how do you fix it?

Colleges may not be able to match your transcript to your file, leaving it marked incomplete. Change the profile to your legal name exactly as on school records, and list your preferred name separately.

You invited two teachers in September and added a new college in October. Why might that college show 'recommenders not invited'?

Recommenders aren't automatically assigned to colleges you add later. Go to My Colleges and assign them to the new college.

One college on your list is test-optional, and you decided not to submit scores there. Your SAT is in the Testing section. How do you keep that college from considering it?

Answer that college's member question about testing with "do not consider my scores." The per-college question controls what each college sees.

What belongs in the additional information section, and what doesn't?

It's for brief, factual context the rest of the application doesn't explain, such as a move, an illness, a family responsibility, or a school policy. It's not for a second essay or more accomplishments, and leaving it empty is normal.

Why should you submit a few days before the deadline instead of the night of?

Servers slow down, payments can fail, and last-minute problems happen near deadlines. Submitting early turns those into minor annoyances and gives you time to confirm submission.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers the kinds of college interviews, how to prepare and practice, what questions to ask, and how to follow up. Interviews are optional at many schools but can add a real voice to an application. After this chapter, students can prepare for any interview format and leave a good impression.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 10 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Interviews 17 Alumni Interview 2 Admissions Officer Interview 2 Evaluative Interview 5 Informational Interview 5 Virtual Interview 2 Interview Preparation 4 Practice Interview 1 Questions to Ask Interviewer 1 Interview Follow-Up 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
  • Chapter 2: How Colleges Evaluate Applicants
  • Chapter 10: Supplemental Essays

docs.title: A Conversation, Not a Test
docs.text:
Many colleges never interview applicants. Of those that do, most treat the interview as optional, and it's rarely what decides an application. But an interview does something nothing else in your file can: it lets a real person hear you think and talk. A good one adds warmth and color to an application. A poorly prepared one is an easy miss to avoid.

The good news is that interviewers aren't trying to catch you out. They aren't testing facts or looking for polished speeches. Mostly, they want to have a genuine conversation with a curious, engaged person. This chapter explains the different kinds of interviews, then covers how to prepare, practice, ask good questions, and follow up.

docs.title: Interviews
docs.text:
A college interview is a conversation, usually 30 to 60 minutes long, between an applicant and someone representing the college: an admissions officer, an alum, or sometimes a current student. Colleges use interviews for two reasons. Some use them to learn more about you, as one more piece of evidence in holistic review (Chapter 2). Others use them mainly to help you learn about the college, and to show interest in you. Many do both.

Policies vary widely, and the right approach depends on the college's policy:

  • Not offered: many large public universities and some private colleges don't interview at all. You don't need to do anything.
  • Optional: offered but not required. These are almost always worth doing if available. An interview is a low-risk way to add a positive data point, and at colleges that track demonstrated interest (Chapter 2), declining one can read as a mild signal of lower interest.
  • Recommended or required: a few colleges strongly encourage or require interviews where they can arrange them. Schedule them early, as soon as you apply or as the college instructs.

Interviews rarely make or break an admission. Readers weigh them lightly compared with your academic record, essays, and recommendations. But in a close decision, an interviewer's report describing you as curious, warm, and engaged can help, and a report describing you as unprepared or uninterested can hurt.

Check each college's interview policy on its admissions website and record it in your tracker. Some colleges require you to request an interview by a certain date, often weeks before the application deadline. Others contact you after you apply.

docs.title: Worked Example: Sorting Interview Policies
docs.text:
Priya checks interview policies for her ten colleges:

  • Six colleges don't offer interviews, including her state flagship. Nothing to do.
  • Three colleges offer optional alumni interviews after you apply. She plans to accept any she's offered.
  • College A, her top reach, offers optional evaluative interviews with alumni, but applicants must request one by October 15 for the Regular Decision round.

Without checking, Priya would have missed College A's request deadline, which falls two months before its application deadline. She requests the interview on October 3 and adds it to her tracker.

docs.title: Kinds of Interviews
docs.text:
Interviews differ in two ways: who conducts them and what they're for. The table below previews the types covered in this section.

Type Who conducts it Main purpose Counts in your file? Admissions officer interview Admissions staff Evaluate you and answer questions Usually yes Alumni interview A graduate of the college Evaluate you, share their experience Usually yes, as one input Evaluative interview Officer or trained alum Assess you for admission Yes Informational interview Student, alum, or staff Help you learn about the college Little or not at all Virtual interview Any of the above, by video Same as in person Same as in person

docs.title: The Admissions Officer Interview
docs.text: An admissions officer interview is an interview conducted by a member of the college's admissions staff, on campus, at a regional event, or by video. Admissions officers often know their region's high schools and may be the same person who reads your file. Their interview notes usually go straight into your application. These interviews tend to be more structured, with questions about your academics, interests, and reasons for applying. Treat them as you would any conversation with someone who has a say in your admission: prepared, honest, and engaged.

docs.title: The Alumni Interview
docs.text: An alumni interview is an interview conducted by a graduate of the college who volunteers to meet applicants in their area, usually at a coffee shop, library, or by video. Selective colleges with many applicants often use alumni interviewers because there are far more applicants than admissions staff could meet. Alumni interviewers are trained by the college and write a short report afterward. That report is one input among many, and readers know alumni vary in style. Alumni interviews tend to be relaxed and conversational, and many interviewers enjoy talking about their own time at the college. Let them. It's a chance to learn something real about the place.

docs.title: The Evaluative Interview
docs.text: An evaluative interview is an interview whose report becomes part of your application and can influence the admission decision. Both admissions officer and alumni interviews are usually evaluative. The interviewer is forming an impression of you, often rating qualities like curiosity, maturity, and fit, and writing it down. That doesn't mean it's adversarial. It means you should prepare: know your application, know why you want this college, and be ready to talk about both naturally.

docs.title: The Informational Interview
docs.text: An informational interview is a conversation meant mainly to help you learn about the college, with little or no role in your evaluation. It may be with a current student, an alum, or staff, and it's often called an "information session" or "chat." Colleges sometimes describe their interviews this way to lower the pressure. Still, treat every interview as if it might count. A poor showing can leave a negative impression that finds its way back, and a strong one never hurts. Use informational interviews to ask the specific questions your school-specific research raised.

docs.title: The Virtual Interview
docs.text:
A virtual interview is an interview held by video call instead of in person. Many colleges now offer them, and they're treated the same as in-person interviews. The conversation is the same, but the logistics matter more:

  • Test your camera, microphone, and internet connection the day before, not the minute the call starts. Also test the specific platform, such as Zoom or Teams.
  • Choose a quiet, well-lit spot with a plain background. Light from in front of you, not behind.
  • Close other apps and silence notifications, including your phone.
  • Look at the camera when you speak, at least some of the time, so you appear to be making eye contact.
  • Join a few minutes early, and have the interviewer's contact information handy in case the connection fails.

docs.title: Worked Example: Fixing the Setup
docs.text: Marcus has a virtual alumni interview with Lakeshore University on a Thursday evening. On Wednesday, he does a test call with his cousin and discovers three problems. The restaurant's back office is noisy. The window behind him turns him into a silhouette. And his laptop's battery lasts only 40 minutes. He moves to his bedroom, turns his desk so the window is in front of him, and plugs in his charger. On Thursday, the call starts on time and runs 45 minutes without a problem. The test call took fifteen minutes and saved him from a stressful start.

docs.title: Interview Preparation
docs.text:
Interview preparation is getting ready to have a natural, engaged conversation about yourself and the college. You're not memorizing answers. Good preparation has four parts.

Know your own application. Reread your activities list, personal essay, and supplements for that college. Be ready to talk about any of it naturally, especially your intended major, your most important activities, and why you're interested in this college.

Research the college specifically. Use your notes from Chapter 10's school-specific research: a program, a class, a professor, a tradition, a student organization. You should be able to say, in your own words, what draws you to this college in particular.

Prepare for common questions. Most interviews include some version of these:

  • Tell me about yourself.
  • Why are you interested in this college?
  • What do you want to study, and why?
  • What do you do outside of class? Which activity matters most to you?
  • Tell me about a challenge you've faced, or a mistake you learned from.
  • What's something you've read, watched, or learned recently that interested you?
  • What would you contribute to our campus?
  • Do you have any questions for me?

For each, think of one or two specific stories or examples you could share. Specific stories make answers memorable, just as they do in essays. Don't write scripts. Rehearsed answers sound rehearsed.

Handle logistics. Confirm the date, time, time zone, and location or link. Plan what to wear: neat and comfortable, a step up from everyday school clothes, but not a suit. Plan to arrive ten minutes early. Bring nothing but yourself, perhaps a copy of your activities resume if the interviewer might want it, and a short list of your questions.

Interviewers are listening for a few things, which is why preparation focuses where it does:

  • Genuine curiosity and engagement. Do you talk about your interests with real energy?
  • Self-awareness. Can you reflect honestly on a challenge or a mistake, not just list accomplishments?
  • Fit. Does the way you talk about yourself suggest you'd contribute something to their community?
  • Conversational ease. Not polish, just the ability to have a normal two-way conversation, rather than a monologue or a string of one-word answers.

docs.title: Worked Example: From Script to Story
docs.text:
Ana's first attempt at answering "Why do you want to study education?" sounds like a speech: "I have always been passionate about helping others, and I believe education is the key to a better future." When she practices it aloud, it feels hollow.

She asks herself what actually made her want to teach, and answers with her essay's story in conversational form: "Honestly, it started with my little brother. When he was struggling to read, I sat with him every night for a couple of weeks, and the moment he finally got it, I wanted to feel that again. Now I tutor at my church, and I've noticed I'm good at seeing when someone's lost before they say so." That answer is specific, sounds like her, and invites a follow-up question, which is exactly what makes an interview a conversation.

docs.title: The Practice Interview
docs.text: A practice interview is a mock interview with a parent, teacher, counselor, or friend, done out loud, before the real one. The goal isn't to memorize answers. It's to get comfortable hearing yourself talk about your story before it matters, and to find which answers come out vague or rambling. Ask your practice partner to use the common questions from the previous section, plus one or two surprises. Afterward, ask them: Which answer was most interesting? Where did I ramble? Did I sound like myself? One or two practice sessions are plenty. More than that can make you sound rehearsed. The practice deck below gives you questions to try, with a timer.

docs.title: Diagram: Interview Practice Deck
docs.text:
Interview Practice Deck

Type: microsim sim-id: interview-practice-deck Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Purpose: Give students a low-pressure way to practice answering common interview questions aloud, with timing and a self-check that encourages specific stories over scripted answers.

Bloom Level: Apply (L3) Bloom Verb: practice, demonstrate Learning Objective: Students will practice answering common college interview questions aloud and demonstrate answers that use a specific example and stay within a natural length.

Canvas layout: - Top: a question card showing one interview question in large type, with its category tag (About you, Why us, Academics, Activities, Challenge, Curiosity, Your questions). - Middle: a circular timer that counts up from 0:00 when "Start answering" is pressed. The ring turns green from 0:30 to 2:00, yellow from 2:00 to 3:00, and orange after 3:00, with a note: "Most good answers run 30 seconds to 2 minutes." - Bottom: after "Stop," a short self-check with createCheckbox items: "I used a specific example or story," "I said why it matters to me," "It sounded like me, not a speech," "I could stop there or keep going if asked." A one-line tip appears for any unchecked item. - Side panel: a "Follow-up" button that reveals a likely follow-up question for the current card (e.g., after "Tell me about an activity": "What's been the hardest part of it?").

Question deck (24 cards, shuffled, filterable by category): the eight common questions from the chapter, plus prompts such as "What's a book or idea you've changed your mind about?", "Tell me about a time you disagreed with someone.", "What do you do when you're not doing schoolwork?", "What would your friends say surprises people about you?", "What will you look for in a roommate?", and "What questions do you have for me?"

Controls (all created in setup() before positioning): createButton "Next question," "Start answering," "Stop," "Follow-up"; createSelect category filter; createCheckbox items for the self-check; createCheckbox "Interviewer mode" that hides the self-check so a practice partner can read questions aloud.

Interaction: The deck never repeats a question until all cards in the filtered set have been shown. A tally shows how many questions have been practiced this session.

Responsive behavior: Call updateCanvasSize() first in setup(); the card, timer, and panel stack on narrow screens.

Implementation: p5.js with createButton, createSelect, and createCheckbox; canvas parented to the main element.

docs.title: Questions to Ask the Interviewer
docs.text: Questions to ask the interviewer are the questions you prepare for the end of the interview, when nearly every interviewer asks, "Do you have any questions for me?" Always have two or three ready. Having none can read as a lack of real interest. Good questions are ones you couldn't answer from the college's website. Questions about the interviewer's own experience are usually a safe, effective choice: What surprised you most about the college? What do you wish you'd known as a first-year? Where did you spend most of your time outside class? You can also ask a specific question from your research: I read about the peer-mentoring program in CS. How common is it for first-years to join? Avoid questions about admission odds, and avoid questions any brochure answers, such as "How big is the campus?"

docs.title: Interview Follow-Up
docs.text: Interview follow-up is the short, sincere thank-you you send your interviewer within a day or two after the interview, usually by email. Thank them for their time, mention one specific thing you enjoyed talking about, and, if it's true, say that the conversation increased your interest in the college. Keep it to three or four sentences. Don't use it to add new accomplishments or ask about your chances. If the interviewer gave you their email, use it. If not, ask the admissions office whether they can pass a note along, or send your thanks through the scheduling email. Then record the interview and follow-up in your tracker, and note anything you learned that might help you decide in the spring.

docs.title: Worked Example: Priya's Thank-You
docs.text:
After her College A interview, Priya emails her alumni interviewer that evening:

"Dear Ms. Patel, thank you for meeting with me today. I loved hearing about the late-night arguments in your first-year writing seminar. It made me even more excited about the seminar program. I'm grateful for your time and your advice about trying the student newspaper. Best, Priya Raman."

It's brief, specific, and genuine. It reminds the interviewer of their conversation and confirms Priya's interest, which is all a follow-up needs to do.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Interviews are conversations, not tests. They rarely decide an admission but can help in a close call. Check each college's policy and request deadline.
  • Admissions officer interviews and alumni interviews are usually evaluative interviews that go into your file. Informational interviews mainly help you learn. Treat every one as if it counts.
  • Virtual interviews count the same as in-person ones. Test your setup the day before.
  • Interview preparation means knowing your application, researching the college, and preparing specific stories for common questions, without scripts.
  • One or two practice interviews, done out loud, build comfort without making you sound rehearsed.
  • Prepare two or three questions to ask the interviewer that a website couldn't answer.
  • Send a short, specific interview follow-up within a day or two.

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
A college offers optional interviews and tracks demonstrated interest. Should you do one?

Yes, almost always. Optional interviews are low-risk chances to add a positive impression, and at colleges that track demonstrated interest, declining can read as lower interest.

What's the difference between an evaluative interview and an informational interview?

An evaluative interview produces a report that becomes part of your application. An informational interview is mainly for you to learn about the college. Still, treat both as if they count.

Rewrite this interview answer to be more specific: 'I like math because it's challenging and interesting.'

One possible answer: "Last spring I spent a whole weekend on one geometry proof our teacher said was optional. When it finally clicked, I wanted more problems like it." Any answer with a specific moment and a reason works.

Name two good questions to ask an alumni interviewer and one to avoid.

Good: "What surprised you most about the college?" or "What do you wish you'd known as a first-year?" Avoid: questions a website answers, or "What are my chances?"

What should an interview thank-you note include, and what shouldn't it?

Include thanks, one specific detail from the conversation, and genuine interest. Don't add new accomplishments or ask about admission chances. Keep it to a few sentences.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers how college pricing and aid work, from net price and the FAFSA and CSS Profile to demonstrated need, types of aid, need-blind admissions, grants, verification, and priority deadlines. It is the foundation for every money decision in the book. Students finish able to estimate a school's real cost and file the FAFSA and, where required, the CSS Profile on time.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
  • Chapter 2: How Colleges Evaluate Applicants
  • Chapter 3: Finding Your Fit
  • Chapter 5: Getting Organized
  • Chapter 12: Filling Out the Common App and Coalition App

docs.title: The Price Is Rarely the Price
docs.text:
Chapter 3 introduced an idea that changes how you look at every college: the sticker price a college publishes is rarely what a family actually pays. Most students receive some financial aid, and the gap between the published price and the real one can be tens of thousands of dollars a year. This chapter explains where that gap comes from.

It's the foundation for every money decision in the rest of the book. You'll start with what financial aid is and where it comes from: the federal government, your state, colleges themselves, and private sources. Then you'll learn the two forms that unlock most aid, the FAFSA and the CSS Profile, and the number they produce, the Student Aid Index, which determines your demonstrated financial need. From there you'll look at the two broad kinds of aid, need-based and merit, how colleges' aid policies differ, and the deadlines that decide how much you get.

Financial aid rules change often. Federal rules changed substantially in 2024 and again in 2026. The details here are current for the 2026–27 and 2027–28 aid years. Always confirm forms, amounts, and deadlines at studentaid.gov and on each college's financial aid website.

docs.title: Financial Aid
docs.text:
Financial aid is money that helps students pay for college, from any source: the federal government, state governments, colleges, and private organizations. It comes in four main forms:

  • Grants: money you don't repay, usually based on financial need.
  • Scholarships: money you don't repay, usually based on merit or specific criteria. Chapter 15 covers them.
  • Loans: money you borrow and must repay, usually with interest.
  • Work-study: a part-time job, usually on campus, whose earnings help pay expenses.

The first two are sometimes called gift aid because you don't pay them back. The last two are self-help aid, because you either repay them or earn them. That distinction matters enormously when you compare offers. A $20,000 aid package made entirely of grants is worth far more than a $20,000 package that's half loans. Chapter 16 shows how to tell them apart on an award letter.

Aid also comes from four sources, each with its own rules:

  1. Federal aid from the U.S. government, the largest source.
  2. State aid from your state government.
  3. Institutional aid from the colleges themselves.
  4. Private aid from employers, foundations, community groups, and other organizations.

Before the diagram below, here are two more terms you'll need. Need-based aid is awarded according to how much your family can afford, and merit aid is awarded for achievement, regardless of need. Both are covered in detail later in this chapter. The map shows how sources, forms, and the need-versus-merit distinction fit together.

docs.title: Diagram: Financial Aid Map
docs.text:

Visual style: A grid with four source columns (Federal, State, Institutional, Private) and four form rows (Grants, Scholarships, Loans, Work-study). Each cell contains small labeled chips for real examples, colored by basis: need-based chips in blue, merit-based chips in gold, chips that can be either in striped blue and gold, and non-need loans in gray. A legend at the bottom explains colors; a bracket on the left marks Grants and Scholarships as "Gift aid — don't repay" and Loans and Work-study as "Self-help aid."

Example chips (each clickable): - Federal × Grants: Pell Grant (need), Federal Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant (need). - Federal × Loans: Direct Subsidized Loan (need), Direct Unsubsidized Loan (not need-based), Parent PLUS Loan (not need-based). - Federal × Work-study: Federal Work-Study (need). - State × Grants: State need-based grant (need). - State × Scholarships: State merit scholarship (merit). - Institutional × Grants: College need-based grant (need). - Institutional × Scholarships: Automatic merit scholarship (merit), e.g., based on GPA and test scores. - Private × Scholarships: Local community scholarship (either), Employer scholarship (either). - Private × Loans: Private bank loan (not need-based; a last resort).

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading an Aid Package by Source
docs.text:
Priya receives this aid estimate from Hillcrest College, whose cost of attendance is $82,000:

  • Hillcrest Grant: $54,000 (institutional, need-based)
  • Hillcrest Merit Scholarship: $6,000 (institutional, merit)
  • Federal Work-Study: $2,500 (federal, need-based)
  • Federal Direct Subsidized Loan: $3,500 (federal, need-based)

Sorting by form, her gift aid is $60,000 and her self-help aid is $6,000. The price her family actually pays, before loans and work-study, is $82,000 − \(60,000 = **\)22,000**, the estimate her net price calculator gave her in Chapter 3. The loan and work-study help her cover that $22,000, but they're not discounts. She'll repay one and earn the other.

docs.title: Grants
docs.text:
Grants are financial aid that you don't have to repay, usually awarded based on financial need. They're the most valuable kind of aid, because every grant dollar directly lowers what your family pays. Grants come from all four sources: the federal government (such as the Pell Grant), states, colleges, and private organizations.

Most grants follow a few patterns:

  • They're usually need-based. The amount depends on your family's financial situation, as calculated from the FAFSA and sometimes the CSS Profile.
  • They usually renew, as long as you file aid forms each year, stay enrolled, make satisfactory academic progress, and your family's finances stay similar. If your family's income rises substantially, your grant may shrink.
  • They're applied directly to your bill. You never receive the money as cash, except for any amount left over after tuition, fees, and on-campus housing are covered.

Grants differ from scholarships mainly in their basis. Grants usually depend on need, and scholarships usually depend on merit or specific criteria. In practice, the terms overlap, and colleges sometimes call a need-based award a "scholarship." What matters most is whether you repay it. If you don't, it's gift aid, whatever it's called.

docs.title: Worked Example: Why Grants Matter Most
docs.text:
Marcus compares two aid offers from colleges with the same $36,000 cost of attendance:

  • College 1: $18,000 in grants and $5,500 in federal loans. Total aid: $23,500.
  • College 2: $10,000 in grants, $5,500 in federal loans, and $8,000 in other loans. Total aid: $23,500.

The totals are identical. But Marcus's family pays $36,000 − $18,000 = $18,000 at College 1, and $36,000 − $10,000 = $26,000 at College 2. College 2 simply lends him more of the difference. Over four years, College 1 costs $32,000 less in money he'll never get back. Looking at the grants, not the total, is what reveals the difference.

docs.title: The Pell Grant
docs.text:
The Pell Grant is the federal government's main need-based grant for undergraduates, awarded to students with the most financial need. You apply for it simply by filing the FAFSA. There's no separate application. For the 2026–27 aid year, the maximum Pell Grant is $7,395 per year for a full-time student, and the minimum award is $740.

The Pell Grant amount depends on your Student Aid Index (covered later), the cost of attendance, and whether you attend full-time. Students with the lowest Student Aid Index receive the maximum, and the award shrinks as the index rises. Since July 2026, students whose Student Aid Index is at least twice the maximum Pell Grant (about $14,790 for 2026–27) aren't eligible. Students whose grants and scholarships from other sources already cover the full cost of attendance also aren't eligible. Pell Grants are portable, meaning they follow you to any eligible college, and they're limited to about six years of full-time study over a lifetime.

Pell Grant eligibility often unlocks other aid too. Many states, colleges, and scholarship programs use it as a signal of need. If you might qualify, filing the FAFSA is essential.

docs.title: Worked Example: Ana and the Pell Grant
docs.text:
Ana's family income is modest. Her mother works part-time, her father works evenings, and they have three children. When Ana files the FAFSA, her Student Aid Index comes out to 0. That qualifies her for the maximum Pell Grant, $7,395 a year for a full-time student.

Over four years, that's about $29,580 in federal grant money she'll never repay, and it goes to whichever college she chooses. Her Pell eligibility also qualifies her for her state's need-based grant and for fee waivers on her applications, and two of her colleges flag it for their first-generation scholarship programs. One form unlocked all of it.

docs.title: Net Price
docs.text:
Net price is what a specific family actually pays for one year at a college: the cost of attendance minus all grants and scholarships. It's the number that matters most when you compare colleges, because it reflects the real cost to your family, not the published price.

\[ \text{Net price} = \text{Cost of attendance} - \text{Grants and scholarships} \]

Loans and work-study are not subtracted, because they're not discounts. Loans must be repaid, and work-study must be earned. They help you pay the net price, but they don't reduce it.

Net price varies enormously by family. Two students at the same college can face very different net prices, because need-based grants depend on each family's finances and merit scholarships depend on each student's record. That's why a college's average net price, as reported by the College Scorecard in Chapter 4, is a useful starting point but not your number.

docs.title: Worked Example: One College, Three Net Prices
docs.text:
Midland State, the fictional public university from Chapter 3, has an in-state cost of attendance of $28,700. Three in-state students receive different aid:

Student Grants and scholarships Net price Loans offered Ana (Pell-eligible) $7,395 Pell + $4,000 state grant + $9,000 Midland grant = $20,395 $8,305 $5,500 Marcus (moderate income) $3,000 state grant + $9,700 Midland grant = $12,700 $16,000 $5,500 A higher-income student $3,000 merit scholarship $25,700 $5,500

All three see the same sticker price. Their net prices range from about $8,300 to $25,700. All three are offered the same federal loan, which shows why loans aren't part of the net price. They're available regardless, and they don't make the college any cheaper.

docs.title: The Net Price Calculator
docs.text: A net price calculator is a tool on every college's website, required by federal law for colleges that offer federal aid, that estimates your net price at that college from your family's financial information. Chapter 3 urged you to use one for every college early in your search, before you get attached to a college you can't afford. Calculators vary in quality. Some ask only a few questions, while others ask nearly as much as the aid forms. Use the most detailed one available, with real numbers from your family's tax return, and treat the result as an estimate rather than a promise. The real number arrives in your award letter in spring.

docs.title: Federal Aid
docs.text:
Federal aid is financial aid from the U.S. Department of Education. It's the largest source of aid in the country and comes in three forms:

  • Grants: mainly the Pell Grant, plus the smaller Federal Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant (FSEOG) for students with exceptional need, which colleges award from limited funds.
  • Loans: Direct Subsidized Loans (for students with need, where the government pays the interest while you're in school), Direct Unsubsidized Loans (available regardless of need), and Parent PLUS Loans (borrowed by parents). Chapter 16 covers loans.
  • Work-study: Federal Work-Study, a part-time job program for students with need.

Federal aid has one gateway: the FAFSA. Every federal grant, loan, and work-study award requires it. Federal aid also has basic eligibility rules. You must generally be a U.S. citizen or eligible noncitizen, have a high school diploma or the equivalent, be enrolled in an eligible program, and make satisfactory academic progress once you're in college.

A common mistake is assuming federal aid is only for low-income families. Federal loans are available to nearly every student who files the FAFSA, regardless of income. Many colleges also require the FAFSA before they'll award their own aid, including some merit scholarships. And many state grants require it too. So the advice is simple: every student should file the FAFSA, even families who expect to qualify for nothing.

docs.title: Worked Example: Why a Higher-Income Family Should File
docs.text:
Casey's parents earn enough that they assume Casey won't qualify for aid, and they plan to skip the FAFSA. Casey's counselor points out three things:

  1. Without the FAFSA, Casey can't borrow even the basic federal student loan, which has lower interest rates and better repayment terms than private loans.
  2. Two of Casey's colleges require the FAFSA before awarding any institutional aid, including merit scholarships.
  3. If the family's situation changes, such as a job loss or a medical crisis, having a FAFSA on file lets the college reassess quickly.

The FAFSA is free and takes most families under an hour. Casey's parents file it in October.

docs.title: The FAFSA
docs.text:
The FAFSA, the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, is the form that determines your eligibility for federal aid, and it's used by most states and many colleges to award their own aid too. It's free. If any website charges you to file it, you're in the wrong place. The official site is studentaid.gov.

The FAFSA asks about your family's finances: income from tax returns, current savings and investments, and some assets. It uses prior-prior year tax information, meaning a student applying for aid in fall 2027 uses the family's 2025 tax return. That's why families can file in the fall, long before the year starts. The form draws tax information directly from the IRS once each contributor gives consent, which makes filing faster and more accurate.

Filing follows a clear sequence:

  1. Create StudentAid.gov accounts (FSA IDs) for the student and each contributor.
  2. Start the FAFSA for the correct aid year. Seniors applying for fall 2027 file the 2027–28 FAFSA.
  3. Invite contributors, such as parents, to complete their sections.
  4. Each contributor gives consent for IRS data to be transferred and completes their section.
  5. List your colleges using their federal school codes. You can list up to 20.
  6. Sign and submit. You'll receive a FAFSA Submission Summary showing your Student Aid Index.
  7. Watch for follow-up. Colleges may request more information or select you for verification.

You file a new FAFSA every year you're in college. The process gets faster after the first time.

docs.title: Worked Example: Ana's Family Files
docs.text:
Ana and her mother sit down together on a Saturday in October. Ana creates her StudentAid.gov account and starts the 2027–28 FAFSA, then invites her mother as a contributor. Her parents file taxes jointly, so only one parent account is needed. Her mother creates her own account, gives consent for the IRS data transfer, and completes the parent section. Most of the tax information fills in automatically.

Ana lists her eight colleges using their federal school codes from her tracker, signs, and submits. Two days later, her FAFSA Submission Summary arrives with a Student Aid Index of 0. The whole process took about ninety minutes, mostly creating accounts and answering household questions, and the free financial aid workshop her mother attended (Chapter 5) made the parent section easy.

docs.title: The FAFSA Opening Date
docs.text: The FAFSA opening date is the day each year's FAFSA becomes available. By law, it must open by October 1 for the following academic year. In recent years, it has opened in late September. The 2027–28 FAFSA opened on September 23, 2026. File as soon as you reasonably can after it opens, because some state and college aid is limited and awarded in order of filing. Opening dates shifted significantly during the FAFSA overhaul of 2024, so always check the current year's date on studentaid.gov.

docs.title: The FSA ID
docs.text: The FSA ID is the username and password for your StudentAid.gov account, which you use to sign the FAFSA electronically and to access your federal aid records. The student and each contributor need their own, created with their own email address and phone number. Create them a few weeks before you plan to file, since verifying a new account can take a day or more. Record yours in your login credentials record from Chapter 5. You'll keep using it through college and beyond, including to manage any federal student loans.

docs.title: FAFSA Contributors
docs.text: FAFSA contributors are the people whose information is required on your FAFSA: you, and, for most students, one or two parents. If your parents are married to each other, both are contributors. If your parents are divorced, separated, or never married and don't live together, the contributor is the parent who provided more financial support in the last 12 months, plus that parent's spouse if they've remarried. Each contributor creates their own StudentAid.gov account, completes their section, and gives consent for their tax information to be retrieved from the IRS. Without consent, you won't receive a Student Aid Index or federal aid. Students in unusual situations, such as those who can't contact their parents or are experiencing homelessness, may qualify to file without parent information. Talk to a college financial aid office for guidance.

docs.title: The Federal School Code
docs.text: The federal school code is the six-character code that identifies a college on the FAFSA, so your information is sent to the right college. Chapter 12's institution codes table listed Iowa's: 001892. Search for each college on the FAFSA itself, or find its code on its financial aid website, and add every college you've applied to or are still considering, up to 20. Adding a college to your FAFSA doesn't commit you to anything. It simply lets that college see your information and build an aid offer.

docs.title: The Student Aid Index
docs.text:
The Student Aid Index (SAI) is the number the FAFSA calculates from your family's financial information to measure your ability to pay for college. It replaced the older Expected Family Contribution starting with the 2024–25 aid year. The SAI ranges from −1,500 to very high numbers. A lower SAI means greater need, and an SAI of 0 or below indicates the highest need.

The most important thing to understand about the SAI is what it isn't. It isn't the amount your family will pay, and it isn't the amount of aid you'll receive. It's an index that colleges use to calculate your eligibility. Colleges and states use it in different ways. Some use it directly to calculate need. Others, especially colleges that use the CSS Profile, run their own formulas and may arrive at a different picture of your family's ability to pay.

The SAI depends mainly on your parents' income and assets, your own income and assets, and your family size. A few rules surprise families. The SAI no longer gives a break for having several children in college at once. And retirement accounts and the family's primary home aren't counted. You'll see your SAI on your FAFSA Submission Summary a few days after filing.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading the Number
docs.text:
Marcus's FAFSA Submission Summary shows an SAI of 9,500. His mother reads it as "we'll have to pay $9,500." That's not quite right. The SAI is an index, and what the family actually pays depends on each college's cost and how much aid it chooses to offer.

What the SAI does tell Marcus:

  • He's not eligible for a Pell Grant at most colleges, since his SAI is too high for meaningful Pell support even though it's below the new cutoff of about $14,790.
  • He'll likely show demonstrated need at colleges whose cost is well above 9,500, as the next section explains.
  • Colleges with generous institutional aid may offer grants that bring his net price close to what his family can afford, and colleges with limited aid may leave a gap.

docs.title: Demonstrated Financial Need
docs.text:
Demonstrated financial need is the difference between a college's cost of attendance and your Student Aid Index. It's the amount of help a college considers you to need:

\[ \text{Demonstrated need} = \text{Cost of attendance} - \text{Student Aid Index} \]

Because the cost of attendance varies by college while your SAI stays the same, your demonstrated need differs at every college. It's highest at the most expensive colleges. A family with an SAI of 9,500 has very little need at a college costing $12,000, but substantial need at one costing $80,000.

Demonstrated need is the starting point for need-based aid. Colleges try to fill it with a mix of grants, work-study, and loans. How much of it they fill, and with what mix, is where colleges differ most. Some fill all of it, mostly with grants. Others fill part of it and leave a gap. The interactive below lets you see how cost, SAI, and aid combine.

docs.title: Worked Example: Need at Three Colleges
docs.text:
Marcus's SAI is 9,500. His demonstrated need at three colleges:

College Cost of attendance − SAI = Demonstrated need Regional public university $24,000 9,500 $14,500 Midland State (in-state) $28,700 9,500 $19,200 Private college with strong aid $79,000 9,500 $69,500

The private college's need figure is the largest by far. Whether that turns into the lowest net price depends entirely on how much of the $69,500 the college actually meets with grants. In Chapter 3, its net price calculator estimated $19,000, which means it planned to meet nearly all of his need, mostly with grants.

Implementation: p5.js with createSlider, createCheckbox, and createButton; canvas parented to the main element.

docs.title: Unmet Need
docs.text: Unmet need is the part of your demonstrated need that a college's aid package doesn't cover. Colleges that don't fill all of your need are said to gap you. For example, if your need is $40,000 and the college offers $25,000 in aid, your unmet need is $15,000. Your family has to cover that on top of the SAI, from savings, income, outside scholarships, or extra loans such as Parent PLUS loans. Unmet need is one of the most important numbers on an award letter, and one of the least visible, since letters rarely state it. Chapter 16 shows how to calculate it.

docs.title: Meets Full Need
docs.text: A college that meets full need commits to covering 100% of every admitted student's demonstrated need, as the college calculates it, with a combination of grants, work-study, and sometimes loans. At these colleges, unmet need should be zero. Fewer than a hundred colleges make this promise, mostly highly selective private colleges and a few public universities for in-state students. Two cautions apply. First, "need" is defined by the college's own formula, often using the CSS Profile, which may expect more from your family than you'd expect. Second, colleges differ in how they meet it. Some use only grants, and others include loans. A college's Common Data Set, Section H, reports what share of need it actually met on average.

docs.title: The CSS Profile
docs.text: The CSS Profile is a detailed financial aid application run by the College Board that about 250 colleges, mostly private, require in addition to the FAFSA to award their own institutional aid. It asks for more information than the FAFSA, such as your family's home equity and, at many colleges, a noncustodial parent's finances, so colleges can award their own grants more precisely. The CSS Profile opens October 1 each year. It costs $25 for the first college and $16 for each additional college, and fee waivers are automatically granted to many lower- and middle-income families. Each college sets its own CSS Profile deadline, often earlier than you'd expect, especially for Early Decision and Early Action applicants. Hillcrest, for example, sets February 15 in Priya's tracker. Check every college on your list. Many, including Iowa, require only the FAFSA.

docs.title: State Aid
docs.text: State aid is financial aid from your state government, usually in the form of need-based grants and merit scholarships for state residents attending college within the state. Most states use the FAFSA to award it, and some have their own additional application. State aid can be substantial, and it often has early or first-come, first-served deadlines that are easy to miss. Some states' deadlines fall months before others'. Look up your state's higher education agency, or ask your counselor, for your state's programs and deadlines, and add them to your tracker. State aid usually applies only at colleges in your state, which is part of why in-state public universities, and some in-state private colleges, are often the most affordable options.

docs.title: Institutional Aid
docs.text:
Institutional aid is financial aid that colleges award from their own funds, including need-based grants, merit scholarships, and sometimes their own loans. For many students, it's the largest source of aid, especially at private colleges with large endowments. It's also the most variable. Two colleges with similar sticker prices can offer completely different amounts of institutional aid to the same student.

Colleges decide institutional aid using their own rules, which is why the same family can receive very different offers:

  • The data they use. Some use only the FAFSA. Others require the CSS Profile or their own forms.
  • Their need formula. Colleges using the CSS Profile may calculate a family's ability to pay differently than the SAI does.
  • Their budget and policy. Some meet full need, while others gap students. Some offer large merit awards, and others offer none.
  • Their goals. Institutional aid is also a tool for shaping the class (Chapter 2). A college may offer more to attract students it especially wants.

The best way to estimate a college's institutional aid before applying is its net price calculator. The second best is its Common Data Set, Section H, which reports the average need-based grant, the share of need met, and how many students receive merit aid without need.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Colleges, Same Family
docs.text:
Priya's family has an SAI of 31,000. Two private colleges, both with costs of attendance around $82,000, make offers:

  • Hillcrest College meets full need using the CSS Profile. Its formula sets her family's ability to pay at about $16,000, and it meets the remaining $66,000 of need with $54,000 in grants, a $6,000 merit scholarship, and $6,000 in work-study and loans. Net price: $22,000, of which work-study and a loan can cover $6,000.
  • College B doesn't meet full need. It offers a $28,000 grant. Net price: $54,000, with a large unmet need.

Both colleges saw the same family. The difference comes entirely from each college's institutional aid policy, which is why Priya ran both colleges' net price calculators before applying, and why she'll compare actual award letters in the spring.

docs.title: Need-Based Aid
docs.text:
Need-based aid is financial aid awarded according to your family's demonstrated financial need, as calculated from the FAFSA and, where required, the CSS Profile. It includes federal and state grants, institutional grants, federal work-study, and subsidized federal loans. The more need you demonstrate, the more need-based aid you're eligible for, though how much you actually receive depends on each college's policy and budget.

Need-based aid has two features worth planning around. First, it's recalculated every year. You file the FAFSA (and CSS Profile, if required) annually, and your aid can rise or fall as your family's finances change. Second, it responds to circumstances. If your family's situation changes significantly, such as a job loss, a death, divorce, or major medical expenses, you can ask the college to reconsider through a professional judgment review. Chapter 16 covers how. Many families who assume they won't qualify for need-based aid are surprised, especially at expensive colleges, where even middle- and upper-middle-income families can show need.

docs.title: Worked Example: Need-Based Aid Changes Over Time
docs.text:
Suppose Marcus enrolls at Lakeshore University. In his first year, his family's SAI is 9,500, and he receives an $18,000 need-based grant. In his second year, his father's restaurant has an unusually good year, and the family's SAI rises to 14,000. His grant falls to $14,000 for the year. In his third year, a slow economy lowers the restaurant's income, and his SAI drops to 7,000. His grant rises to $20,000.

Nothing about Marcus changed, but his need-based aid did, because it follows his family's finances. That's why he files his FAFSA every October, as soon as it opens.

docs.title: Merit Aid
docs.text:
Merit aid is financial aid awarded for achievement, such as grades, test scores, talents, or leadership, rather than financial need. Most merit aid comes from colleges themselves as institutional scholarships. Some is automatic, awarded at admission based on GPA and test scores, like Iowa's merit scholarships in the case study. Some requires a separate application or an invitation to compete. Some states also offer merit scholarships for residents.

Merit aid is most common at colleges trying to attract strong students. That means you're most likely to receive large merit awards at colleges where your record is near the top of the admitted class, often your target and safety schools (Chapter 3). The most selective colleges usually offer no merit aid at all. Every admitted student is strong, so they award aid only by need.

Two questions matter for every merit award: Is it renewable? And what do I need to keep it? Many merit scholarships require a minimum college GPA, often 3.0 or higher, and full-time enrollment. Losing one after your first year can raise your cost sharply.

docs.title: Worked Example: Merit Aid at a Safety
docs.text:
Casey's 3.40 GPA and 24 ACT place Casey near the top of the admitted class at a regional public university, which offers automatic merit scholarships by GPA and test score. Casey's admission letter includes a $4,000-per-year scholarship, renewable for four years with a 3.0 college GPA.

At Iowa, Casey's 24 ACT falls short of the score cutoff for its larger merit awards, as Chapter 6 noted (about 26 ACT or 1230 SAT). That's one reason Casey considered a retest. A two-point gain could have meant several thousand dollars a year at Iowa, while the regional university's award was already in hand. Merit aid rewarded Casey's record most at the college where Casey stood out most.

docs.title: How Colleges Use Financial Information in Admission
Need-Blind Admissions
docs.text: Need-blind admissions is a policy in which a college decides whether to admit you without considering whether you'll need financial aid. Your ability to pay plays no role in the admission decision. Most public universities and many private colleges are need-blind, at least for U.S. applicants. A smaller group of highly selective colleges are both need-blind and meet full need, which is the most generous combination available. Need-blind admission doesn't, by itself, mean a college will meet your need. A need-blind college can admit you and still leave you with unmet need. Check both policies separately.

docs.title: Need-Aware Admissions
docs.text: Need-aware admissions, sometimes called need-sensitive admissions, is a policy in which a college may consider an applicant's ability to pay when making some admission decisions, usually for the last portion of the class, when its aid budget is nearly spent. Many private colleges with limited aid budgets are need-aware. Applying for aid at a need-aware college can slightly lower your chances at the margin. But not applying for aid when you need it is far worse, because you'd be admitted without aid you can't do without. Colleges publish their policies. Search the financial aid website for "need-blind" or "need-aware." In most cases, apply for aid if you need it.

docs.title: Deadlines That Decide How Much You Get
Verification
docs.text: Verification is the process of confirming the information on your FAFSA. Your college's financial aid office asks you to submit documents such as tax transcripts, W-2 forms, or a verification worksheet. About a third of FAFSAs are selected each year, some at random and some because information seems inconsistent or estimated. Being selected doesn't mean anyone suspects you of anything. It's routine. But your aid isn't final until verification is complete, so respond quickly to any request, check your applicant portal and email often, and keep copies of what you send in your filing system's financial aid folder (Chapter 5). Delays in verification can delay your aid offer and, at colleges with limited funds, reduce it.

docs.title: The Aid Priority Deadline
docs.text: An aid priority deadline is the date by which you must file the FAFSA, and the CSS Profile if required, to receive full consideration for a college's or state's aid. Chapter 5 introduced priority deadlines in general. Aid priority deadlines are among the most important, and many fall before your application deadline. Iowa's priority deadline for the 2027–28 FAFSA, for example, is December 1, 2026, two months before its regular application deadline. Missing an aid priority deadline doesn't usually make you ineligible, but it can mean you're considered only for whatever aid remains. Record every college's and your state's aid deadlines in your tracker, and file the FAFSA as early as you can after it opens.

docs.title: First-Come, First-Served Aid
docs.text: First-come, first-served aid is financial aid that a college or state awards in the order applications arrive, until its funds run out. Many state grant programs and some colleges' own grants work this way. Iowa's financial aid office describes much of its aid as first-come, first-served from a limited pool. At these places, filing in October rather than February can mean thousands of dollars in grants that a later filer, with the same need, never sees. If any college or state on your list awards aid this way, filing early is one of the simplest ways to lower your cost.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Filers, Same Need
docs.text:
Two students with identical finances apply to the same public university, whose state grant program is first-come, first-served:

  • Student 1 files the FAFSA on October 3. She's awarded a $4,000 state grant and a $6,000 university grant.
  • Student 2 files on March 10, after the university's December 1 priority deadline. By then, the state grant fund has run out, and the university's remaining grant funds are small. She's offered a $1,500 university grant and larger loans.

Same need, same college, a difference of $8,500 a year in free money, determined entirely by when each student filed.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Financial aid comes from federal, state, institutional, and private sources, as grants, scholarships, loans, and work-study. Grants and scholarships don't need to be repaid. Loans and work-study do, or must be earned.
  • Net price is cost of attendance minus grants and scholarships, not loans. Estimate it with each college's net price calculator.
  • Federal aid requires the FAFSA, which every student should file. It opens by October 1, and recently in late September. Each FAFSA contributor needs an FSA ID and must give consent. Add each college with its federal school code.
  • The FAFSA produces your Student Aid Index, which isn't what you'll pay. Demonstrated financial need equals cost of attendance minus the SAI. Unmet need is the part a college doesn't cover. Colleges that meet full need cover it all.
  • The Pell Grant is the main federal need-based grant, up to $7,395 for 2026–27. State aid and institutional aid add more, and some colleges require the CSS Profile for their own aid.
  • Need-based aid follows your family's finances each year. Merit aid rewards achievement and is largest where you stand out. Check renewal rules.
  • Need-blind admissions ignores ability to pay. Need-aware admissions may consider it at the margin. Apply for aid if you need it.
  • Respond quickly to verification. File before every aid priority deadline, and file early anywhere aid is first-come, first-served.

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
A college's cost of attendance is $40,000. You receive $15,000 in grants, $3,000 in scholarships, $5,500 in loans, and $2,500 in work-study. What's your net price?

Net price = cost − grants and scholarships = \(40,000 − (\)15,000 + \(3,000) = **\)22,000**. Loans and work-study help you pay it but don't reduce it.

Your Student Aid Index is 12,000. What's your demonstrated need at a college costing $65,000? At one costing $11,000?

\(65,000 − 12,000 = **\)53,000 at the first. At the second, cost is below your SAI, so demonstrated need is $0**.

Your family's income is high, and you expect no need-based aid. Should you still file the FAFSA? Why?

Yes. It's required for federal student loans, many colleges require it for their own aid and some merit scholarships, and it lets a college respond quickly if your family's circumstances change.

What's the difference between a college that is need-blind and one that meets full need?

A need-blind college doesn't consider ability to pay when deciding admission. A college that meets full need covers 100% of your demonstrated need once admitted. A college can be one without the other.

Your state's grant program is first-come, first-served, and your top college's aid priority deadline is December 1. When should you file the FAFSA?

As soon as possible after it opens in the fall, well before December 1. Filing early gives you the best chance at limited state and college funds.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers finding automatic, competitive, outside, and local scholarships, deciding which are worth applying for, reusing essays, keeping renewable awards, and avoiding scams and award displacement. It extends the aid picture with money students apply for or earn automatically. After this chapter, students can build a focused scholarship list and spot a scam.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: How Colleges Evaluate Applicants
  • Chapter 10: Supplemental Essays
  • Chapter 14: Understanding Financial Aid

docs.title: Money You Find, Money That Finds You
docs.text:
Chapter 14 covered the aid that comes from filing forms: federal, state, and college aid based on your family's finances and your record. Scholarships add another layer. Some arrive automatically with your admission letter. Others you have to find, apply for, and win. Scholarship money is real, but finding it takes more than typing "scholarships" into a search engine, and some of what you'll find is designed to take your money rather than give it.

This chapter is about spending your scholarship time where it pays off. You'll start with what scholarships are and the main kinds: automatic merit awards, competitive scholarships, and outside scholarships, including the local ones students most often overlook. Then you'll learn how to judge eligibility, estimate whether an application is worth your time, prioritize a list, and reuse essays without falling into the recycled-essay trap. The chapter ends with three things that protect the money you win: renewal rules, scam warning signs, and award displacement.

docs.title: Scholarships
docs.text:
Scholarships are financial aid you don't have to repay, usually awarded for merit, talent, or specific qualifications rather than financial need alone. Like grants, they're gift aid, so every scholarship dollar lowers your net price (Chapter 14). Unlike most grants, many scholarships require you to do something to earn them, such as meeting a GPA standard, submitting an essay, or competing against other applicants.

Scholarships come from two broad places, and the difference shapes your strategy:

  • College scholarships come from the colleges themselves, as part of institutional aid. Many are automatic. Some require a separate application.
  • Outside scholarships come from anyone else: businesses, community groups, foundations, religious organizations, professional associations, employers, and national programs.

The table below previews the kinds of scholarships covered in this chapter. Each gets its own short section after it.

Kind Who awards it How you get it Competition Automatic merit A college Admission plus meeting its criteria None beyond admission Competitive A college or outside group A separate application, often with essays Moderate to very high Outside Businesses, foundations, organizations A separate application Varies widely Local Community groups near you A separate application, often through your school Usually low

docs.title: Worked Example: Where Priya's Scholarship Money Comes From
docs.text:
By April, Priya has scholarship offers from three sources:

  • Hillcrest College: a $6,000-per-year merit scholarship, awarded automatically with her admission (Chapter 14).
  • Her state flagship: a $3,000-per-year honors college scholarship, awarded after a separate application and a short essay.
  • Her town's Rotary Club: a $1,500 one-time scholarship, for which she competed with about 20 students from her county.

The Hillcrest award came with no extra effort. The flagship award took one essay. The Rotary scholarship took an application, an essay, and an interview. All three lower what her family pays, but they took very different amounts of work. Matching effort to likely payoff is what this chapter is about.

docs.title: Automatic Merit Scholarships
docs.text: Automatic merit scholarships are awards a college gives to admitted students who meet published criteria, usually GPA and test scores, with no separate application. You're considered simply by applying, and the award typically appears in your admission letter or aid offer. Many public universities and private colleges use them to attract strong students. Iowa's merit scholarships, described in the case study, are an example. Check each college's scholarship page for its criteria and deadlines. Some automatic awards require you to apply by an early deadline, such as Early Action, or to submit test scores. At test-optional colleges, an automatic award with a score cutoff is one of the strongest reasons to submit a score (Chapter 6).

docs.title: Competitive Scholarships
docs.text: Competitive scholarships are awards you must apply for, usually with essays, recommendations, interviews, or a portfolio, and that are judged against other applicants. They include colleges' named scholarships and honors awards as well as many outside scholarships. Some are small and local. Others, such as large national programs, attract tens of thousands of applicants for a handful of awards. Competitive scholarships reward the same strengths admissions does, which are specific essays, strong recommendations, and depth in activities, so your application materials are a head start. Because they take real time, the expected-value thinking later in this chapter matters most for them.

docs.title: Outside Scholarships
docs.text:
Outside scholarships, also called private scholarships, are scholarships from organizations other than your college or the government: businesses, foundations, civic and religious groups, professional associations, employers, and national programs. They usually follow you to whichever college you attend, though some are restricted to certain colleges, states, or majors.

Outside scholarships vary enormously. Some are worth $500, others $10,000 or more. Some take a short form, others multiple essays. Some are renewable, many are one-time awards. Where to look, roughly in order of payoff for your time:

  1. Your high school counseling office, which often keeps a list of local and regional scholarships.
  2. Your parents' or your own employers. Many companies offer scholarships for employees' children. Ask the human resources office.
  3. Community and identity-based organizations, such as Rotary, Kiwanis, and Lions clubs, religious organizations, cultural associations, and nonprofits serving first-generation and other students.
  4. Professional associations in your intended field, such as nursing, engineering, or education.
  5. National scholarship search engines, useful for volume but heavily competitive.

Outside scholarships also have a catch that surprises many families: winning one can reduce the aid your college offers, through award displacement. That's covered at the end of this chapter. The money is still worth winning, but you need to know how your college will treat it.

docs.title: Worked Example: Ana's Outside Scholarship List
docs.text:
Ana's counselor gives her a list of 30 local and regional scholarships. Ana also finds six more through her mother's employer, her church, and a nonprofit for first-generation students. She adds them to a scholarship tab in her tracker with the amount, deadline, requirements, and eligibility for each.

When she checks eligibility, 14 of the 36 don't fit. Some require a major she isn't planning, residence in another county, or a parent in a specific union. That leaves 22, still far too many to apply for well. The rest of this chapter shows how she narrows them.

docs.title: Local Scholarships
docs.text: Local scholarships are scholarships offered by organizations in your own community, such as civic clubs, local businesses, credit unions, churches, school foundations, and community foundations, usually for students from a specific town, county, or high school. They're often the best-kept secret in scholarship searching. They're rarely listed on national search engines, so far fewer students apply, sometimes only a handful. A $1,000 local award with 15 applicants can be a much better use of your time than a $10,000 national award with 20,000 applicants. Your school counselor, your local community foundation's website, and local newspapers and organizations are the best places to find them. Many have spring deadlines, so check in January.

docs.title: Scholarship Search Engines
docs.text: Scholarship search engines are free websites, such as the College Board's BigFuture scholarship search, Scholarships.com, and Fastweb, that match you to scholarships based on a profile you fill out. They're useful for finding national and regional awards you'd never hear about otherwise. Use them with three cautions. First, they're crowded. Large national awards on these sites attract enormous applicant pools. Second, profiles can generate marketing. Use your dedicated email (Chapter 5), and read privacy settings before sharing details. Third, never pay for a search. The best search tools are free, and any service charging to "find" scholarships for you is a warning sign, as you'll see in the scams section.

docs.title: Scholarship Eligibility
docs.text: Scholarship eligibility is the set of requirements you must meet to be considered for a scholarship: GPA, test scores, financial need, intended major, residence, school, background or identity, activities, or affiliation with an organization. Read the full eligibility rules before you start an application, not after. Many students waste hours on scholarships they can't win because of a requirement buried on page two, such as a county residence rule or a minimum GPA. Eligibility also determines your odds. The narrower the eligibility, the fewer the applicants. A scholarship for "first-generation students from Johnson County planning to study education" may have only a few eligible applicants, and Ana is one of them.

docs.title: The Expected Value of Applying
docs.text:
The expected value of applying is a way of estimating whether a scholarship is worth your time by combining its amount, your chance of winning, and the hours it takes. The idea is simple: a likely $1,000 can be worth more than an unlikely $10,000. To compare scholarships, estimate the expected dollars per hour of work:

\[ \text{Expected value per hour} = \frac{\text{Award amount} \times \text{Chance of winning}}{\text{Hours to apply}} \]

Your chance of winning is an estimate. For local awards, divide the number of awards by the likely number of applicants. Your counselor may know how many students applied last year. For national awards, assume the odds are low, often well under 1%, unless you're exceptionally well matched. The numbers don't need to be precise. Even rough estimates reveal which applications deserve your evenings.

docs.title: Worked Example: Comparing Three Scholarships
docs.text:
Marcus estimates the expected value of three scholarships:

Scholarship Amount Estimated chance Hours Expected value per hour National tech scholarship $10,000 0.5% (1 in 200) 8 \(10,000 × 0.005 ÷ 8 ≈ **\)6** County community foundation $2,000 10% (3 awards, ~30 applicants) 4 \(2,000 × 0.10 ÷ 4 = **\)50** Local restaurant association $1,000 25% (1 award, ~4 applicants) 2 \(1,000 × 0.25 ÷ 2 ≈ **\)125**

The national scholarship sounds the most exciting, but per hour, it's the weakest use of his time. The local restaurant association award, which he's eligible for through his family's business, is worth about twenty times as much per hour. Marcus applies for all three, but he writes the local applications first and gives them his best effort, and he spends no more than his eight planned hours on the national one. The calculator below lets you compare your own list.
