docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small interactive simulations, each focused on one idea from the book. Every chapter embeds its sims, and each one also has its own lesson page with a fullscreen link and teaching notes.

Every sim below is marked built (orange dot): implemented and awaiting the author's review.

docs.title: Chapter 1: The College Landscape and Application Rounds
docs.text:
• College Admissions Process Roadmap: An interactive road map of the six stages of the college admissions process, with a drag-and-drop quiz on their order.
  • Senior Year Admissions Timeline: An interactive timeline of one senior year in admissions, with a personal track that changes as you choose Regular Decision, Early Action, or Early Decision.
  • College Type Sorter: A drag-and-drop sorting activity: classify twelve real colleges as public or private and as a research university or liberal arts college, then decide which public research universities are flagships.
  • Admission Rate Calculator: Calculate a college's admission rate from its applications and admits, and see why a surge in applications lowers the rate even when admits stay the same.
  • The Journey of an Application File: A swimlane flowchart that walks an application through an admissions office, showing who touches the file at each of seven steps.
  • Application Round Explorer: Answer five questions about one college and one student, and the explorer recommends an application round, explains why, and shows its deadline, decision, and commitment dates.

docs.title: Chapter 2: How Colleges Evaluate Applicants
docs.text:
• Annotated Transcript Explorer: Explore a fictional high school transcript region by region and learn what each part tells an admissions reader.
  • GPA Calculator: Calculate an unweighted GPA from your own courses and see how credits, single grades, and a college's core-only recalculation change the result.
  • Rigor in Context: See why course rigor is judged against what your high school offers: compare the share of available advanced courses taken, not the raw count.
  • Holistic Review Rating Explorer: Compare applicant files with similar grades and see how a first reader's separate Academic, Activities, and Personal ratings respond to each part of the file, and to context.
  • Regent Admission Index Calculator: Run the University of Iowa's Regent Admission Index formula and see how GPA, ACT score, core courses, and residency decide whether you clear the admission threshold.
  • Middle 50% Range Plotter: Plot your GPA and ACT score against a college's middle 50% range and see whether you fall below, inside, or above it.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Finding Your Fit
docs.text:
• College Self-Assessment Builder: A five-step self-assessment of majors, size, setting, culture, and cost that turns your answers into a ranked priority profile with dealbreakers.
  • Campus Size and Setting Explorer: Compare typical campus experiences across twelve combinations of school size and setting, highlight your target zone, and pin the colleges on your list.
  • Cost of Attendance Builder: Build a college's cost of attendance from tuition, room and board, and indirect costs, and compare how residency and housing choices change the total.
  • Reach, Target, Safety Classifier: Classify a college as a reach, target, or safety for you from your GPA and test score, its admission rate and middle 50% ranges, and its financial fit.
  • Balanced College List Builder: Build a college list of eight to twelve schools across reach, target, and safety, and check live whether it is balanced and includes an affordable safety you'd be glad to attend.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Researching and Narrowing Your College List
docs.text:
• Research Tool Matrix: A matrix showing which college research tools best answer which questions, from admission chances and cost to campus culture.
  • College Outcomes Comparison: Compare retention, four-year, and six-year graduation rates for up to four colleges, and see which gaps are a reason to ask questions.
  • List Narrowing Funnel: Run Marcus's 18-college long list through three narrowing passes (fit, balance, and picturing yourself there) and watch each cut get logged with its reason.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Getting Organized
docs.text:
• College Requirements Matrix: Compare application requirements across every college on your list, spot the one-of-a-kind requirements before they're missed, and total the workload.
  • Getting Organized Setup Checklist: An interactive checklist of the five first steps and the core setup tasks for getting organized, with a progress ring and a note on why each task matters.

docs.title: Chapter 6: The SAT and ACT Question
docs.text:
• SAT-ACT Score Converter: Convert between SAT totals and ACT composites with the official concordance, and place the converted score in a college's middle 50% range.
  • Score Submission Planner: Compare your SAT or ACT score with every college on your list and get a college-by-college recommendation on whether to submit it, with the reason shown.
  • Superscore Calculator: Calculate an SAT or ACT superscore from several test dates and compare it with your best single-sitting score.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Your Senior Year Course Load
docs.text:
• Advanced Course Pathways Compared: Compare Advanced Placement, the International Baccalaureate, and dual enrollment on sign-up, commitment, assessment, college credit, and fit, and find the pathway that matches your situation.
  • When Colleges See Senior Grades: A timeline of when colleges receive senior-year course and grade information, and how that timing differs for early, regular, and deferred applicants.
  • Senior Schedule Balance Planner: Build a draft senior schedule and weekly commitments, then compare the rigor signal it sends with the weekly hours it demands, to find a sustainable plan.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Activities and Resume
docs.text:
• Depth vs. Breadth Activity Map: Plot activities by years of involvement and weekly hours to see the difference between a deep activity profile and a broad one, then plot your own.
  • Activity Entry Builder: Draft a Common App-style activity entry within the real character limits and get instant feedback on action verbs, specifics, and hours.
  • What Counts as an Activity?: Decide whether fourteen everyday commitments, from jobs and family duties to hobbies, belong on your activities list, and see which activity type each would go under.

docs.title: Chapter 9: The Personal Essay
docs.text:
• Essay Topic and Prompt Matcher: Test a candidate essay topic against the qualities of a strong personal story, and see which Common App prompts it fits.
  • Show-Don't-Tell Practice: Practice telling a general claim apart from a specific showing sentence, then write and check your own showing revision.
  • Personal Essay Structure Explorer: See how the parts of a personal essay work together under three common structures, and plan your own essay with a 650-word budget.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Supplemental Essays
docs.text:
• Why Us Specificity Checker: Test a Why Us essay draft for specificity: highlight generic phrases and specific details, and run the swap test with another college's name.
  • Supplement Planner: Enter every supplemental essay prompt on your list, group them by type to see where one core essay can be adapted, and schedule the writing backward from deadlines.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Letters of Recommendation
docs.text: • Recommender Comparison Tool: Compare possible teacher recommenders on how well they know you, how recently they taught you, subject, and reliability, and see which two would write the strongest, most complementary letters.

docs.title: Chapter 12: Filling Out the Common App and Coalition App
docs.text: • Pre-Submission Checklist: A college-by-college review of your Common App application before you press Submit, so common errors are caught first.

docs.title: Chapter 13: Interviews
docs.text: • Interview Practice Deck: Practice answering 24 common college interview questions out loud, with a timer, likely follow-ups, and a quick self-check.

docs.title: Chapter 14: Understanding Financial Aid
docs.text:
• Financial Aid Map: An explorable map of where financial aid comes from (federal, state, institutional, private), the forms it takes, and which kinds are need-based or merit-based.
  • Need and Aid Calculator: See how cost of attendance, the Student Aid Index, and a college's aid package combine into demonstrated need, net price, and unmet need.

docs.title: Chapter 15: Scholarships
docs.text:
• Scholarship Priority Calculator: Rank scholarships by expected dollars per hour of work, see how renewability and reusing an essay change the ranking, and fit the best ones into the hours you have.
  • Scholarship or Scam?: Practice spotting scholarship scams by deciding whether twelve realistic offers look legitimate or like a scam, and naming the sign that decides it.

docs.title: Chapter 16: Comparing Award Letters
docs.text:
• Award Letter Decoder: Translate any financial aid award letter into standard numbers: sort each line into free, earned, or borrowed money, then see the real net price and out-of-pocket cost.
  • Award Letter Comparison Chart: Compare up to four financial aid offers side by side on first-year net price, out-of-pocket cost, projected four-year cost, and debt.

docs.title: Chapter 17: Waiting and Managing Anxiety
docs.text: • What Can I Control?: Sort common waiting-period worries into what you can act on and what's out of your hands, and turn each controllable worry into a small next step.

docs.title: Chapter 18: Handling Decisions
docs.text: • Decision Response Guide: An interactive guide to the next steps and deadlines for every kind of admission decision: acceptances, Early Decision outcomes, deferrals, waitlists, denials, and offers for a different program or term.

docs.title: Chapter 19: Making Your Final Choice
docs.text: • Final Choice Comparison Matrix: Compare two to four finalist colleges with a weighted decision matrix of cost, fit, outcomes, distance, and gut sense, and see which factors drive the result.

docs.title: Chapter 20: Getting Ready for Fall
docs.text:
• Summer-to-Move-In Countdown: Organize every task between committing to a college and move-in day on a timeline, check them off, and watch for the summer-melt risks that keep admitted students from arriving.
  • Personal Application Roadmap: Build a complete, college-specific application roadmap with 19 stops, from list-building to fall move-in.

docs.title: Other tools
docs.text: • Learning Graph Viewer: explore all 342 concepts in the book and how they depend on each other.

docs.title: Activity Entry Builder
docs.text: Run the Activity Entry Builder MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Let students draft a Common App-style activity entry within the real character limits and get feedback on action verbs, specifics, and measurable impact.

Learning objective: Students will compose an activity entry within the Common App's character limits and revise its description to lead with an action verb and include specific, measurable detail.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 8: Activities and Resume.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Fill in the activity type, grades, timing, hours, position, organization, and description. Counters show the Common App limits (50, 100, and 150 characters) and turn orange near the limit and red over it.
  • Watch the Reader's view card update. Text beyond 150 characters appears struck through in red.
  • Read the Feedback panel: an action verb first, a number, no "I" or filler, no repeated position, and realistic hours, plus total hours per year.
  • Load a preset to compare the chapter's entries. Sam — tutoring before and after show a weak draft and its revision. Copy entry text copies your entry.

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text:
You can add this MicroSim to any web page by adding this to your HTML:

<iframe src="https://bakullberg.github.io/College-Admissions-ebook/sims/activity-entry-builder/main.html"
        height="692px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will compose an activity entry within the Common App's character limits and revise its description to lead with an action verb and include specific, measurable detail.

Bloom level: Create (L6) — compose, revise

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school juniors and seniors, and the parents, counselors, and mentors helping them.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15–20 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 8 that introduces this MicroSim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Before and after (4 min): Load Sam's two drafts and list every check the revision fixes.
  2. Revise Sam yourself (5 min): From the before draft, write your own revision before loading the after version. Compare.
  3. Your best activity (8 min): Write the entry for your strongest activity until every check passes.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
• Why does the first word of a description matter so much?
  • What kinds of numbers can make an activity concrete?
  • What should you cut first when a description runs over 150 characters?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Students write an entry that passes every check, stays within all character limits, and shows an action, a specific detail, and a result.

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Chapter 8: Activities and Resume — the chapter this MicroSim supports.

docs.title: Admission Rate Calculator

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Let students compute admission rates and see why the number of applications, not just the number of admits, drives selectivity.

Learning objective: Students will calculate a college's admission rate from its applicant and admit counts and explain how a change in applications changes the rate even when the number of admitted students stays the same.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 1: The College Landscape and Application Rounds.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Move Applications received and Students admitted. The formula updates with your numbers, and the icon grid fills one icon per percentage point.
  • Read the selectivity band and the "About 1 in N" line under the percentage.
  • Press College A (40,000 / 6,000) or College B (9,000 / 6,300) to load the chapter's worked examples.
  • Press Application surge (+25%) to raise applications while holding admits constant, and read the caption.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will calculate a college's admission rate from its applicant and admit counts and explain how a change in applications changes the rate even when the number of admitted students stays the same.

Bloom level: Apply (L3) — calculate

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school juniors and seniors, and the parents, counselors, and mentors helping them.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 1 that introduces this MicroSim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Check the worked examples (3 min): Load College A and College B and confirm their rates (15% and 70%) by hand.
  2. Predict, then test (4 min): Before pressing Application surge twice, predict the new rate. Then press it and compare.
  3. Look up a real school (3 min): Find one college's applicants and admits on its website or the Common Data Set and enter them.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
• Why can a college's admission rate fall even when it admits the same number of students?
  • Does a 15% admission rate mean you personally have a 15% chance? Why not?
  • What band is a college with 25,000 applicants and 5,000 admits in?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Students compute an admission rate correctly from two counts, place it in the right selectivity band, and explain the effect of an application surge in their own words.

docs.text:
Students will classify a four-year college as public or private and as a research university or liberal arts college, and explain the clue in its description that decides each label.

Bloom level: Understand (L2) — classify

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school juniors and seniors, and the parents, counselors, and mentors helping them.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10–15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 1 that introduces this MicroSim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Sort the deck (6 min): Place all twelve cards. Aim for at least ten on the first try.
  2. Explain one surprise (3 min): Pick Dartmouth College or St. Mary's College of Maryland and explain in one sentence why its name doesn't decide its category.
  3. Your list (5 min): Add three schools you are considering. Check each one's website to answer the three questions accurately.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
• Why is every flagship a public research university, but not every public research university a flagship?
  • Which clue in a profile tells you a school is public?
  • Why might a public liberal arts college be rare?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Students sort at least ten of twelve cards correctly on the first try and can name the deciding clue for any card.

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Chapter 1: The College Landscape and Application Rounds — the chapter this MicroSim supports.

docs.title: Cost of Attendance Builder
docs.text: Run the Cost of Attendance Builder MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Show students how a college's cost of attendance is built from tuition, room and board, and indirect costs, and how residency and housing choices change the total.

Learning objective: Students will break down a cost of attendance into direct and indirect costs and compare how residency and housing choices change the total.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 3: Finding Your Fit.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Choose Residency and Housing to fill in Midland State's figures for that scenario.
  • Edit any of the five items to enter a different college's published numbers.
  • Choose a Compare against scenario to draw a second bar, and read the dollar difference below the chart.
  • Hover over any segment to see its amount, whether the college bills it, and what it covers. Reset to Midland State restores the chapter example.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will break down a cost of attendance into direct and indirect costs and compare how residency and housing choices change the total.

Bloom level: Analyze (L4) — break down, compare

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school juniors and seniors, and the parents, counselors, and mentors helping them.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10–15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 3 that introduces this MicroSim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read the example (3 min): Confirm that tuition is about 40% of Midland State's in-state total. What makes up the other 60%?
  2. One change at a time (4 min): Compare in-state on campus with in-state living with family. Which items change, and by how much?
  3. A real college (6 min): Find one college's published cost of attendance and enter all five items.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
• Why would a student who looks only at tuition underestimate the real cost?
  • Which costs on the chart can you control, and which can't you?
  • Why do indirect costs still matter even though the college doesn't bill them?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Students break a published cost of attendance into direct and indirect costs and explain how one residency or housing change affects the total.

docs.text: 1. Chapter 3: Finding Your Fit — the chapter this MicroSim supports.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Give students a single interactive guide to the next steps for every kind of admission decision, including Early Decision cases, so no response or deadline is missed.

Learning objective: Students will select the decision they received and carry out the correct next steps, including deadlines, for acceptances, denials, deferrals, waitlists, and Early Decision outcomes.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 18: Handling Decisions.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Click a decision to open its chain of steps, or click any step to read it. Gold steps are deadlines.
  • Use ◀ Back and Next step ▶ to walk the chain, and check Mark this step done as you finish each one. Done steps turn green.
  • Under I have multiple decisions, choose up to three decisions to see their chains side by side, with every deadline collected in one list.
  • On narrow screens, the guide opens one decision at a time.

docs.text:
Students will select the decision they received and carry out the correct next steps, including deadlines, for acceptances, denials, deferrals, waitlists, and Early Decision outcomes.

Bloom level: Apply (L3) — execute, respond

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school juniors and seniors, and the parents, counselors, and mentors helping them.

docs.text: 10 minutes, then as decisions arrive

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 18 that introduces this MicroSim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Walk one chain (3 min): Open Waitlist and read every step. Why should you deposit elsewhere by May 1 even if you hope to come off the waitlist?
  2. ED outcomes (3 min): Compare the Early Decision acceptance chain with the Deferral chain. When are you released from the binding commitment?
  3. Your decisions (4 min): As decisions arrive, choose them in the multiple-decision dropdowns and mark steps done.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
• What should you do first when an Early Decision offer isn't affordable?
  • Why is depositing at two colleges a problem?
  • How can you keep a denial in perspective?

docs.text: Students list the correct next steps and deadline for three different decisions without the guide.

docs.title: Depth vs. Breadth Activity Map
docs.text: Run the Depth vs. Breadth Activity Map MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Let students see the difference between a deep activity profile and a broad one by plotting each activity's years of involvement against its weekly hours, then plot their own activities.

Learning objective: Students will compare activity profiles by years of involvement and weekly hours, and distinguish a profile that shows depth from one that shows breadth alone.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 8: Activities and Resume.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Each bubble is one activity: farther right = more years, higher = more hours per week, bigger = more hours per year. Gold = a leadership or growing role.
  • Use Show Applicant A, Show Applicant B, or Show both to compare the chapter's two profiles.
  • Add up to ten of your own activities with the form. They appear as blue outlines. Click one of your bubbles to edit it, or Clear mine to start over.
  • Read the summary lines for how many activities fall in the shaded depth zone (3+ years and 5+ hours a week).

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will compare activity profiles by years of involvement and weekly hours, and distinguish a profile that shows depth from one that shows breadth alone.

Bloom level: Analyze (L4) — compare, distinguish

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school juniors and seniors, and the parents, counselors, and mentors helping them.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10–15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 8 that introduces this MicroSim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Compare profiles (4 min): Applicant A lists ten activities and Applicant B four. Which shows more total time? Which shows more depth?
  2. Plot yourself (6 min): Add your own activities with honest hours. How many land in the depth zone?
  3. Plan senior year (3 min): Pick one activity you could move toward the depth zone or into a growing role this year.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
• Why can four activities tell a reader more than ten?
  • Does an activity have to be in the depth zone to be worth listing?
  • What counts as a 'growing role' if you don't have a title?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Students distinguish a deep profile from a broad one using years, hours, and role, and identify one of their own activities with the most depth.

docs.title: Essay Topic and Prompt Matcher
docs.text: Run the Essay Topic and Prompt Matcher MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Help students test an essay topic against the qualities of a strong personal story and see which Common App prompts it fits, reinforcing that the story comes before the prompt.

Learning objective: Students will assess a candidate essay topic against criteria for a strong personal story and select the Common App prompts it fits.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 9: The Personal Essay.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Type your topic in a few words, then answer the five questions about it.
  • The prompt cards light up green for a strong fit and yellow for a possible fit. Prompt 7 always works.
  • The Story strength meter scores how specific the story is, whether it reveals something new, and whether you know what it means. The tip line suggests a next step, including advice for common topics.
  • Try the presets: Ana — reading with my brother, The big game, and Translating at the doctor. Hover over a prompt card for its summary, and read the exact wording on the Common App site.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will assess a candidate essay topic against criteria for a strong personal story and select the Common App prompts it fits.

Bloom level: Evaluate (L5) — assess, select

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school juniors and seniors, and the parents, counselors, and mentors helping them.

docs.text: 10–15 minutes

docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 9 that introduces this MicroSim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Ana's story (3 min): Load Ana's preset. Why does her story fit three prompts?
  2. Rescue the big game (4 min): Load The big game. Change only the specificity and meaning answers to reach Strong. What would the essay have to be about?
  3. Your topics (6 min): Test two or three of your own candidate topics. Which one scores Strong?

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
• Why should you choose the story before the prompt?
  • What makes a common topic work anyway?
  • Why does a single moment often make a stronger essay than a long summary?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Students evaluate two candidate topics and justify choosing one using specificity, what it reveals, and its meaning.

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Chapter 9: The Personal Essay — the chapter this MicroSim supports.

docs.title: Personal Essay Structure Explorer
docs.text: Run the Personal Essay Structure Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Show how the parts of a personal essay work together under three common structures, and let students plan their own essay with a word budget that totals 650.

Learning objective: Students will plan a personal essay by choosing a structure and organizing its parts within a 650-word budget.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 9: The Personal Essay.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Choose a Structure: Narrative arc, Montage, or Idea-driven. The bar splits 650 words among that structure's parts.
  • Click any part of the bar to read its job and a sample excerpt. Hover to see its word count and share.
  • Drag the sliders to plan your own word budget. The total turns orange over 650 and gray under 500.
  • Try the presets: Ana's outline, Too much story, and All reflection.

docs.text:
Students will plan a personal essay by choosing a structure and organizing its parts within a 650-word budget.

docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 9 that introduces this MicroSim.

1. Ana's plan (3 min): Click each part of Ana's outline and read the excerpt. Where does the reflection start?

  • When would a montage serve a story better than a narrative arc?

docs.title: Final Choice Comparison Matrix
docs.text: Run the Final Choice Comparison Matrix MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Help students compare two to four finalist colleges with a weighted decision matrix that combines cost, fit, and outcomes, and see which factors drive the result.

Learning objective: Students will weigh their finalist colleges on cost, academic fit, social fit, outcomes, and personal sense using weights that reflect their own priorities, and justify a final choice by identifying the factors that most influence it.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 19: Making Your Final Choice.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Type your finalists' names, set a weight (0–5) for each factor, and score each college 1–5.
  • Enter four-year net prices to score cost automatically (lowest price = 5), or check Override cost scores to score cost yourself.
  • Each college's bar is split by factor; the leader is outlined in gold. What's driving this? names the two factors with the biggest weighted difference between the top two.
  • Use Add factor for your own criteria and Add college or Remove college for up to four finalists. Load the Priya or Marcus preset to see the chapter's examples. Hover over a bar segment for weight × score.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will weigh their finalist colleges on cost, academic fit, social fit, outcomes, and personal sense using weights that reflect their own priorities, and justify a final choice by identifying the factors that most influence it.

Bloom level: Evaluate (L5) — weigh, justify

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school juniors and seniors, and the parents, counselors, and mentors helping them.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 19 that introduces this MicroSim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Priya's matrix (4 min): Load Priya's preset and confirm 95 vs. 86. Which factors favor the flagship?
  2. Change the weights (4 min): Raise Cost to 5 and lower Gut sense to 2. Does the leader change? What does that tell you?
  3. Your finalists (7 min): Enter your own finalists and weights, then compare the total with your gut.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
• Why isn't the highest total automatically the right choice?
  • What does it mean when your gut disagrees with the total?
  • Which factor would you never trade away?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Students build a matrix for their finalists and justify their choice by naming the factors that drive the result.

docs.title: Financial Aid Map
docs.text: Run the Financial Aid Map MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Give students a single, explorable picture of where financial aid comes from, what forms it takes, and which kinds depend on need versus merit.

Learning objective: Students will classify types of financial aid by source (federal, state, institutional, private), form (grant, scholarship, loan, work-study), and basis (need or merit), and explain which kinds must be repaid.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 14: Understanding Financial Aid.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Each chip is a real kind of aid. Its column is the source and its row is the form. Blue = need-based, gold = merit, blue-and-gold = either, gray = not based on need.
  • Grants and scholarships are gift aid (never repaid). Loans and work-study are self-help aid.
  • Click any chip to read what it is and what unlocks it. Hover over a source header for a one-line description.
  • Use the filter buttons to show only gift aid, only need-based aid, or only what the FAFSA unlocks.

        height="622px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will classify types of financial aid by source (federal, state, institutional, private), form (grant, scholarship, loan, work-study), and basis (need or merit), and explain which kinds must be repaid.

Bloom level: Understand (L2) — classify, explain

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school juniors and seniors, and the parents, counselors, and mentors helping them.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 14 that introduces this MicroSim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. The FAFSA's reach (3 min): Press Show only what the FAFSA unlocks. How much of the map does one form open?
  2. Gift vs. self-help (3 min): Press Show only gift aid. Which sources give gift aid in more than one form?
  3. Your plan (4 min): List the chips you could realistically receive and what you must file to get each one.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
• Why is a dollar of grant aid worth more than a dollar of loan aid?
  • Which aid can you get only by filling out a separate application?
  • Why should a family file the FAFSA even if they don't expect need-based aid?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Students classify six aid examples by source, form, and basis, and correctly say which must be repaid.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Chapter 14: Understanding Financial Aid — the chapter this MicroSim supports.
  2. Federal Student Aid — the official FAFSA and federal aid site.

docs.title: GPA Calculator
docs.text: Run the GPA Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Let students calculate an unweighted GPA from their own courses and see how credits, individual grades, and core-only recalculation change the result.

Learning objective: Students will calculate an unweighted GPA from a list of courses and demonstrate how a college's core-only recalculation can produce a different number.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 2: How Colleges Evaluate Applicants.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Each row is one course: type its name, pick a grade and credit value, and check the box if it is a core academic course.
  • Both readouts update immediately: the GPA for all courses and the core-only GPA many colleges recalculate.
  • What moved it? names the course whose last change shifted the GPA, and by how much.
  • Use Add course and Remove last for up to eight rows, Load Priya's year to restore the chapter example (3.64 and 3.60), and Show the math to see the sums.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will calculate an unweighted GPA from a list of courses and demonstrate how a college's core-only recalculation can produce a different number.

Bloom level: Apply (L3) — calculate, demonstrate

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school juniors and seniors, and the parents, counselors, and mentors helping them.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10–15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 2 that introduces this MicroSim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Check the example (3 min): With Priya's year loaded, confirm 20.0 ÷ 5.5 = 3.64 and 18.0 ÷ 5.0 = 3.60 using Show the math.
  2. Credit weight (4 min): Change Health from A to C, then change AP Chemistry from B to C. Which change moves the GPA more, and why?
  3. Your own year (6 min): Enter your own courses from last year and compare your all-courses and core-only GPAs.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
• Why does a half-credit course move the GPA less than a full-credit one?
  • Why might a college's core-only GPA differ from the one on your transcript?
  • When could dropping electives raise a GPA, and when could it lower it?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Students calculate an unweighted GPA by hand for a new set of courses, match the calculator's result, and explain why the core-only GPA differs.

docs.title: Holistic Review Rating Explorer
docs.text: Run the Holistic Review Rating Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Show how holistic review produces separate ratings for different parts of an application, and how context changes those ratings, so students see why identical numbers can lead to different outcomes.

Learning objective: Students will compare applicant files with similar academic numbers and attribute differences in reader ratings to specific parts of each file.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 2: How Colleges Evaluate Applicants.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Choose Applicant A, Applicant B, or Dana, then click the folder tabs to read each part of the file.
  • Change Activities depth, Essay specificity, or Recommendation detail one at a time. The rating that changes flashes gold.
  • Uncheck Reader has the school profile to see why context matters for a small-school applicant like Dana.
  • Hover over any rating box to see what that level means. The model is simplified, and the three ratings are never added together.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will compare applicant files with similar academic numbers and attribute differences in reader ratings to specific parts of each file.

Bloom level: Analyze (L4) — compare, attribute

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school juniors and seniors, and the parents, counselors, and mentors helping them.

docs.text: 15 minutes

docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 2 that introduces this MicroSim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Same numbers, different files (5 min): Compare Applicants A and B tab by tab. Which ratings differ, and which parts of the file cause the difference?
  2. One change at a time (5 min): Starting from Applicant A, change only the essay, then only the recommendations. Which single change helps most?
  3. Context (5 min): Load Dana and uncheck the school profile. Explain in one sentence why the Academic rating changes.

docs.title: Discussion Questions

  • Which parts of an application can you still change in senior year?
  • What does the school profile tell a reader that the transcript can't?

docs.text: Run the Interview Practice Deck MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Give students a low-pressure way to practice answering common interview questions aloud, with timing and a self-check that encourages specific stories over scripted answers.

Learning objective: Students will practice answering common college interview questions aloud and demonstrate answers that use a specific example and stay within a natural length.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 13: Interviews.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the question, press Start answering, and answer out loud. The ring turns green between 30 seconds and 2 minutes, yellow until 3 minutes, then orange.
  • Press Stop, then check the self-check items that are true. A tip appears for anything unchecked.
  • Press Follow-up to see a question an interviewer might ask next, and Next question for a new card. The deck won't repeat until every card in the category has been shown.
  • Filter by category, or check Interviewer mode to hide the self-check so a practice partner can read the questions to you.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will practice answering common college interview questions aloud and demonstrate answers that use a specific example and stay within a natural length.

Bloom level: Apply (L3) — practice, demonstrate

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school juniors and seniors, and the parents, counselors, and mentors helping them.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15–20 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 13 that introduces this MicroSim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Warm up (5 min): Answer "Tell me about yourself" twice. Aim for under two minutes with one specific story.
  2. Partner practice (10 min): In Interviewer mode, a partner reads five questions and the follow-ups; switch roles.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will plan their supplemental essays by organizing prompts by type, identifying where core material can be adapted, and scheduling each piece before its deadline.

Bloom level: Create (L6) — plan, organize

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school juniors and seniors, and the parents, counselors, and mentors helping them.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15–20 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 10 that introduces this MicroSim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read Priya's plan (4 min): Load Priya's list. How many essays does she write fresh, and how many does she adapt?
  2. Find the crunch (4 min): Switch to Calendar view. Which week is orange, and what would you move earlier?
  3. Your plan (10 min): Clear the board and enter every supplement on your own list.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
• Why can a community essay be adapted but a Why Us essay can't?
  • How does seeing every prompt in August change your fall?
  • Which pieces would you write first, and why?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Students produce a plan in which no week has more than three pieces and every core essay is scheduled before its adaptations.

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Chapter 10: Supplemental Essays — the chapter this MicroSim supports.

docs.title: What Can I Control?
docs.text: Run the What Can I Control? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Help students practice separating worries they can act on from worries they can't during the waiting period, and turn each controllable worry into a small next step.

Learning objective: Students will classify common waiting-period worries as within or outside their control and plan one concrete action for each controllable worry.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 17: Waiting and Managing Anxiety.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the worry, then choose I can do something about this or Out of my hands.
  • Read the feedback. For worries you can act on, edit the suggested next step and press Save step.
  • My plan collects every step you save and counts the worries you let go. It's kept in this browser when storage is available.
  • Press Next ▶ for the next worry, or Start over to clear your plan and reshuffle.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will classify common waiting-period worries as within or outside their control and plan one concrete action for each controllable worry.

Bloom level: Apply (L3) — classify, plan

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school juniors and seniors, and the parents, counselors, and mentors helping them.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 17 that introduces this MicroSim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Sort the deck (6 min): Work through all fourteen worries and save at least three steps.
  2. Schedule it (2 min): Put each saved step into your calendar with a day and time.
  3. Let go (2 min): Pick one worry from the Out of my hands pile and write what you'll do instead when it comes up.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
• Why does checking the portal ten times a day make waiting harder?
  • Which of your worries has a next step you could take this week?
  • Who can you talk to when the waiting feels heavy?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Students sort the deck and produce a plan with at least three concrete, scheduled next steps.

docs.title: References
docs.text: 1. Chapter 17: Waiting and Managing Anxiety — the chapter this MicroSim supports.

docs.title: What Counts as an Activity?
docs.text: Run the What Counts as an Activity? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Challenge the assumption that only school-sponsored activities count, by having students classify real-life examples and see which activity type each would be listed under.

Learning objective: Students will classify everyday commitments as listable activities or not and explain which activity type each belongs to and why.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 8: Activities and Resume.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the scenario card and press List it or Probably not.
  • Read the feedback: the recommended answer, the Common App activity type, and the reason.
  • Gray-area cards show It depends, with what would make them count. They aren't scored.
  • Press Next ▶ for the next card and Restart to shuffle the deck. The tally collects the activity types you've discovered.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will classify everyday commitments as listable activities or not and explain which activity type each belongs to and why.

Bloom level: Understand (L2) — classify, explain

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school juniors and seniors, and the parents, counselors, and mentors helping them.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 8 that introduces this MicroSim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Play the deck (6 min): Work through all fourteen cards.
  2. Gray areas (2 min): For the video games card, describe a version that would clearly count.
  3. Your hidden activities (2 min): List one commitment of your own that you hadn't thought of as an activity.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
• Why do family responsibilities count as activities?
  • What makes a paid summer program weaker than a part-time job on an application?
  • When does a hobby become an activity?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Students correctly classify at least nine of the eleven clear-cut cards and explain one gray-area card's condition.

docs.title: Why Us Specificity Checker
docs.text: Run the Why Us Specificity Checker MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Help students test a Why Us draft for specificity by running the swap test and highlighting generic phrases, so they can see where research and personal connection are missing.

Learning objective: Students will critique a Why Us essay draft by applying the swap test and assessing whether each sentence names a specific college detail and connects it to the writer.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 10: Supplemental Essays.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Enter the college's name and a different college's name, then paste your draft.
  • Press Check. Orange sentences contain generic phrases, green sentences contain a likely specific detail, and a blue underline marks a detail connected to you.
  • Press Swap test to see your draft with the other college's name. If it still makes sense, it isn't specific enough.
  • Load Priya — first draft and Priya — revision to compare the chapter's example. The checker uses simple patterns and can't judge quality.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will critique a Why Us essay draft by applying the swap test and assessing whether each sentence names a specific college detail and connects it to the writer.

Bloom level: Evaluate (L5) — critique, assess

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: High school juniors and seniors, and the parents, counselors, and mentors helping them.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10–15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read the section of Chapter 10 that introduces this MicroSim.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Priya's two drafts (4 min): Check both drafts. Which details in the revision would be impossible to write about another college?
  2. Swap your own (5 min): Paste one of your Why Us drafts and run the swap test.
  3. Add two details (6 min): For each orange sentence, replace the generic phrase with a specific course, program, place, or person, and say why it matters to you.

docs.title: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
• What makes a detail specific to one college?
  • Why isn't a specific detail enough on its own without a connection to you?
  • Where can you find details that most applicants won't mention?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Students revise a Why Us draft until it fails the swap test and every specific detail connects to them.

docs.title: References
